sections.heading: Why this matters
sections.markdown:
Debugging Solidity is a longstanding pain point, and the root cause is structural. The compiler (solc) does not emit the rich debug information debuggers need: variable types, scopes, and runtime locations. Without a standard for that data, every debugging tool reverse-engineers compiler behavior, which breaks whenever the compiler changes.

The 2025 Solidity Developer Survey (925 responses) re-confirmed this. The three most requested improvements, step-through debugging, variable and state inspection, and transaction replay, map directly to what a standard debug format enables. The need is sharpest in production, where deployed contracts are immutable and the cost of not understanding behavior is highest.

This RFP funds implementing the [ethdebug format](https://ethdebug.github.io/format/) directly in solc. The end state:
* solc emits standardized debug data covering storage variables, local variables, memory, calldata, and per-instruction context
* That data survives the full compilation pipeline, including all optimizer passes, so it works on production builds
* Debuggers, frameworks, monitoring tools, explorers, and agents can read one shared standard instead of reconstructing compiler internals

sections.heading: The team
sections.markdown:
This RFP is a co-sponsorship opportunity brought by **Argot Collective** and **Walnut**. The ethdebug format is developed by Argot engineer Nicholas D'Andrea. The solc implementation is done by Walnut. We expect them to do this work.

This is not a competitive tender in the usual sense. The project is already in progress with the first three milestones funded and underway, so there is no open challenge window. A challenger just doesn’t make sense in this case.

Argot Collective is the anchor backer. A public goods nonprofit, Argot has committed up to $151,000 of the $279,000 project budget. This RFP raises the remaining $127,000: $85,500 to finish the project and additional $43,000 to ensure ecosystem adoption by every user of the solc compiler.

* The implementation is underway at Walnut, with the first three milestones below funded by Argot.

* The full six-milestone implementation of ethdebug in solc, from test infrastructure through the optimized production pipeline

sections.markdown:
* Building end-user debugger UIs. This funds the compiler-level data, not the tools that read it. Walnut is building soldb, the first ETHDebug consumer - a CLI-based debugger and tracer for Solidity.
* The ethdebug format specification itself, which Argot maintains separately.
* Ongoing maintenance beyond the grant period, beyond the maintenance plan required below.

sections.heading: Commitments
sections.markdown:
1. **Open source.** All work merged under solc's existing license, no closed-source dependencies.
2. **Upstream, not a fork.** Deliverables land in the official solc repository, or are open pull requests under active review by the Solidity team. A private fork does not count.
3. **Machine-checkable acceptance.** Debug data output is validated by an automated test suite in public CI against the ethdebug format schemas.
4. **Production coverage proven.** Final acceptance requires debug data demonstrated correct on optimized builds.
5. **Maintenance plan.** A documented plan for keeping ethdebug output current as solc and the optimizer evolve.

sections.heading: Why this matters
sections.markdown:
With the rise of AI-generated contracts, a growing number of non-developers and beginners are creating and deploying smart contracts. This expands the attack surface, as these users often do not know which security checklists apply to their code or how to fix flagged vulnerabilities. Historically, over $8 billion in user funds has been lost specifically to smart contract execution flaws, according to an empirical study in Science Direct.

Integrating a consistently maintained and tagged Cyfrin Security Checklist directly into RemixAI solves this. Users get automated, contract-specific filters (such as ERC-20, NFT, or staking), actionable AI-guided fixes, and automated Foundry invariant tests that validate checklist findings with counterexample execution traces.

sections.heading: Why this matters
sections.markdown:
The problem is larger than DeFi protocol losses alone. Argus covers the Ethereum ecosystem: DeFi on Ethereum, Ethereum layer 2s, and the base-layer clients that run the network.

As of 13 November 2026, Ethereum DeFi has about $39.4 billion locked (https://defillama.com/chain/ethereum). Ethereum layer 2s secure about $35.1 billion (https://l2beat.com/scaling/tvs). Those figures move day to day; they show the scale of funds that sit on live contracts, on layer 2s, and behind the clients that process them.

Losses span more than one layer. Immunefi's 2026 Ecosystem Vulnerability Scoreboard puts DeFi protocol losses at $680 million in 2025, and says 89% of those losses came from protocol logic exploits (https://immunefi.com/blog/research/the-ecosystem-vulnerability-scoreboard-6-years-of-defi-loss-data/). One of those incidents, the Balancer V2 composable stable pools exploit, lost $128 million across Ethereum and several layer 2s. That same report keeps centralized exchange failures separate: exchanges absorbed over $1.6 billion in infrastructure-class losses in 2025, led by the $1.5 billion Bybit compromise. Chainalysis counted over $3.4 billion stolen across the industry from January through early December 2025 (https://www.chainalysis.com/blog/crypto-hacking-stolen-funds-2026/). DeFi protocol losses are only one slice of that picture.

The Glamsterdam gas changes (Ethereum Improvement Proposal 8037 and 8038) showed the same gap at the base layer. ChainSecurity and the Ethereum Foundation found deployed contracts that rely on gas invariants the upgrade would break (https://blog.ethereum.org/2026/11/06/glamsterdam-8037-8038).

After this work, users of Ethereum DeFi, layer 2s, and the base layer are safer because confirmed bugs in live systems have been reported to the teams that run them. Anyone can point to a report, and to acknowledgment or other proof that outside teams accepted those issues, plus a public fix when possible.

sections.heading: Why this matters
sections.markdown:
Ethereum security teams face high volumes of fragmented threat information across incidents, malicious-domain lists, attacker infrastructure, private reporting channels, on-chain observations, and external research publications. As blockchain security has matured, attackers have increasingly targeted operational infrastructure, developers, credentials, and software supply chains alongside smart contracts, creating a growing need for intelligence that connects these threats to practical defensive actions. These sources differ in structure, reliability, and sharing restrictions. Teams must spend significant analyst time reconciling them before determining whether a threat affects their systems and what defensive action to take.

SEAL already has visibility into incidents and malicious campaigns across the Ethereum ecosystem. This initiative will make that intelligence easier to use through validated records with supporting evidence, relevant alerts delivered to affected teams, and recommendations that specify concrete defensive actions. Participating organizations will be able to integrate intelligence into their existing security tooling and contribute observations through controlled information-sharing channels.

sections.heading: Why a grant: what already exists
sections.markdown:
SEAL Intel builds on an established operational threat intelligence program rather than creating a new intelligence organization from scratch. SEAL already receives threat information through incident response, ecosystem reporting channels, security research, and trusted relationships with blockchain organizations. The grant will fund the incremental engineering, automation, intelligence processing, and integrations needed to turn those existing capabilities into a more scalable intelligence service.

**Existing foundation and grant-funded additions**

| Existing SEAL capability | Additional work funded by this grant |
|---|---|
| Incident and intelligence intake through SEAL reporting channels | Connect selected intake workflows to a shared intelligence pipeline, preserving source provenance and sharing permissions |
| Existing analyst research and threat intelligence workflows | Automate selected collection, normalization, deduplication, enrichment, and correlation tasks |
| Existing OpenCTI-related intelligence capabilities | Build and document additional integrations, Ethereum-specific data conventions, and production workflows |
| Public security research, intelligence reports, and malicious-domain contributions | Produce consistent, evidence-linked records, actionable recommendations, and machine-readable distribution |
| Established relationships with ecosystem organizations | Support integrations and independently verified operational adoption of the new intelligence feeds |

**Existing operational capabilities and track record**

- **Ecosystem intelligence network:** SEAL maintains more than 100 communication channels and hotlines connecting DeFi protocols, centralized exchanges, infrastructure providers, and other blockchain organizations. These relationships provide direct visibility into incidents and emerging threats.

- **24/7 incident and intelligence intake:** SEAL operates `@seal_911_bot` and `@seal_tips_bot`, supporting incident reporting, intelligence submissions, initial response coordination, and information sharing.

- **Phishing detection and blocklisting:** SEAL reports identifying approximately 5,000–10,000 malicious frontends weekly and contributes intelligence to ecosystem phishing blocklists. Its integration with MetaMask's eth-phishing-detect helps malicious frontends become blocked rapidly after identification.

- **Malware and threat actor research:** SEAL investigates DPRK-linked threat actors, malware-as-a-service operations, social engineering campaigns, malicious infrastructure, and software supply-chain compromises. Research outputs include indicators of compromise, attacker tactics and techniques, campaign analysis, and coordinated defensive actions.

- **Public intelligence and research:** SEAL publishes threat research, incident analysis, and operational statistics through SEAL Radar and maintains public research repositories and datasets.

- **Existing intelligence infrastructure:** SEAL already conducts structured intelligence research and maintains OpenCTI-related capabilities for organizing and analyzing threat information.

These capabilities give SEAL a significant operational advantage: direct incident visibility, researchers who understand both traditional cybersecurity and Ethereum-specific threats, and established relationships with organizations positioned to act on intelligence.

**Why grant funding is needed**

While SEAL already collects and analyzes intelligence, many processes still require manual collection, reconciliation, enrichment, and distribution. This grant will connect existing workflows, automate repeatable processing tasks, improve intelligence quality and consistency, and provide integrations that enable security teams to consume and act on intelligence more efficiently.

**Public evidence and references**

- SEAL Radar: https://radar.securityalliance.org/
- SEAL GitHub: https://github.com/security-alliance
- Lazarus Group research: https://lazarus.group/
- Public Lazarus intelligence dataset: https://github.com/security-alliance/lazarus-group-data
- Binance incident research: https://radar.securityalliance.org/tradertraitor-vs-contagious-interview-a-look-at-binances-initial-incident-report/
- DPRK malware research: https://radar.securityalliance.org/vs-code-tasks-abuse-by-contagious-interview-dprk/

sections.heading: In scope
sections.markdown:
SEAL Intel will expand its existing threat intelligence operations into an automated, analyst-validated service for Ethereum and its Layer 2 ecosystem. The grant funds new integrations, intelligence processing, distribution tools, and partner adoption—not the creation of a new intelligence team.

**1. Collection and normalization**

Build connectors for curated public and permissioned sources, including security research, malicious-domain feeds, incident reports, on-chain observations, and trusted reporting channels. Preserve source provenance, confidence, and sharing restrictions. Extract and deduplicate information from structured and unstructured reports, normalize it using STIX 2.1 with Ethereum-specific indicators (wallet addresses, contracts, transaction hashes, malicious dApp domains), and classify threats by category and affected participant type.

**2. Processing, correlation, and analyst review**

Automate enrichment and correlation against existing SEAL intelligence and incident observations, subject to permissions. Analysts review records before release for correctness (validity, source reliability, false positives), enrichment (supporting evidence and links to infrastructure, incidents, malware, and campaigns), and relevance (affected organizations, urgency, defensive actions). Outputs are evidence-linked, analyst-approved intelligence records. SEAL's differentiator is combining automation with direct incident visibility and researchers experienced in Ethereum threats; the technology reduces repetitive work so analysts can provide actionable guidance rather than raw indicator lists.

**3. Alerts, recommendations, and feeds**

Deliver flash alerts for active threats; tailored defensive recommendations for protocols, exchanges, wallets, and infrastructure providers; periodic campaign and threat reports; and authenticated TAXII 2.1 and REST feeds for integration into existing security tooling. Provide filtering by threat category, participant type, and authorized sharing level, plus API documentation and onboarding guidance.

**4. ISAC collaboration**

Connect selected existing SEAL reporting and ISAC workflows to enable two-way intelligence exchange. Approved participants can submit observations, receive relevant alerts, request context, and coordinate on shared threats. Apply contributor permissions, optional redaction or anonymization, and TLP 2.0 restrictions. Provide contributor feedback where confidentiality permits. This strengthens existing coordination rather than building a new messaging or incident-response platform.

**5. Security and quality**

Implement vetted access, role-based permissions, provenance, TLP-aware distribution, audit logs, and correction or withdrawal procedures for stale or inaccurate intelligence. Protect restricted sources and review automated outputs for false positives and malicious submissions.

**6. Pilot and verification**

Integrate independent Ethereum ecosystem organizations, gather operational feedback, and measure source coverage, extraction quality, analyst effort, alert delivery speed, feed/API usage, contributions, and documented defensive actions. An independent reviewer verifies the quantitative acceptance criteria specified separately in the milestones.

**Use of funds:** The proposed six-month $267,000 budget covers engineering ($108,000), intelligence analysis ($54,000), partner integration ($60,000), delivery management ($15,000), infrastructure ($18,000), and independent review ($12,000), subject to confirmation. Existing SEAL capabilities and previously funded work are excluded from duplicate reimbursement.

sections.heading: Out of scope
sections.markdown:
The initiative does not include:

- Guaranteed prevention of all exploits, phishing campaigns, or security incidents.
- Replacement of participating organizations' existing security operations or incident-response teams.
- Unlimited custom threat investigations, security assessments, or consulting services for individual organizations.
- Automated changes to participant systems, including credential rotation, patching, or blocking.
- Development of an entirely new endpoint security, blockchain monitoring, messaging, or incident-response platform.
- Expansion into unrelated blockchain ecosystems beyond the agreed Ethereum and Layer 2 scope.
- Redistribution of restricted or confidential intelligence without authorization.
- Private donor services or features not expressly included in the approved grant scope and milestones.

The grant expands SEAL's existing intelligence capabilities and coordination workflows. It does not replace SEAL 911 or create a separate incident-response organization.

sections.heading: Commitments
sections.markdown:
SEAL will deliver the agreed grant-funded capabilities and provide independently verifiable evidence against the approved milestones. Evidence will include documented source integrations, intelligence-processing workflows, analyst review procedures, distribution mechanisms, and operational adoption by independent Ethereum ecosystem organizations.

**Long-term sustainability:** SEAL intends to maintain the capabilities developed through this initiative as part of its existing intelligence operations after the six-month grant period. Sustainability will be supported through continued ecosystem funding and a proposed enhanced Intel/ISAC donor offering, currently envisioned at $50,000 annually per participating organization. The proposed offering would provide participating organizations with access to SEAL Intel services, including invitation-only private intelligence briefings, quarterly threat intelligence reports, and relevant intelligence feeds and alerts. This model is prospective and does not represent committed revenue.

**Public-good outputs and access:** Grant-funded public-good deliverables will be distinguished from additional donor-supported services. Intelligence involving sensitive incidents, private sources, or confidential reporting will remain subject to contributor permissions, confidentiality requirements, and applicable TLP restrictions.

**Licensing:** SEAL will specify the licenses and publication commitments applicable to grant-funded software, documentation, schemas, and other deliverables in the final grant agreement. Restricted intelligence and confidential source material will not be publicly released where doing so would violate applicable permissions.

**Maintenance:** Named maintainers, the minimum post-grant support period, and the operating budget required to sustain the funded capabilities will be confirmed before the grant agreement is finalized.

**Measurement and accountability:** The initiative will be evaluated against agreed quantitative milestones covering source integration, normalization, automated extraction accuracy, analyst productivity, alert delivery, intelligence distribution, and independent partner adoption. Public evidence will be provided where appropriate, with sensitive information redacted or made available to the independent reviewer through approved access arrangements.

Any exceptions concerning source-code publication, restricted intelligence, or other standard grant requirements will be expressly disclosed and agreed before implementation.

sections.heading: Why this matters
sections.markdown:
Some of the largest losses in Ethereum's history happened at its bridges: honeypots of locked funds guarded by small signer sets that rely on reputation rather than contract logic or validity proofs, prioritizing UX over security. Ronin, Poly Network, BNB Bridge, Wormhole, and Nomad all sit near the top of the [Rekt leaderboard](https://rekt.news/leaderboard/), and each broke the layer that decides which cross-chain messages are valid. 

EEZ turns cross-chain execution into an Ethereum primitive. A contract on one rollup calls a contract on another rollup, or on L1, and uses the return value in the same transaction, with the result checked on Ethereum. That takes the bridge out of these flows:

- Moving assets between rollups no longer needs a third-party contract holding pooled assets, so there is no bridge pool for an attacker to drain.
- Atomic multi-chain actions, such as a swap funded from another rollup, complete fully or revert together, within one L1 block, provided a builder includes the bundle.
- A smaller attack surface. Today a protocol copies itself onto every network it reaches, and duplication breeds bugs: version drift, per-chain initialization mistakes, maintenance across every copy. The Balancer v2 exploit drained the same code chain by chain. With EEZ a protocol deploys once, where it is easiest to audit and secure, and a fix applies everywhere. 

Every Layer 2 becomes a true extension of Ethereum: one account and one contract address across connected chains, with wallets routing sends so funds sent to the wrong chain can stop being lost. Ethereum L1 stays as secure as it is today, since its consensus does not depend on EEZ. What changes is the layer above it: cross-chain validity is decided by checks on Ethereum instead of by a signer set's reputation, the locked-fund pools that made bridges worth attacking disappear, and the code that can lose user money across chains collapses to one set that Ethereum can see and everyone can audit.

**What each rollup keeps.** Each rollup declares the proof systems it accepts and how many must agree, and every cross-chain outcome is checked on L1 against them; the composer that builds each bundle can at most stall calls. Based rollups, like the first Gnosis deployment, go further: sequencing happens inside the L1 block, and anyone can rebuild the chain from L1 data alone. Today one attestation signer runs the check by re-executing each block window, so until more proof systems are added, a chain's safety rests on that signer. The audit covers the signer, the multi-prover design it plugs into, and how each rollup locks its configuration down.

**What independently tested guarantees change.** Every rollup that adopts EEZ inherits the same contract set on Ethereum. Its cross-chain attack surface becomes that reviewed set plus its own configuration, instead of a bridge it built and audited alone. Every later adopter shares one review, and a fix reaches all of them at once. The same sharing is the risk: a flaw in the shared set is a flaw everywhere, which is why no chain should adopt it on the EEZ team's word alone. The audit turns these guarantees from a design claim into something a rollup can rely on; the testnet lets outside chains verify it, and mainnet adoption shows they did.

With audited EEZ, users and teams will be able to:

- Move assets between rollups with no third-party pool holding funds for an attacker to drain.
- Run atomic multi-chain actions, such as a swap funded from another rollup, that complete fully or revert together within one L1 block, provided a builder includes the bundle.
- Deploy a protocol once, where it is easiest to audit, and serve every connected chain from that one deployment, so a fix applies everywhere.
- Use one account and one contract address across connected chains, with wallets routing sends so funds sent to the wrong chain can stop being lost.
- Adopt a shared, independently audited contract set instead of building and auditing a bridge alone, with every later adopter sharing the same review and every fix reaching all of them at once.

EEZ is not a dapp and not a product. It is an Ethereum public good: an open, permissionless protocol for synchronous composability between Ethereum rollups. The core EEZ contract has no admin role. Each connected rollup keeps its own contract, whose owner sets the accepted proof systems, verification keys, and threshold. That design puts the security of the whole system on its smart contracts, which is exactly what this grant puts under independent review.

sections.heading: Why this matters
sections.markdown:
A zkVM proves that a guest program ran. It cannot show whether the program implements Ethereum correctly. Wrong opcode results, gas charges or state updates can produce valid proofs of invalid Ethereum results. Bugs in EVM code shared with the regular client may also affect ordinary nodes.

Nethermind will prove its Amsterdam EVM against an independently reviewed Lean specification, through CIL and optimised RISC-V. The team will check EthLib definitions against Ethereum specifications and fixtures before reuse. A public manifest will identify proved methods that also appear unchanged in regular-client builds. The proof excludes production-only methods and JIT-generated code.

LeanCIL could also help verify C# components of other Ethereum projects. Nethereum provides .NET libraries for transaction signing, wallets and EVM interaction, alongside tooling for Solidity development in VS Code. Applying LeanCIL to Nethereum would require separate work beyond this grant.

sections.heading: Why a grant: what already exists
sections.markdown:
LeanCIL is being built to verify compiled .NET code, including Nethermind's EVM. It proves supported CIL methods and composes contracts. Its instruction model, runtime support and proof automation do not yet cover the full EVM. This grant funds the missing capabilities and the EVM proofs.

EVMYulLean and `il2rv64` provide starting points for the other proof stages. EthLib defines and proves EVM rules in Lean, with some Amsterdam gaps. Nethermind will review these components before reuse, reducing duplicate work.

sections.heading: In scope
sections.markdown:
- Extend EVMYulLean to Amsterdam using reviewed EthLib definitions and lemmas. Check fork rules, gas charges and state changes against Ethereum specifications and fixtures.
- Extend LeanCIL for the CIL instructions and .NET runtime behaviour reached by the EVM. Bind proofs to method bytes and metadata, automate checks and prove all reachable EVM-owned methods.
- Extend `il2rv64` to prove that the optimised RISC-V code matches the compiled CIL, then compose the refinement proofs.
- Prove precompile dispatch, gas charges, return data and failures under explicit contracts, excluding their algorithms.
- Publish proofs, coverage, assumptions, build identities and comparisons of proved methods shared with the regular client.
- Measure independent Ethereum nodes running a release containing those methods.

sections.markdown:
- Formal verification of the entire regular Nethermind EVM or its JIT-generated code. Production CIL that differs from the guest is excluded.
- Precompile algorithms, the full stateless guest, witness and SSZ processing, tries, block orchestration and zkVM provers.
- Completion of LeanCIL for arbitrary .NET programs, all EthLib modules, other clients, L2 plug-ins or native targets.

sections.heading: Why this matters
sections.markdown:
Two gaps, one cause.

- Coverage: the platform indexes 8 chains, and the same attackers, the same bytecode and the same Ethereum-issued assets are on dozens more. Ethereum L2s with billions in value, such as Mantle, is not covered by the platform today.
- Backtesting: an alert that has never been run against a real attack is an untested guess. Replaying an alert over history needs call traces and logs in a form that can be scanned quickly. We compress older data to stay within capacity, and a backfill on compressed data slows from milliseconds to tens of minutes per day of history.

The cause is storage. Adding chains without more disk makes the compression problem worse. Adding disk without more chains leaves the ecosystem's value uncovered.

Who is safer: any team on the covered chains, whose alerts can be replayed over past exploits before they rely on them, and incident responders, who get the decoded internal-call trace of an attack transaction the same day on chains whose explorer shows no traces. Every new chain is an Ethereum L2 whose value settles on Ethereum. Attackers reuse Ethereum exploit code across all of them.

Backfill becomes a normal step when creating an alert, from the web app and the CLI.
- Decoded traces for responders: the internal-call trace of any transaction on a funded chain, queryable in DedaubQL and exportable from the CLI.
- Unlimited access for SEAL and SEAL 911 members: unlimited active alerts with backfill and decoded traces without rate limits, for 36 months from the first new chain going live.

sections.heading: Why this matters
sections.markdown: Ethereum's security model is based on independent verification, but most applications abandon that property at the RPC boundary. The problem becomes more severe across L2s and bridges, where one application may trust several independent read infrastructures. The April 2026 KelpDAO incident (https://www.corpuscore.tech/blog/the-code-was-fine-thats-the-problem) showed the direct consequence: compromised RPC infrastructure caused a verifier to attest to a non-existent source-chain event, releasing about $292 million on the destination chain (https://unchainedcrypto.com/layerzero-links-292-million-kelp-dao-bridge-exploit-to-north-koreas-lazarus-group/). colibri moves verification to the application edge: data is accepted only together with evidence that the client verifies locally.

sections.heading: The team

sections.heading: Why a grant: what already exists
sections.markdown: colibri has been in production since November 2025 and runs on Ethereum, Gnosis and the OP Stack. The verifier, the execution and consensus proofs, and a zk-compressed consensus proof already exist. Bindings are available for JavaScript/TypeScript, Swift, Kotlin/Java, Python, Dart/Flutter and Rust. This grant pays for what is missing: the chain adapter framework, the per-network support table, the fallback protocol and the new networks. A team starting from scratch would first have to build the verifier itself.

sections.heading: In scope
sections.markdown:
- Hardening only the reusable multi-chain verification components required by this grant: common proof interfaces, explicit verification/trust modes, cross-chain conformance tests, live-chain testing and reproducible CI. General Ethereum-core work unrelated to multi-chain adoption is excluded.
- A public, machine-readable support table for every network (the Verification Capability Model): what colibri verifies natively, what it verifies only partially, and where it relies on the fallback. Applications read the active mode for each request. 
- A chain integration framework: standardized chain/consensus adapter interfaces where possible, reusable L2 verification components, an integration SDK, conformance and live-chain tests, test vectors, compatibility checks, and a documented process for adding a network.
- A witness-based verification fallback protocol for networks without native proofs yet: defined security assumptions, integration with the Capability Model, applications always able to identify fallback use, no silent downgrade, a migration path to native verification, reference implementation, test vectors, and documentation.
- Integration support for L2 teams and cross-chain protocols adopting colibri verification.
- At least 2 reference network integrations on materially different architectures, selected only where their chain-specific engineering is not being paid by another foundation, grants program or commercial integration budget.

sections.heading: Out of scope
sections.markdown:
- Integrations into wallets, DeFi protocols and other dApps. A companion initiative covers them.
- Networks that are not Ethereum or one of its L2s, this grant covers Ethereum L2s and bridges only. 
- New language bindings such as Go. They belong to the companion dApp initiative. 
- Pragmatic Adaptive Privacy (PAP). A companion initiative covers it. 
- Transaction simulation and the open transaction-security foundation. A companion initiative covers them, built on the verified data this grant delivers. 
- Commercial vRPC, prover services, and integration work for RPC providers.
 - The full integration cost of chains that have their own foundation, grants program or integration budget. They may pay separately for chain-specific engineering, support and maintenance beyond the reusable components funded here.

sections.heading: Commitments
sections.markdown:
- **License:** the verifier, chain adapters, support table, fallback protocol and test suites are released under an OSI-approved open-source license. Commercial vRPC and prover services built on top are not covered.
- **Maintenance:** corpus.core maintains the chain integrations and the support table after the grant, funded by commercial products built on the open core.
- **Pinned targets:** a public support table covering at least 6 Ethereum L2 networks and at least 5 L2 networks using colibri verification in a production product run by the chain team, 2 of them from the named list, and at least 3 cross-chain protocols using colibri verification in production.
- **Exception requested:** a merged upstream pull request counts toward the bridge target when the bridge's own release schedule delays production use.

initiatives.summary: colibri turns blockchain reads from a trust assumption into a cryptographic check. This grant makes that security model reusable across Ethereum’s L2s a production multi-chain verification framework, a public capability table for L2 networks, and an explicit capability/fallback model with no silent downgrade. Success means at least 5 L2 networks use colibri verification in their own production products and at least 3 cross-chain protocols use it where a false read can move real value. Chain-specific engineering that can be funded by a chain foundation is explicitly excluded.

sections.heading: Why this matters
sections.markdown:
- **Screen implants.** In October 2026, Ledger confirmed a hidden implant in at least one device sold through a reseller. The implant read the recovery phrase off the Ledger device's screen during setup and sent it out over a mobile network. Reported losses exceed $86 million (BleepingComputer, Ledger).
- **Blind signing.** In February 2025, Bybit lost about $1.5 billion after its Safe signers approved a malicious upgrade they could not read on their devices (BlockSec).
- **No way to check.** Most hardware wallet owners cannot verify that their device runs the published firmware on a genuine chip.

After this grant, an Ostros owner creates a recovery phrase that a screen implant never sees in full, reads Ethereum transactions in plain language before signing, and confirms their firmware and chip are genuine.

This grant is one step toward a goal of a hardware wallet that owners can verify end to end, from an open-source chip through open software to a device they can open and inspect. CrossBar builds both the chip and the wallet, so this goal can be reached. Any hardware wallet can reuse the split recovery phrase method, the attestation design and the owner verification tool, the way distributions build on Linux. A follow-on initiative will (1) make the device openable, and (2) let owners inspect the chip inside their own wallet.

sections.heading: Why a grant: what already exists
sections.markdown:
- **The chip:** Daric, CrossBar's security chip with published RTL, SDK and documentation, features a 350 MHz RISC-V core with an MMU, 4 MB of ReRAM, crypto accelerators, a true random number generator, a key store, glitch sensors and a security mesh. Its post-quantum library (ML-DSA, ML-KEM) is NIST CAVP-validated on the RISC-V core.
- **The software:** Xous runs on Ostros with a fully open bootloader, core drivers, an e-ink UI, seed generation and key management. The firmware build is deterministic.
- **The Ethereum signer:** The shared Ethereum signer (https://github.com/ethereum/ethereum-app) runs on Ostros hardware with verifiable signing (ERC-8213), demoed at Devcon 8.
- **Developers:** The Founders Edition ships to developers in late November 2026, and teams have applied to build apps on it. At Devcon 8, 196 developers signed up for CrossBar's Dabao hackathon and picked up a free board with the same die, so they already use the RISC-V, Rust and Xous tools Ostros needs.
- **In use and openly reviewed:** Ostros builds on the open Xous environment (OS and secure boot), where findings from public reviews of the Daric die are fixed. The Baochip version of that die shipped in every DEF CON 34 badge (August 2026). At Devcon 8, CrossBar guided about 250 attendees one by one through IRIS inspections, on their own chip or on a demo chip.

The secure chip and the operating system already exist, so the grant covers the security features and their adoption.

sections.heading: In scope
sections.markdown:
- **Attestation:** Each Ostros can prove it carries a genuine Daric chip, set up in a new factory personalization flow. The split recovery phrase and the app loader both build on it.
  - Technical: A key generated inside the chip at personalization, checked against a published CrossBar root, as a per-device certificate or anonymous attestation (scheme chosen during the grant).
- **Clear signing:** Ostros shows Ethereum transactions in plain language (ERC-7730), or the verifiable digest (ERC-8213) when no descriptor exists.
- **Web companion:** Connects Ostros to any Ethereum app through WalletConnect.
  - Technical: USB or Bluetooth; the device decodes and displays each request itself, so the companion never decides what the owner sees.
- **Owner verification:** A public guide and tool to rebuild the firmware, match its hash and check the attestation.
- **Split recovery phrase:** Features a 24-word phrase: 12 words show on the Ostros screen and 12 go to the owner's computer over a connection the computer checks comes from a genuine Daric chip. An implant on the screen never sees the full phrase, so an attacker needs both an implant and malware on the computer (method by Nicolas Bacca, Devcon 8).
  - Technical: The computer accepts its 12 words only after checking that the session key is signed by the device's attestation key. The 12 words an implant could see leave more than 120 bits of the phrase unknown.
- **App loader and developer kit:** Outside teams install security apps without rebuilding the firmware, with an emulator and system API documentation.
  - Technical: Each app runs in its own Xous process, isolated by the MMU, under a permission model that limits what each app can reach.

sections.heading: Out of scope
sections.markdown:
- Planned follow-on initiative: (1) the openable device, and (2) research into Daric chip inspection in the Ostros package.
- Drivers not needed for these features (power management, fingerprint, NFC, vibrator, LED), the app store website and MPC on the RISC-V core: CrossBar builds these with its own funds.
- Apps for other chains (Bitcoin and others).

sections.heading: Commitments
sections.markdown:
- Software under Apache 2.0; chip RTL and board design files under CERN-OHL-W, except the bus fabric, USB PHY and analog blocks, which do not process data.
- Pinned targets: Release firmware rebuilds bit-identically from source, the full recovery phrase never appears on the Ostros screen, and no secret is shared across devices.
- Ostros works with any Ethereum app and does not require a proprietary companion app.
- Public vulnerability disclosure process; fixes ship as signed, reproducible firmware.
- CrossBar maintains the grant deliverables for at least 12 months after the final milestone (security fixes, firmware updates, review of outside pull requests).
- CrossBar publishes the IRIS rig design, software and Devcon 8 reference images under open licenses.

initiatives.summary: Ostros™ is CrossBar's hardware wallet, open from the chip to the apps. It runs on Daric, CrossBar's open-core RISC-V security chip, and the Rust-based Xous operating system. This grant adds chip attestation, clear signing, a recovery phrase a screen implant cannot read, an owner check that firmware and chip are genuine, an independent security review, and an app loader for outside security apps. The grant is paid out as wallets add Ostros support, owners verify their own devices, and outside teams build security apps on it.

sections.heading: Why this matters
sections.markdown:
Smart contracts can be decentralized and independently verified, while the frontend used to interact with them still depends on centralized infrastructure. An attacker who compromises a dApp's domain, DNS, hosting platform or CDN can serve modified code that alters transaction parameters, and browsers do not check that the code they receive is the code the dApp team published. In February 2025, attackers modified the JavaScript served by the Safe wallet interface used by Bybit and drained its cold wallet without exploiting any contract bug ([Sygnia](https://www.sygnia.co/blog/sygnia-investigation-bybit-hack/), [NCC Group](https://www.nccgroup.com/research/in-depth-technical-analysis-of-the-bybit-hack/)). Frontend compromises also hit BadgerDAO ([TRM Labs](https://www.trmlabs.com/resources/blog/trm-investigates-badgerdao-defi-protocol-hacked)) and KyberSwap ([CoinDesk](https://www.coindesk.com/tech/2022/09/01/defi-platform-kyber-network-discloses-265k-exploit-vows-to-reimburse-all-funds)).

Gateways that serve dApps from IPFS face the same risk: in April 2026, attackers hijacked eth.limo's DNS for about five hours ([eth.limo post-mortem](https://discuss.ens.domains/t/eth-limo-dns-hijack-post-mortem/22079)), and a compromised gateway can serve modified code for every site it delivers.

DappFence protects the users of every dApp that deploys it, including dApps served through IPFS gateways. Wallet defenses such as transaction simulation and clear signing check the transaction; DappFence checks the code that builds and presents it, so a modified interface is blocked before the user is asked to sign.

sections.heading: The team
sections.markdown:
**Coinspect** does the work. Andres A., the main author of the current DappFence codebase, leads development and works full-time on this grant (https://github.com/a-d-j-i).

Coinspect is a security research and auditing firm founded in 2014: https://www.coinspect.com.

Coinspect develops and owns the DappFence repository and has pledged $27,000 of the funding goal. There is no other funding for this work.

sections.heading: Why a grant: what already exists
sections.markdown:
DappFence already has a working implementation. Automated browser tests show that a modified page, script or external resource, including the DappFence script, is blocked, that new signed releases load without being blocked, and that attempts to wipe DappFence from the browser are detected.

On a user's first visit, the site installs a Service Worker that the browser keeps between visits. On later visits, that Service Worker verifies the frontend's code against manifests signed by the dApp's publisher and blocks any file that does not match. No external service, browser extension or dedicated infrastructure is involved: the script and the signed manifest are served from the dApp's own hosting, and an attacker who controls that hosting cannot forge a valid manifest without the publisher's private signing key. An attacker who tries to remove DappFence has to replace a Service Worker script whose expected hash is in the signed, public manifest, so such an attack is straightforward to monitor.

The repository contains:

- The Service Worker runtime (@dappfence/core), with a report-only mode for gradual rollout.
- A warning page and emergency panel shown when tampering is detected, and a status endpoint with verification results and block history.
- Manifest tooling (@dappfence/manifest-tools) that hashes a build, signs the manifest and verifies signatures.
- Initial build integrations for Next.js and Vite.
- A test application and an end-to-end browser test suite.

The current implementation remains a prototype and requires hardening before production use. The grant pays for hardening, release and adoption, not for building what already exists.

sections.heading: In scope
sections.markdown:
- Runtime hardening: Close the known gaps in the verification runtime, including stronger verification of a dApp's own Service Worker.
- Signing and release workflow: Harden manifest generation, signing and verification.
- Integration tooling: Finish and publish the Next.js and Vite integrations and extend them where production deployments require it.
- Compatibility: Run the end-to-end test suite on Chrome and Firefox, and against sample applications built with each supported integration.
- Production deployments: Deploy in live, publicly accessible dApps, starting with one and growing to the adoption target, and resolve the issues each deployment surfaces.
- Support: Direct assistance to dApp teams integrating DappFence.
- Documentation: Integration, onboarding, signing and release guides for dApp teams, and a threat model stating what DappFence protects against and what it does not.

sections.heading: Out of scope
sections.markdown:
- First visits and the protection window: Trust is established on a user's first visit. The browser downloads the DappFence script again once 24 hours have passed since its last check, so returning users have a protection window of up to 24 hours when the script is served with a long cache lifetime. Two cases are therefore not covered: a user whose first visit happens while the site is already compromised, and a compromise that persists beyond the protection window, after which the attacker's script can replace the Service Worker on returning users' browsers.
- Supply chain and signing keys: Verification confirms that users run the release the publisher signed. It does not assess whether that release is safe: malicious code added before signing, through a compromised dependency or build pipeline, passes verification, as does code signed with a compromised key.

sections.heading: Commitments
sections.markdown:
- Code published under the MIT license, with development public in the repository.
- Coinspect maintains the public repository for 6 months after the last milestone, at no further cost: reviewing and merging contributions and publishing releases to npm.
- DappFence has no business model yet; further development after the grant will need new funding.

initiatives.summary: DappFence is an open-source, client-side security system designed to protect users from compromised web frontends. The February 2025 Bybit theft, in which attackers manipulated the Safe wallet interface to deceive signers and steal approximately $1.5 billion, demonstrated why Ethereum security must extend beyond smart contracts to the interfaces people use to interact with them. DappFence verifies frontend assets against an authenticated integrity manifest and blocks resources that do not match the version defined by that manifest. Coinspect will bring the implementation to production-ready, validate it in production deployments, finish and publish its integration tooling, and drive adoption by dApps.
initiatives.title: DappFence: Verifiable Frontend Security

sections.heading: Why this matters
sections.markdown: The security boundary of a wallet or dApp does not end at key custody. Applications continuously make security-relevant decisions from RPC data: balances, allowances, bytecode, storage, logs, name resolution and eth_call results. If those reads are manipulated, the application can display false state, route funds incorrectly or construct a transaction from a false premise. colibri replaces the RPC provider as a source of truth with locally verified proofs. Manipulated reads are a proven attack path: in April 2026, compromised RPC infrastructure (https://www.corpuscore.tech/blog/the-code-was-fine-thats-the-problem) fed false chain data to KelpDAO's bridge verifier and released about $292 million (https://unchainedcrypto.com/layerzero-links-292-million-kelp-dao-bridge-exploit-to-north-koreas-lazarus-group/). Every wallet that trusts its RPC provider depends on the same kind of infrastructure.

sections.heading: Why this matters
sections.markdown:
This protects people whose funds sit in exploitable contracts or on leaked keys: a white hat who finds them can take them first and send them somewhere lawful. Today we leave that money on the table for the worst people in the world. White hats hold back because they want legal cover first, someone else to do the work of returning the money second, and pay third. Give them a destination they trust and they will rescue funds like mad, many just for the lulz.

- North Korea takes billions from our industry ([FBI](https://www.ic3.gov/PSA/2025/PSA250226)). UN monitors found crypto theft brings in as much as half of its foreign income and helps bankroll its nuclear program ([NK News](https://www.nknews.org/2024/03/north-korea-relies-on-crypto-theft-for-up-to-half-of-foreign-income-un-report)).
- At least 220,000 people may be held in scam compounds in Myanmar and Cambodia alone, forced to run scams that include crypto fraud ([UN News](https://news.un.org/en/story/2023/08/1140187)).
- Anthropic measured the value AI agents could exploit from real, previously hacked contracts doubling roughly every 1.3 months ([Anthropic](https://www.anthropic.com/research/smart-contracts)). You fight AI with AI, once white hats have somewhere safe to send what they find.

sections.heading: In scope
sections.markdown:
Legal setup (a new entity or an existing one), custody, an owner portal and a public case page, plus case work through month 12: outreach that brings rescuers' cases in, the operator's own rescues, intake, owner searches, ownership checks and returns. That covers known owners (a protocol, company or token holders), paid back within weeks, and unknown owners (weak or leaked keys), paid as they prove their claims.

The ideal service gives white hats legal cover when they hand funds over and pays their bounties without KYC. Where the law stops short of that, propose the design that gets closest and say where it falls short; once this RFP is funded, we pick the proposal that works and comes closest. The fee design here is a starting idea too: the team picks the legal structure, custody setup and tools, and may propose any design that solves the same problem, as long as owners pay for their rescue, the rescuer's bounty and operator's fee come only from returns, and unclaimed funds stay open to claims.

sections.heading: Out of scope
sections.markdown:
- Rescues that need red-teaming or breaking into someone's computer or systems, this is not accecptable: rescues must start from public information, such as open-source code, onchain data or keys already published
- Tracing and freezing stolen funds
- Assets on chains other than Ethereum and its L2s

sections.heading: Existing work
sections.markdown:
- [SEAL Whitehat Safe Harbor](https://frameworks.securityalliance.org/safe-harbor/whitehat/) lets a white hat step in only during an exploit under way or imminent, on a protocol that adopted it, for a bounty usually 10% capped at $1 million ([SEAL](https://securityalliance.org/safe-harbor)). A good start with a narrow use: a white hat may not act on a known hole before an attacker does.
- [DART](https://assetrecovery.io/) (Digital Asset Recovery Technologies) and the independent Crypto Recovery Trust it works with are the closest model: a Wyoming statutory trust with an independent trustee takes crypto from white hats, gives them legal cover and returns it to verified original owners where the law allows.
- About 70,500 ETH from TheDAO's 2016 refund contracts is still unclaimed a decade later ([thedao.fund](https://thedao.fund)): even a famous refund never reaches every owner.
- [Kleros](https://kleros.io/) arbitration, for disputed claims.

This RFP aims to go further than Safe Harbor: if a white hat can take exposed money, they should.

sections.heading: Who we expect to do this
sections.markdown:
Nobody is pre-selected. A winning team pairs legal operations with BD and outreach people that white hats and incident-response groups already trust, since adoption pays only when rescuers hand funds over and owners are found. It needs no onchain engineering expertise.

Drafted with TheDAO Security Fund; the idea was built by Griff Green from conversations with SEAL 911, DART, TheDAO's lawyers and other teams. DART has a clear head start and may bid, as may TheDAO's lawyers.

sections.heading: Hard requirements
sections.markdown:
1. Victims pay for their rescue with a haircut on the return or a fee to collect it. That funds an equal rescuer bounty and operator fee, paid only on returns to verified owners: An example payout scheme could be: 2% each of the first $10 million, 0.25% to $100 million, 0.06% to $1 billion and 0.01% above (about $200,000 each at $10 million, $425,000 at $100 million and $1 million at $1 billion). Tiers apply per case, and a case is one incident with all its related addresses, chains and staged returns. Rates may rise case by case, within a published ceiling and set before the case is accepted, when few owners are likely to come forward. The proposal shows how the fee sustains the service after the grant, even with few claims and zero yield.
2. Published rules for proving ownership, including for leaked or weak keys (a signature from the exposed key proves nothing on its own), and a dispute path to a neutral arbiter.
3. A licensed firm's legal opinion covers custody, money transmission, sanctions, unclaimed property, how far rescuers can be paid without KYC, and what protection rescuers get when they hand funds over. Every return and bounty is sanctions-screened.
4. Funds nobody claims become an endowment: once they count as lost or abandoned under applicable law or a rule the operator publishes before the rescue, the operator may stake them or earn other low-risk yield and keep that yield, but every claim stays open and the principal stays available to pay it for at least 7 years from the rescue.
5. Rescued funds, including any staked under Hard requirement 4, sit only in audited code, such as an unmodified Safe, or with an independent trustee or regulated custodian, kept apart per case and from the operator's own funds, and the operator can't move them alone.
6. A public case page lists every deposit, return and endowment balance, each valued in USD at its block by a published onchain query: Chainlink feed, else relevant DEX TWAP (e.g. Uniswap v3 TWAP); anything else counts as $0.
7. Rescuers may stay unnamed in public. Where the law requires identity checks for bounties, the proposal says which checks and why, and the legal opinion in Hard requirement 3 confirms them. Owners' identities and evidence stay with the operator; the technical reviewer inspects counted case files and keeps no copies.
8. Code is open source, under a license the bidder states.
9. A case counts only if the funds were rescued after the award starts and its case page links the onchain trail from exploited contract or leaked address to owner. The technical reviewer also confirms the owner had the funds before the incident, no protocol could have recovered the funds itself, the owner is not the operator, its staff or an affiliate, the exposed contract or key was not deployed or funded by the rescuer, the operator or their affiliates, counted rescuers are not each other's staff or affiliates, and in each adoption milestone at most one counted rescuer is the operator or tied to it. Milestones count what owners receive, after bounty, fee and gas.
10. The operating legal entity signs an indemnification agreement with every white hat who hands it funds, so if a white hat is sued over a good-faith rescue handed to the service, the entity covers their legal defense.

initiatives.summary: Our industry's security holes fund North Korea's weapons programs, scam compounds full of trafficked people, and countless cybercriminals. Black hats find exposed money and take it, while white hats who find the same holes warn the team and hope the money stays there long enough to be rescued; with AI speeding up attacks, that is a losing strategy. This RFP funds a legal entity that takes what white hats rescue, gives them legal cover, pays them without KYC, and earns its fee only when owners get their money back. Our goal is an army of white hats rescuing money everywhere they can, in effect an open bug bounty on all of Ethereum.
initiatives.title: RFP: An Open Bug Bounty Program for All of Ethereum: White Hat Rescued Funds Distribution Service

sections.heading: Why this matters
sections.markdown:
- Bybit (2025, about USD 1.5B) and Radiant (2024, about USD 50M): compromised signing interfaces, hardware wallets that could not render a Safe delegatecall, signers approving a hash.
- ERC-7730 is a real improvement, and this builds on it. It also adds at the moment a single point of trust (the descriptor signing key and its review queue) and cannot express computed meaning: Safe `safeTxHash`, ERC-4337 `userOpHash`, shielded transfers.
- Protocols fund their own audits; the shared signing flow has no owner. The EF Trillion Dollar Security report lists blind signing among the main user-facing risks.

What people can do afterwards:

- **Semantic clear signing.** A proof attests a computation, so the device can show what a Safe hash commits to, what a batch does on net, or a shielded transfer bound to the commitment it signs. It closes a concrete attack: a compromised host swaps the commitment (Tornado), precommitment (Privacy Pools) or note key (Railgun) in a deposit for one it controls.
- **No registry, no permission.** Each contract compiles its rules with the open toolchain and publishes `h_rules` in its own storage or ENS name: nothing to submit, no per-vendor pipeline.
- **Policy-bound signing for AI agents.** The device signs an agent's proposal with no button press when the proof shows it fits a policy the user enrolled; a compromised agent gets no proof outside it.

sections.markdown:
ZKNOX (Paris, 2025): 30+ open-source repositories, three hardware-wallet applications, three EIPs, public security analyses of privacy protocols and wallets, Ethereum Foundation grants, four hackathon prizes in two years including two first prizes, the latest at ETHGlobal Cannes 2026 for the proof of concept this grant starts from. sections.markdown:
- ZKlarity (March 2026): clear-signing circuit for 13 Aave v3 actions and a Groth16 verifier running natively in a Ledger Nano S+ secure element, 2.8 s per verification: https://github.com/ZKNoxHQ/ZKlarity
- ETHGlobal Cannes 2026, first prize in the Ledger track: end-to-end demonstrator with an on-device storage proof checking the rules commitment in an ENS record.
- Streaming STARK verifier on the same device: a 97 KB proof streamed in 414 chunks with about 8 KB of RAM.
- Railgun joinsplit circuits in gnark with a test setup ceremony, and a Railgun signer on Nano S+.

The grant pays for generalisation, hardening, integrations, adoption and review of running code.

sections.heading: In scope
sections.markdown:
The prover (dapp, relayer or the user's wallet software) computes `readable` from `tx` and the protocol's rules and proves `h_tx = H(tx)`, `h_readable = H(readable)` and `readable = Render(rules, tx, context)` for rules identified by `h_rules`. The device recomputes both hashes from the bytes it signs and displays, verifies the proof and shows the string with a trust level, without parsing ABI or seeing private context. `h_rules` is anchored by the protocol (contract slot, registry or ENS record) and checked through a storage proof.

Deliverables:

- ERC draft with threat model, proof envelope, anchoring paths, trust indicator and agent policy envelope.
- ERC-7730-to-circuit compiler: all v1 field formats, nested calldata, `safeTxHash` and `userOpHash` binding, reproducible verification-key build, differential tests against viem and ethers.
- Embedded verifier v1.0 in C99 on BLS12-381 and BN254 for Nano S+, Nano X, Stax and Flex; self-hostable prover; Ledger app and Kohaku integrations.
- Five DeFi protocols end to end on the device: Aave v3, Safe (`execTransaction` with nested decoding and `safeTxHash` binding), Uniswap v3/v4, Lido, Morpho.
- Tornado Cash (`deposit`, `withdraw`), Privacy Pools (`deposit`, `withdraw`, `ragequit`) and Railgun (`shield`, `transact` spend authorisation, `unshield`) on the device: amounts, recipient, fee and change recomputed from the note plaintexts, and the commitment, precommitment or npk proven to derive from a note or key the wallet holds; circuits native to BN254; one negative vector per protocol where the host substitutes the commitment and the device refuses.
- Policy-bound signing for AI agents. A policy selects allowed protocols and functions with pinned addresses and constrains the rendered parameters (token in a set, amount at most a ceiling, recipient equal to the signer); the compiler turns it into one circuit with hash `h_policy`. The device verifies against (`h_tx`, `h_readable`, `h_policy`) and signs without a confirmation screen. Enrolment is a clear-signing event with a human (canonical policy text, `h_policy`, a signature cap); revocation is a button press. The ERC-8004 `agentWallet` is the device key, with `h_policy` published as Identity Registry metadata.
- Version 2: a hash-based STARK (KoalaBear, Poseidon2, FRI, Plonky3/SP1 format) replaces the verifier, streamed in phase order in 240-byte chunks with about 8 KB of RAM on the device. No trusted setup, so publishing rules is a single transaction by the contract owner; a pairing-free, plausibly post-quantum device; rules written as a Rust program compiled to an AIR.
- Independent review of the compiler, the privacy circuits and the embedded verifier; integration guides for wallet vendors and protocols.

sections.heading: Out of scope
sections.markdown:
- A descriptor registry or a vendor review pipeline: protocols anchor their own rules.
- Software wallets other than Kohaku and devices other than Ledger's (stretch goals).
- Privacy-protocol renderers under version 2: BN254 hashing is non-native in a 31-bit field, so they are evaluated only.
- Policies with time state (no trusted clock on the device).

sections.heading: Commitments
sections.markdown:
- Every deliverable under Apache-2.0 or MIT, built and tested in public CI.
- ZKNOX maintains the compiler, both verifiers and the Ledger and Kohaku integrations for 12 months after the last milestone at no further cost (security fixes, SDK updates, review of external pull requests) and runs the hosted prover for the same period; a Docker image allows self-hosting after that.
- Pinned targets: verification at most 3.0 s (BLS12-381) and 2.5 s (BN254) on Nano S+; 5 DeFi and 3 privacy protocols on the device; STARK verifier with no trusted setup, at most 16 KB of RAM and 128 KB of proof.
- No exception requested.

initiatives.summary: Hardware wallets sign bytes they cannot interpret, and clear signing today depends on a descriptor registry signed by the wallet vendor. This grant funds an open standard and toolchain in which the device verifies a zero-knowledge proof that the string it displays is the correct rendering of the bytes it signs, under rules the protocol itself commits on-chain. It ships an ERC draft, a compiler, an embedded verifier, Ledger and Kohaku integrations, five DeFi protocols including Safe, ZK clear signing of Tornado Cash, Privacy Pools and Railgun, policy-bound signing for AI agents, an independent review, and a second verifier that moves from Groth16 to a STARK streamed into the device.

sections.heading: Why this matters
sections.markdown:
Your keys, your devices, your multisig process, your access controls... these matter as much as your smart contracts:

- Bybit lost nearly $1.5B in ETH in February 2025 after attackers took over one Safe developer's computer ([Chainalysis](https://www.chainalysis.com/blog/bybit-exchange-hack-february-2025-crypto-security-dprk/)).
- KelpDAO lost about $292M in April 2026 through compromised RPC nodes, "not a smart contract hack" ([Chainalysis](https://www.chainalysis.com/blog/kelpdao-bridge-exploit-april-2026/)).

Serious teams already buy OpSec audits, and all of that work is invisible, while the findings often wait on a to-do list. After TheDAO hack, shipping an unaudited contract became negligent. OpSec audits need the same shift, and SOC 2 checklists were never built for stolen keys and tricked signers. Teams that complete an OpSec audit and fix what it finds get listed on a public board.

A rating only matters if missing it costs something, the way no bank works with a firm that fails compliance. Once the exchanges, protocols, bridges, L2s and wallets that move the money require a current listing, weak OpSec costs a team its listings and integrations, and users are safer from stolen keys, hijacked laptops, tricked signers and poisoned infrastructure.

sections.heading: In scope
sections.markdown:
This RFP pays for coordination: getting the OpSec audit firms working together, then getting the businesses that move the money to require an OpSec audit. The board is the easy part.

Bidders have complete freedom in how they get there, including their own milestones, within the hard requirements below. What matters is three outcomes: more teams get OpSec audits, teams act on them by fixing what they find, and the OpSec audit firms coordinate as one coalition, ideally one that outlives the grant on member dues and runs shared services like red teaming. This money funds only the coordinator.

One possible approach:

- A simple public board of teams that completed an OpSec audit and fixed every critical and high finding, with their auditor and dates. It may also show facts anyone can check onchain, such as timelocks, multisig thresholds and outflow limits, the way L2BEAT Stages shows rollup trust assumptions.
- The founding firms list the teams they audit first, with a clear path for any qualified OpSec firm to join. The coalition decides.
- Shared outcome goals in place of one rigid checklist, such as "after a compromise, the team can trace affected systems and the root cause within 24 hours", built on SEAL's frameworks, with the auditor answering for the result.
- A six-month check-in, and a verification committee that spot-checks listings.
- Member dues, equal votes for founding firms and a neutral name. Fees from listed teams only if the coalition chooses, the same fee whatever the result.
- The first organizations that require a current listing.

sections.heading: Out of scope
sections.markdown:
- Performing the OpSec audits (the OpSec audit firms do that)
- Requiring every firm to adopt one shared standard (the coalition may agree one if it helps)
- A heavy platform build

sections.heading: Existing work
sections.markdown:
- [SEAL Security Frameworks](https://frameworks.securityalliance.org/): SEAL's open OpSec, multisig, treasury and incident frameworks, the natural base for the standard.
- [SEAL Certifications](https://securityalliance.org/our-work/certifications): modular certifications assessed by auditors SEAL accredits, recorded as onchain attestations. Bids may build the standard and rater roster on it; a bid that starts fresh explains why.
- [L2BEAT Stages](https://l2beat.com/stages): the model, a public maturity rating for rollups.
- [Coinspect Wallet Security Ranking](https://wallets.coinspect.com/): a quarterly public security score for Ethereum wallets.

sections.heading: Who we expect to do this
sections.markdown:
Nobody is pre-selected. The dream candidate is a credible coordinator who can get 4+ OpSec audit firms to work together (if you have ever tried to get six companies to agree on anything, you know that's the real work here), then get the protocols and wallets that matter to write a listing into their policies.

A strong bid reads like a founder pitch: one credible lead or a lean team, its own plan, and why audit firms and protocols will take its call. The OpSec audit firms that back this RFP before the vote each name one ETHSecurity Badge holder to the panel that reviews bids, and the panel's majority picks the coordinator.

The longterm goal of this initiative is to bootstrap an organization that can make Operational Security Audits as necessary as smart contract audits. We expect in the long run for this organization to provide many shared services for the OpSec auditors, such as becoming a certification authority, red teaming projects on the board, etc. 

Drafted by Griff Green of TheDAO Security Fund, with feedback from several OpSec audit firms. Griff runs no audit firm and will not bid.

sections.heading: Hard requirements
sections.markdown:
1. Listing only. The board shows a team's name, its auditor, dates and facts already public onchain (timelocks, multisig thresholds, rate limits), never its gaps, findings or why a team is missing.
2. Fixed before listed. A team is listed only after its auditor confirms every critical and high finding is fixed.
3. Human-led audits. Only human-led, crypto-specific OpSec audits earn a listing; an automated or AI-only scan, or a generic SOC 2 or ISO 27001 report, never does.
4. Open and tool-agnostic. Any rules under CC BY 4.0, board code under MIT, and a listing is reachable with any tools or vendors.
5. Listings expire. A listing lasts at most 12 months and is suspended on a disclosed incident or material change until the team is re-audited.
6. Built to last. The coalition and board keep running after the final milestone on money other than TheDAO's, with a maintenance plan in the bid.
7. **Neutral coordinator.** The coordinator is not an OpSec audit firm, because whoever runs the coalition would gain an edge over the firms it convened.

initiatives.summary: Every team says it takes OpSec seriously, but nobody can check. This RFP funds a neutral coordinator to get at least 4 OpSec audit firms working together, so more teams get OpSec audits and fix what they find, with a public board of the teams that did (every gap stays private). Then the list gets teeth: protocols, bridges, L2s, wallets and exchanges make a current listing on the board a condition of doing business.

sections.heading: Why this matters
sections.markdown: The signing interface is itself part of the security boundary. In the February 2025 Bybit incident, compromised Safe infrastructure presented signers with a benign-looking operation while malicious transaction data changed control of the wallet; about $1.46 billion was stolen (https://www.a16zcrypto.com/posts/article/bybit-hack-lessons). Hardware wallets protect keys, but they cannot protect a user who authorizes a malicious effect they cannot independently understand. colibri can simulate locally on verified state, independent of the dApp or RPC that constructed the transaction. This grant makes that independent check enforceable before signing and deploys it in real signing flows.

sections.heading: The team
sections.markdown:
corpus.core (Germany) does the work.
- **Simon Jentzsch, Chief Architect.** Worked on TheDAO (2016), co-founder of slock.it, built the Universal Sharing Network and Incubed (IN3), the first minimal verification client for Ethereum. Co-author of EIP-1186 (eth_getProof), the Merkle-proof standard most Ethereum light clients use for state verification.
- **Steffen Kux, Vision & Product.** Head of the project business at slock.it from 2017, with industrial clients such as Siemens and Energy Web Foundation. Worked on Incubed, CEO of dm3, Co-founder of corpus.ventures.
- **Jork Leonhardt, Business & Ecosystem.** COO at slock.it, co-founder of Tokenize.it and corpus.ventures.
Track record: colibri has been in production since November 2025 and is integrated in the Ethereum Foundation's Kohaku wallet SDK, the Freedom browser, Ambire and beel.com (formerly Tokenize.it).

https://github.com/corpus-core/colibri-stateless
https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-1186

sections.heading: Why a grant: what already exists
sections.markdown: colibri already executes eth_call locally on verified state. A transaction-security prototype runs on top of it: local simulation and evaluation by a small local model, fully in the browser, already integrated in the Kohaku wallet SDK (https://github.com/ethereum/kohaku-extension/tree/HEAD/src/web/modules/sign-account-op/components/ColibriSimulationResult). This grant turns the prototype into an open foundation: structured effects, a deterministic rule engine, a wallet-facing policy interface and test vectors. A team starting from scratch would first need a client that verifies state locally, because a simulation on unverified data inherits the same trust problem.

sections.heading: In scope
sections.markdown:
- Local transaction simulation on verified state. 
- Structured effect extraction: token transfers, approvals, NFT movements, balance changes, ownership and upgrade changes, reverts. 
- A baseline deterministic rule engine with an extensible rule and policy interface. 
- A machine-readable result that wallets use to block, warn or require extra confirmation, demonstrated in a reference signing flow.
 - An open interface for local explanation components, with a reference integration of a local model. Security decisions never depend on the model, and transaction data never goes to a hosted LLM. 
- Reproducible test vectors for normal, suspicious and malicious transactions. 
- Integration support for wallets and signing tools adopting it.

sections.heading: Out of scope
sections.markdown:
- Advanced commercial transaction-security capabilities: domain-specific language models, model weights, training data, specialized analyzers and rule sets, threat intelligence. corpus.core may license these separately. 
- Training custom models. The reference integration uses an existing local model runtime. 
- Hosted or managed services. 
- The verification core, new chains, general dApp integrations and PAP. Companion initiatives cover them.

sections.heading: Commitments
sections.markdown:
- **License:** local simulation, effect extraction, the baseline rule engine, the policy and explanation interfaces, the reference integrations and the test vectors are released under an OSI-approved open-source license. Commercial extensions built on top are not covered. 
- **Maintenance:** corpus.core maintains the open foundation after the grant, funded by commercial transaction-security products built on it. 
- **Pinned targets:** at least 5 new wallets or signing tools show colibri’s verified simulation results in their production signing; at least 2 from the list in the adoption milestone or teams whose multisig governs over $100 million onchain.
- **Exception requested:** a merged upstream pull request counts toward the target when the integrating team's own release schedule delays production use.

initiatives.summary: A secure key does not help when the signer is shown one transaction and authorizes another effect. The Bybit attack demonstrated the scale of this failure mode. This grant turns colibri's verified local simulation into an open pre-sign security layer: independently reconstruct transaction effects from cryptographically verified state, apply deterministic security policies, and return machine-readable block/warn/confirm decisions that wallets can enforce before signing. The result must ship in at least 5 production signing flows.
