sections.heading: Why this matters
sections.markdown:
Most exploits drain a protocol over several transactions, across minutes or hours. The funds still in the contract after the first transaction can be rescued, but only by someone who sees the attack at once, understands the bug fast enough to reuse it defensively, and has legal cover to do it. That almost never happens. The SEAL whitehat rescue list records 25 rescues worth about $80.7M since 2022, and only 5 of them were done under Safe Harbor, although 33 protocols holding $60.7B have adopted it (safeharbor.securityalliance.org). Whitehats hold back because reusing the attacker's path is legal risk, and because nobody runs rescue capacity as a standing service.

Who is safer: users of Safe Harbor adopters on Ethereum mainnet, Arbitrum One, OP Mainnet and Base (Aave, Lido, Sky, Uniswap, Pendle, Euler, Balancer, Polymarket and 25 others). From what: an exploit in progress, while part of the funds is still in the contract. What anyone can point to afterwards: at least 5 adopters that verified their rescue playbook and know Defimon as a responder, a published benchmark of minutes from attack transaction to root cause, a public incident log, and, when an exploit hits an adopter, funds returned to its on-chain recovery address, confirmed by the protocol and by SEAL 911.

The money at stake, from the DefiLlama hacks dataset (api.llama.fi/hacks, pulled November 11, 2026; DeFi protocols on Ethereum mainnet or an Ethereum L2, centralized exchanges excluded):

- 2025: 70 incidents, $447M lost, of which 56 contract-level exploits worth $364M.
- 2026 to date: 130 incidents, $557M lost, of which 111 contract-level exploits worth $414M.
- Three Safe Harbor adopters were exploited in the last 12 months: Balancer V2 ($128M, November 2025), Makina ($4.2M, 2026, $3.4M returned under Safe Harbor), Lazy Summer ($6M, 2026).

How much of that is rescuable: Decurity reconstructed the per-transaction drain timelines of 10 multi-transaction exploits from 2022 to 2026 (rescue-window.decurity.io). In 6 of the 10, more than 80% of the funds at risk were still on the contract 5 minutes after the first attacker transaction, and 6 of the 10 drains lasted longer than an hour. Where a bot acted inside that window (Squid, Foom), 81% to 82% of the funds at risk came back the same day; where nobody did (CrossCurve, $2.76M), less than 1% came back.

Why the rescue has to be autonomous: 49% of vulnerable contracts are exploited within 30 days of deployment and 85% of vulnerable proxy implementations within 30 days of the upgrade (time-to-hack.decurity.io). Incidents are spread evenly across all four 6-hour blocks of the UTC day, so a human responder misses most of the 5-minute windows, and a playbook written once goes stale at the adopter's next upgrade.

sections.heading: The team
sections.markdown:
Decurity does the work. The rescue is fully autonomous: Defimon's agent detects the exploit, identifies the vulnerable function and the funds still at risk, and moves them to the protocol's registered recovery address from the playbook, so the protocol holds its funds again before anyone at Decurity is awake. People do the follow-up, none of it time-critical: notifying SEAL 911 and the protocol's security contact, the incident log entry, and KYC where the agreement requires it for the bounty. Arseniy Reutov, CTO and co-founder, leads the program (QuickNode case study: https://www.quicknode.com/blog/real-time-defi-exploit-detection). Arseniy holds an ETHSecurity Badge and will abstain from rating and ranking this initiative.

Public cases where Defimon rescued funds or warned the team before the drain:

- Foom.cash, February 26, 2026: $1.84M rescued on Ethereum and returned the same day; Foom.cash paid a 10% security fee:
    - https://defimon.xyz/blog/foom-cash-whitehat-rescue-february-2026
- Squid Router, April 7, 2026: $512K rescued:
    - https://x.com/DefimonAlerts/status/2041530294369386806
- Veil.cash: 2.025 ETH rescued
    - https://x.com/Veildotcash/status/2025293773891404225
- Secured.finance: alert 45 minutes before the hack
    - https://x.com/DefimonAlerts/status/2096855557575458950
- Ajna.finance: team alerted one hour before the hack
    - https://x.com/DefimonAlerts/status/2093632180656263283
- Guru.fund: team alerted before 85% of funds were drained
    - https://x.com/DefimonAlerts/status/2080679061265739844
- Olas.network, Yam.finance: governance takeovers reported
    - https://x.com/DefimonAlerts/status/2096432367908933790
    - https://x.com/DefimonAlerts/status/2095019159847313766
- Kpk.io: proxy backdoor reported
    - https://x.com/DefimonAlerts/status/2079618207569133651
- CPIMP: several projects notified
    - https://x.com/DefimonAlerts/status/2003167362829418679

No other funder pays for this scope. Defimon's paid feed ($200 per month) and Signals channel ($50 per month) fund detection today; nothing funds standing rescue capacity.

sections.heading: Why a grant: what already exists
sections.markdown:
Everything the grant extends is live:

- Detection on Ethereum, Arbitrum, Optimism, Base and Polygon with an LLM-verified confirmed-attacks stream and early detection of attacker contracts, proxy upgrades and malicious governance proposals.
- An AI agent that, given an attack transaction, identifies the vulnerable function and the balances still exposed, and executes the rescue. Measured on real incidents: Squid Router was rescued 4 minutes after the first attacker transaction, $512K of $623K at risk (82%); Foom.cash 16 minutes after the first exploit transaction landed on Base, which included recognizing the same flaw in the separate Ethereum deployment, $1.84M of $2.26M at risk (81%).
- The operational experience of those rescues. Foom.cash also showed the gap this grant closes: the protocol had no Safe Harbor terms, no recovery address and no responder it knew, so the return relied on goodwill on both sides.

The grant pays for the part nobody funds: per-adopter rescue readiness (registry data, recovery addresses verified with the protocol, pre-written rescue paths), benchmarking the root-cause agent, private transaction submission, legal review of the runbook against the Safe Harbor terms, and running the agent and its follow-up process for 12 months. A from-scratch build of detection plus rescue capacity would cost several times this budget.

sections.heading: In scope
sections.markdown:
- Covered chains: Ethereum mainnet, Arbitrum One, OP Mainnet and Base. These are the chains Defimon runs detection and rescue on today.
- A rescue playbook for every Safe Harbor adopter with at least $10M on a covered chain: recovery address and scoped assets read from the SafeHarborRegistry (0x326733493E143b8904716E7A64A9f4fb6A185a2c), bounty and identity terms, security contact, and a pre-written rescue execution path. A public index shows the terms; the execution paths stay private.
- Playbooks kept current: every implementation upgrade of an adopter's scoped contracts, which Defimon already detects, triggers a re-verification of that adopter's playbook within 7 days.
- Playbooks verified with the adopters themselves: recovery address, scoped contracts and security contact confirmed by the protocol, and Defimon introduced as a responder it should expect to hear from. Where an adopter's agreement requires Named identity (Aave, Sky, Euler, Balancer, Silo, Makina, Origin, Reserve and others), Decurity completes KYC and sanctions screening at payout, as the agreement requires.
- The root-cause agent benchmarked on replayed historic exploits, with the replay set and results published.
- Private transaction submission (Flashbots Protect or equivalent) and the go/no-go checklist from the SEAL Whitehat Rescue Guide: active or imminent exploit, independence from the attacker, net benefit, return within the agreement deadline, SEAL 911 notified.
- The rescue agent running against every covered adopter for 12 months, and a public incident log: every rescue-candidate event on an adopter is logged with acted or not acted, and why.
- Free rescue-grade alert feed for SEAL 911 members for the grant period.
- Outreach to protocols holding over $100M that have not adopted Safe Harbor, to add them to the registry.

sections.heading: Out of scope
sections.markdown:
- Rescues on protocols that have not adopted Safe Harbor. Those are legal risk for the whitehat; a legal destination for such funds is the subject of the separate RFP "An Open Bug Bounty Program for All of Ethereum: White Hat Rescued Funds Distribution Service" on this board.
- Initiating an exploit, acting on a known vulnerability before an attack starts, or bug bounty reporting. Rescues start only during an active or imminent exploit.
- Any chain other than Ethereum mainnet, Arbitrum One, OP Mainnet and Base. Defimon also runs detection on Polygon PoS, BNB Chain, Avalanche and Hyperliquid, and nothing on those chains counts toward any deliverable or milestone.
- Tracing or freezing funds the attacker already moved, and negotiating with attackers.

sections.heading: Commitments
sections.markdown:
- The rescue runbook, the adopter index, the replay benchmark set and the incident log are published under CC BY 4.0. The rescue execution tooling stays closed, because it would help attackers as much as defenders.
- Every rescue under this program returns funds to the protocol's registered recovery address within the agreement deadline and is reported in the public incident log. Decurity keeps only the bounty the agreement defines. Rescues are rewarded by Safe Harbor bounties, never by this grant.
- Decurity keeps the rescue agent running against every covered adopter for at least 12 months after the last milestone, paid from Safe Harbor bounties and feed revenue, at no further cost to the fund.
- Decurity staff, affiliates and Decurity's own contracts never count toward any milestone.

initiatives.summary: Defimon detects DeFi exploits in under a second and has returned over $2.5M to victims. This grant turns that into an autonomous rescue agent for the 33 protocols that adopted the SEAL Whitehat Safe Harbor: a rescue playbook per adopter, verified with the protocol, and an agent that identifies the root cause and the funds still at risk within minutes and moves the remaining funds straight to the protocol's registered recovery address, with no human in the loop. Safe Harbor bounties pay for running it after the grant.

sections.heading: Why this matters
sections.markdown:
Security review has shifted a great deal of effort onto LLM-assisted tooling over the last eighteen months. That shift has been productive and remains accessible to teams through frontier models and private tools, but it is also incomplete. They are weakest precisely where fuzzing is strongest, particularly on regression detection and avoidance as developers ship new or harden existing code.

**Current state:**

Many teams know the above, but very few run fuzzing continuously. The reasons are mostly operational:

- Compute: Meaningful fuzzing is measured in sustained core hours. Most teams cannot justify that as a standing line item for a single codebase, so it never gets budgeted.
- Time: Someone has to write harnesses that generate inputs structured enough to reach deep code rather than bouncing off input validation.
- Software: Teams that do try usually run a fuzzer in GitHub Actions or a similarly time-boxed CI runner, yielding a few minutes of fuzzing per commit. That is only enough to replay an existing corpus and generate suitable code coverage.

sections.heading: In scope
sections.markdown:
- A documented CLI or front-end UI
- Running continuous fuzzing campaigns across multiple tenants in a secure manner
- Ability to allocate compute across multiple projects and scale it up and down efficiently and on demand
- Capability to hand off harnesses, corpora, and knowledge to users
- Documentation so teams can maximally self-serve

**On the milestone plan:**

Amounts below are shown as a share of the awarded budget, with an indicative figure at a $150,000 award.

sections.heading: Out of scope
sections.markdown:
- Manual audits and code review. This program funds fuzzing infrastructure.
- Authorship of harnesses and tests
- Publishing exploit detail or proof-of-concept code for anything still unpatched
- A guaranteed bug count. Fuzzing finds what it finds; the commitment is to compute and process.
- Triage of findings
- Incident response
- Any other professional services

sections.heading: Existing work
sections.markdown: None named.

sections.heading: Who we expect to do this
sections.markdown:
The strongest bidder is a team that has run continuous fuzzing at scale before, over months rather than for the duration of an audit, and can show the following evidence: campaigns sustained, coverage figures, bugs found and disclosed. Proposals should be explicit about:

- Coverage of languages and frameworks
- Compute: State the sustained core hours you can field and where they come from
- User Experience: How does the user access the tool? Is it via service request only? A CLI? A dedicated User Interface? Briefly describe the user flow as it will exist should the grant be awarded.

The proposal will likely be best served by a single grant recipient, but the RFP can certainly be considered for multiple participants if that best serves the needs of the ecosystem.

sections.heading: Hard requirements
sections.markdown:
1. Aggregated results measured and published: Aggregate and abstracted statistics for coverage, findings, etc., updated at least quarterly on a public page. Bug counts alone are not an acceptable measure of a fuzzing program.
2. Siloed User Experience: Users may only see their own findings for security purposes. This must be available to be considered for the grant.
3. No user lock-in: Harnesses must build and run on standard open source fuzzing tooling. Every project keeps its harnesses, corpus, and documentation under an open license at no further cost, and must be able to keep running them without paying the grantee anything.

initiatives.summary: The Ethereum ecosystem is lacking a solution for scalable, continuous, and compute-intensive fuzzing campaigns for projects. For each project to subscribe to their own solution would be costly and could have diminishing returns over time to make it a worthwhile investment of time, money, and human capital. We are requesting proposals from applicants who have developed or can develop tools to orchestrate fuzzing at scale, assign compute resources efficiently, and flex these resources up and down in an agile manner so that any team can orchestrate their own fuzzing campaign for themselves. A self-serve model. This RFP would fund the construction and maintenance of such a tool.
initiatives.title: RFP: Community Fuzzing Tooling for Ethereum Ecosystem Projects

sections.heading: Why this matters
sections.markdown:
Every valid finding left unfixed waits for the next attacker to find it. Users are safer when someone both sides trust owns the job of getting it fixed.

- Bounties work where programs exist: [Immunefi](https://immunefi.com/) has paid researchers over $140M. Code with no bounty, no maintainer or a program that never answers has no such path.
- Without a broker we expect researchers to drop findings rather than chase unbountied teams, since a lone researcher asking for payment risks looking like an extortionist.

sections.heading: In scope
sections.markdown:
The goal: validated findings get fixed, including in unmaintained code, and researchers get paid, bounty or no bounty. Bidders have complete freedom in how they get there, including their own milestones, within the hard requirements below. This RFP is a starting point and will change; the final milestones are agreed with the selected team.

One possible approach, the one the milestones below follow:

- Build relationships with real bug hunters, validate their exploits, and take each finding to the owner with the full details and an offer to help fix it.
- Charge for it: fees from teams, a cut of researcher payments, commissions on bounty submissions it files and defends, or another model.
- Keep a working line to SEAL's war rooms for findings that turn into live attacks.
- Use the security contacts published under the companion security-contact RFP without depending on them.

sections.heading: Out of scope
sections.markdown:
- Bug hunting itself.
- Whitehat rescues of funds at risk ([separate RFP](https://initiatives.thedao.fund/initiative/an-open-bug-bounty-program-for-all-of-ethereum-white-hat-res) on this board).
- Bugs in shared code where several teams must fix together (the companion coordinated-patching RFP).

sections.heading: Existing work
sections.markdown:
- [Zero Day Initiative](https://www.zerodayinitiative.com/about/): Web2's trusted broker since 2005. It pays researchers, then gives the vendor the details and a 120-day deadline ([policy](https://www.zerodayinitiative.com/advisories/disclosure_policy/)).
- [SEAL 911](https://securityalliance.org/seal-911): a free emergency hotline that has coordinated over 200 war rooms for active or imminent incidents. The broker handles findings not under active exploit.

sections.heading: Who we expect to do this
sections.markdown:
An independent for-profit company: an audit firm with an AI bug-hunting pipeline, a bounty platform, or a new firm. The best pitch answers one question: why will researchers and teams both trust you? A clear connection to SEAL, whose war rooms bring together major security crews, is a strong plus. Nobody is pre-selected.

Drafted by TheDAO Security Fund from a conversation with EthSec (ethsecurity.org) and Consensys. Consensys Diligence may bid. A fix counts toward the milestones of only one initiative on this board. EthSec, TheDAO Security Fund and Giveth will not bid.

sections.heading: Hard requirements
sections.markdown:
1. **Disclosure never depends on payment.** The affected team receives the full finding at first contact, with no condition, before any payment request.
2. **Terms first.** Payment terms, the same for every team, are published before any team is contacted. A law firm's opinion on the model goes to the technical reviewer, with its summary published, before the first payment request.
3. A finding goes only to the teams that must fix it, never sold or licensed to anyone else.
4. Nothing about an unfixed finding is published, including which team is slow to respond.
5. Every finding is validated with a working proof of concept before any team is contacted.
6. Researchers may stay unnamed in public.
7. **Outside means unaffiliated:** no shared owner, staff or funding with the selected team. A payment or fix counts only when payer and researcher are also unaffiliated with each other, and each finding is a separate root cause.
8. Ethereum and L2 code only.
9. **A business that pays for itself.** The broker is a for-profit company that charges for its service, with a business model in the bid that covers its costs after the grant.

initiatives.summary: In the age of AI, team inboxes fill with junk bug reports, so whether a real bug gets fixed comes down to who sends it and whether the team trusts them. This RFP seeds a for-profit broker that builds relationships with real bug hunters and validates their exploits. It takes serious findings to teams across Ethereum that trust it, sees them fixed and the researcher paid, and lives on its fees.
initiatives.title: RFP: A Bug Broker That Gets Ethereum Bugs Fixed and Researchers Paid, Bounty or No Bounty

sections.heading: Why this matters
sections.markdown:
During an Ethereum security incident, time is a critical resource. Responders need to establish what happened, identify the affected assets, follow the funds, and prepare the evidence needed for their next action. Every manual handoff between logs, transaction views, attribution results, and investigation notes consumes part of that response window. Funds can move again while the team is still assembling its first coherent account.

This initiative funds an open-source module that reduces the work between receiving incident evidence and producing a verified response package. It connects off-chain evidence with Ethereum activity, reconstructs the attack timeline, maps supported fund movements, and flags transfers to attributed exchange addresses. The intended users are protocol and exchange security teams, incident-response firms, and law-enforcement investigators.

**Less time assembling evidence. More time to act on it.**

sections.heading: The team
sections.markdown:
The proposed recipient is the ForensIQ team, backed by HackenProof. The proposer reports an existing MVP with user and role management, case creation, file uploads, AI file analysis, and integrations with Crystal and Etherscan. These components provide a head start; the grant pays for the additional investigation module and its validation, not rebuilding the SaaS foundation.

The head start combines working ingestion and analysis components with existing blockchain integrations and access to prospective pilot users through HackenProof. Reuse should let the team spend the grant on cross-source reconstruction, response exports, and field validation. Before the agreement is finalized, a baseline demonstration and reuse inventory will make those savings checkable. The module is at MVP stage; measured investigation outcomes will come from the pilots.

HackenProof's existing relationships provide a route to pilot users. The proposer identifies law-enforcement partners in Ukraine and the Netherlands as intended first testers and plans to invite Hacken and other cybersecurity partners.

sections.heading: Why a grant: what already exists
sections.markdown:
[Crystal](https://crystalintelligence.com/crystal-expert-for-law-enforcement/) provides blockchain investigation capabilities, including fund tracing and case organization. These are substantial existing capabilities; neither timeline visualization nor transaction tracing alone is the novelty proposed here.

The proposed advance is an independently deployable, evidence-linked workflow connecting selected incident logs to Ethereum transfers and response preparation, evaluated against investigators' existing processes. The first milestone will document feature overlap, identify components worth reusing, and fix the specific workflow improvement to be tested.

sections.heading: In scope
sections.markdown:
- Ethereum mainnet, native ETH movements, and ERC-20 transfers; support for relevant execution traces must be documented against the selected data provider.
- Two or three log formats chosen with pilot users during the first month, plus supporting file evidence with stable source references.
- A shared timeline with normalized timestamps, original timestamps retained, and explicit handling of unknown time zones or uncertain ordering.
- Fund-flow views linking transfers to transaction hashes and addresses, with documented tracing assumptions.
- Crystal attribution integration and Etherscan transaction-data integration, with documented access requirements.
- Incremental case updates and configurable polling alerts for supported transfers to addresses attributed to exchanges, including source, retrieval time, and uncertainty. Provider delays and polling intervals are visible.
- Evidence-linked attack hypotheses, human-reviewed containment recommendations for agreed scenarios, and an exportable investigation package. Exchange action remains at the recipient exchange's discretion.
- Standalone deployment, public documentation, reproducible test fixtures, and independent pilot evaluation.

**What this pays for:**

Consider an illustrative investigation: a team provides access logs, incident files, and suspicious transaction hashes. The module places relevant events on one timeline, links each finding to its source, traces supported transfers, and checks available address attribution. If funds reach an address attributed to an exchange, the investigator gets an alert and an evidence package to review for an escalation request. The team can start reviewing supported findings while the broader investigation continues.

The funded contribution is the connection between those steps: evidence normalization, traceable correlations, incremental updates, and a consistent response export. Existing blockchain intelligence supplies attribution. AI helps organize evidence and propose explanations; an investigator verifies conclusions and chooses actions. Recommendations will cover a small set of incident scenarios agreed with pilot users, rather than promise a reliable diagnosis for every attack.

Success means shorter time to a verified timeline and a usable escalation package, with correctness measured alongside speed. Pilot results will establish whether and where the module saves time; no improvement percentage is claimed in advance.

The open-source core will ingest supported logs and supplied Ethereum data, produce timelines and fund-flow views, and export evidence without a ForensIQ account. Commercial attribution is an optional enrichment using the operator's own credentials. Without it, exchange identity can remain unknown. Public fixtures allow the complete workflow to be evaluated without purchasing third-party access.

**On the milestone plan:**

The six-month plan allocates roughly four months to development and two to pilots and refinement. Pilot recruitment and data-access arrangements start in month one. The proposed cost basis is $120,000 for team work ($20,000 per month), $10,000 for infrastructure and external services, and $5,000 for independent review, all included in the milestone amounts. Team work covers backend and data integration, AI/evidence analysis, investigator-led validation, and pilot delivery. Staffing allocations will be fixed in the final plan; these figures do not imply four full-time hires. Service costs and reviewer fees must be validated before contracting. Payments are tied to acceptance, not monthly payroll.

sections.heading: Out of scope
sections.markdown:
- Other chains and L2s, cross-chain bridge tracing, and claims to resolve movement through mixers.
- A proprietary address-labeling database or redistribution of third-party data without permission.
- Universal log ingestion, autonomous remediation, automatic freeze-request submission, or guaranteed recovery.

sections.heading: Commitments
sections.markdown:
1. **Open source and independently usable.** All code developed for the funded module is released under an OSI-approved license. The license is fixed in the agreement. No paid ForensIQ account is required, and necessary reused dependencies must permit standalone distribution.
2. **Evidence before conclusions.** Findings include source references. Observations, hypotheses, and attribution are distinguishable. Missing evidence and unresolved paths remain visible.
3. **Safe handling of case material.** Deployment documentation explains where data is processed, external-provider access, and retention settings. External AI processing requires explicit configuration. Untrusted file contents cannot trigger external actions.
4. **Reproducible acceptance.** Public fixtures, commands, expected outputs, and evaluation reports let an independent reviewer reproduce the core workflow. Sensitive investigation materials are not published.
5. **Independent adoption.** At least three external teams use the module on investigation material and publicly confirm use, or authorize a named independent reviewer to confirm use publicly with identifying details omitted. Attendance at a demo does not count.
6. **Maintenance.** ForensIQ maintains the module for at least 12 months after completion of the pilot phase, covering bug fixes, security updates, and integration compatibility. HackenProof's own budget backs this commitment. Future grants may support expansion but are not a condition of maintenance.

**Note on the adoption milestone**

Public confirmations disclose no sensitive evidence. Participation and publication arrangements must be agreed with pilot teams. Private cases can use the independent attestation route; other qualified teams can also satisfy the criteria. The independent reviewer must be able to verify that the three teams are distinct and external to the recipient. The final milestone accounts for approximately 37% of the budget.

initiatives.summary: ForensIQ is building an open-source module that connects off-chain incident evidence (logs, files, transaction hashes) with Ethereum activity to reconstruct attack timelines, trace fund flows, and flag transfers to attributed exchange addresses. It replaces the manual handoffs between logs, block explorers, and attribution tools with one evidence-linked workflow that produces a verified response package faster. The grant funds the missing connective layer on top of ForensIQ's existing MVP (case management, Crystal and Etherscan integrations), not a rebuild of the platform. Success is measured through pilots with protocol, exchange, and law-enforcement investigators, tracking time to a verified timeline and correctness rather than a promised percentage improvement.

sections.heading: Why this matters
sections.markdown:
Exploited contracts do not stop draining when the news cycle ends. Radiant Capital's lending pools on Arbitrum and BNB Chain were taken over in October 2024, and the attacker's implementation is still installed. It still calls transferFrom on wallets with open approvals: about 2,200 wallets were drained in 2025 and about 170 more in 2026 through September 13, all to one receiver address (0x070ca92f568037d351666b3918a0f6ba7ad20ed1), with the latest drain two days before this was written. Radiant's DAO scoped these approval losses at $7.7M for 2024 and $1.2M for the first quarter of 2025 and did not compensate them. Revoking is the only protection those wallets have.

The same pattern repeats at every scale. Multichain disclosed a router bug on January 18, 2022 and asked users to revoke; the first drain came 16 hours later, and a month on 3,101 of 7,962 affected addresses still had not revoked (Multichain post-mortem). During that incident Multichain built an ad-hoc approval-revoke API that SushiSwap, SpookySwap and AAVE integrated to warn users. Multichain is gone and nothing replaced it. In January 2026 SwapNet drained $13.43M from 18 Matcha users, 17 of them in the 45 minutes between the first attack and the pause (Matcha post-mortem).

Today a user learns they are exposed only by opening the Revoke.cash page for that exploit, one chain at a time. Wallets and explorers have no data source to warn their own users. After this initiative, any wallet can tell a user "you are still approved to exploit X on chain Y" the moment they open it, and anyone can check the ecosystem-wide numbers.

sections.heading: The team
sections.markdown:
**Rosco Kalis** does the work. He created Revoke.cash in 2019 as the first token approval management tool and has worked on it full-time since 2022, growing it to 100+ networks, NFT and Permit2 support, batch revoking, and the exploit checker. He maintains the public exploit list and the spender data this initiative builds on. Revoke.cash received Optimism RetroPGF funding and is the tool protocols point their users to after an incident, most recently in Matcha's SwapNet post-mortem.

Track record: https://github.com/rkalis, https://x.com/RoscoKalis, https://revoke.cash/about.

No other funder pays for this scope. The Optimism Foundation and the Monad Foundation sponsor batch revoke fees on their chains, which is unrelated to this work.

sections.heading: Why this matters
sections.markdown:
A Safe is a contract on Ethereum. Its owners and threshold are on-chain, and anyone can execute a transaction once it carries enough owner signatures to meet the threshold. In the standard flow, everything before that step happens off-chain, through the hosted Safe{Wallet} frontend that Safe Labs operates and the Safe Transaction Service behind it. Self-hosting that stack means running the Client Gateway, the Transaction Service and a tracing archive node for internal-transaction indexing, so few teams do.

In July 2024, WazirX lost roughly $235M from a Safe multisig managed through Liminal Custody, whose interface showed a routine transfer while the signatures authorized a malicious contract upgrade. In October 2024, malware on the computers of Radiant Capital's signers showed a clean transaction while their hardware wallets received different calldata; the signers signed blind instead of checking the domain and message hash on the device, and lost roughly $50M. In February 2025, malicious JavaScript in the hosted Safe{Wallet} frontend showed Bybit's signers one transaction while their hardware wallets signed another, and roughly $1.5B left the Safe. These incidents are different manifestations of the same underlying problem: the software presenting a transaction to a signer cannot be treated as a trusted part of the signing boundary.

Assume Safe's hosted frontend and Transaction Service disappear tomorrow. A non-technical multisig signer should still be able to:

- open this UI from a local copy or the IPFS release
- connect a hardware wallet
- rebuild the transaction from the Safe's on-chain state (owners, threshold, nonce, contract version) and the parameters they were sent, then recompute its hashes locally
- verify exactly what they are signing
- exchange signatures with the other owners through ordinary files or links
- execute the transaction using only a JSON-RPC endpoint

No Safe account, Safe backend, project-operated server, indexer or technical help required. That is Vitalik's walkaway test.

sections.heading: In scope
sections.markdown:
This RFP pays for finishing, hardening and maintaining a local-first Safe UI with minimal dependencies and trivial deployment. Optimise for the least technical signer rather than the developer running the UI. Deliverables:

- Ethereum Mainnet, Safe contract versions v1.3.0 and v1.4.1 at minimum
- Production hardening of an existing codebase, or a fresh build
- The full lifecycle against one standard JSON-RPC endpoint: load a Safe from chain state, propose, sign, exchange signatures, execute, manage owners and threshold, arbitrary contract calls
- Signature exchange without a server: signed transaction packages exported and imported through ordinary files or shareable links, with nested Safe (EIP-1271) support and approveHash as the on-chain alternative
- Verification: enter or import a transaction's full SafeTx parameters and recompute the EIP-712 domain hash, message hash and safeTxHash locally, with calldata decoded offline from a bundled selector database or a user-supplied ABI
- Hardware wallet signing on Ledger and Trezor at minimum, over WebUSB or WebHID or through a vendor library bundled with the app
- A command-line tool or local API that returns the hashes and decoded calldata for a given Safe address, chain ID and transaction parameters, for scripts and AI agents
- Reproducible IPFS builds with fixed import settings, an ENS name whose contenthash resolves to the current release, and docs for running locally and verifying a build
- 12 months of maintenance after the first tagged release (expected within 3 months of funding), and a business plan for the years after

sections.heading: Out of scope
sections.markdown:
- Full Safe{Wallet} parity (Safe Apps, swaps, staking, onramps)
- Hosted backends or indexers, including a team-run web server for this UI (the IPFS and ENS release is in scope)
- Chains beyond Ethereum Mainnet
- Mobile apps
- New smart contracts

sections.heading: Existing work
sections.markdown:
- [localsafe.eth](https://github.com/Cyfrin/localsafe.eth) (Cyfrin, MIT), live at [localsafe.eth.limo](https://localsafe.eth.limo). Its README calls it "still a project in early development": Safe v1.4.1 only, no transaction history; last release v0.3.1, June 18, 2026.
- [Eternal Safe](https://github.com/eternalsafe/wallet) (GPL-3.0), a Safe{Wallet} fork (app v1.26.2) that needs only an RPC URL. Received a Safe Grants Program grant; maintained by Devan Non; signature "smart links" are encoded rather than encrypted; v1.4.1 by default.
- [Safe's own monorepo](https://github.com/safe-global/safe-wallet-monorepo) (GPL-3.0). Self-hosting it means the [Client Gateway](https://github.com/safe-global/safe-client-gateway), the [Transaction Service](https://github.com/safe-global/safe-transaction-service) and a tracing archive node ([Safe docs](https://docs.safe.global/core-api/api-overview)).
- Hash-verification tools: [safe-tx-hashes-util](https://github.com/pcaversaccio/safe-tx-hashes-util), [OpenZeppelin Safe Utils](https://github.com/OpenZeppelin/safe-utils), [Cyfrin safe-hash](https://tools.cyfrin.io/safe-hash). They verify hashes only.

A bid built on another codebase should show it meets these hard requirements with fewer runtime dependencies.

sections.heading: Who we expect to do this
sections.markdown:
Nobody is pre-selected. Teams that have already shipped Safe frontends or signing tools, including the people behind localsafe.eth and Eternal Safe, will be judged on that record, and the budget is $120,000 either way. Safe contributors are welcome to bid or to co-fund.

Co-drafted by Griff Green and pcaversaccio, both Curators of TheDAO Security Fund. pcaversaccio maintains [safe-tx-hashes-util](https://github.com/pcaversaccio/safe-tx-hashes-util), listed above.

sections.heading: Hard requirements
sections.markdown:
1. **Open source.** An OSI-approved license, MIT or GPL-3.0 expected, and a public repository from the first commit of funded work.
2. **RPC only, nothing project-operated.** Every flow works against a standard JSON-RPC endpoint. Runtime dependencies are minimised, with no dependency on a hosted SaaS, proprietary API, mandatory backend, indexer, telemetry service, analytics provider or project-operated infrastructure, and no analytics or telemetry in the UI.
3. **Signature exchange without a server.** Signed transaction packages export and import through ordinary files or shareable links. Imported signatures are checked against the transaction's safeTxHash and the Safe's current owner set before they are accepted: signature recovery for EOA owners, an isValidSignature call for contract owners. Off-chain signatures work for nested Safes through EIP-1271, and on-chain approval through approveHash is supported as an alternative.
4. **Hardware wallets.** Ledger and Trezor at minimum, over WebUSB or WebHID or through a bundled vendor library. Before signing, the UI shows the EIP-712 domain hash, message hash and safeTxHash. The device shows the domain hash and the message hash, and the signer matches those against the UI and an independent hash tool. Vendor libraries are bundled and served with the app, with no popup, iframe or metadata fetched from a vendor's servers and no separate bridge daemon to install.
5. **Undecodable calldata stays unverified.** Calldata the UI cannot decode is shown as raw bytes with an unverified label, never as safe to sign.
6. **Verifiable builds.** Reproducible from a tagged commit to the published IPFS CID with fixed import settings, by an unaffiliated user without the team's infrastructure; the ENS contenthash resolves to the current release.
7. **Trivial deployment.** Open a local copy or the IPFS release, connect a hardware wallet, and work. Nothing to install beyond that.
8. **A maintenance and business plan in the proposal.** Who maintains the UI for the 12 months after the first tagged release, and how it is paid for after that.
9. **Public evidence for every milestone.** Recordings, transaction hashes, CIDs, test runs and named parties confirming, all published.

sections.heading: Why this matters
sections.markdown:
**ValOS is currently the only open-source standard for Ethereum validator operational security.** Other industry standards exist, but they restrict how people can use, modify or build upon them.

ValOS is free for anyone to adopt, adapt and extend, including for commercial use. This makes security controls accessible to more operators, while allowing auditors, monitoring platforms, ratings providers and other security companies to build their own tools and services to assess, monitor and improve infrastructure security.

**The ValOS standard has already been developed and gone through two rounds of updates and improvements. The next step is adoption.** The priority now is to put this work into practice, with organisations implementing security controls in their day-to-day operations to reduce risks, prevent failures and improve Ethereum infrastructure resilience.

**VOAP brings the same openness to adoption.** It helps operators implement ValOS security controls and security providers independently assess, monitor and support those practices. Together, they help ensure security improvements are not just documented, but implemented and maintained over time.

The programme will openly share adoption approaches, progress, challenges and lessons learned, while protecting confidential and security-sensitive information.

**Each adoption makes the next one easier.** Others can learn from what works, reuse proven security practices and build on previous work instead of starting from scratch. This allows security improvements made by one organisation to benefit others across Ethereum.

As more organisations adopt ValOS, their practical experience can also help improve the standard, keeping its security controls relevant as Ethereum infrastructure and risks evolve.

**The goal is not simply to have an open security standard, but to put it to work — building an open, community-driven security ecosystem where more operators implement stronger security controls, independent providers help maintain them, and shared learning makes Ethereum infrastructure safer and more resilient.**

sections.heading: The team
sections.markdown:
**[Lionscraft](https://www.lionscraft.io/) has been the lead contributor, coordinator and maintainer of D.U.C.K. and subsequently ValOS since the initiative began in 2023.** Over nearly three years, Lionscraft has led the development, publication and ongoing improvement of the standard, its security controls, tools and best practices.

The initiative has involved contributions from 20 organisations across Ethereum staking, node operations, cybersecurity, risk and assurance. Lionscraft coordinated their participation, bringing together organisations with different expertise and levels of involvement. Some were major contributors to the standard and its supporting resources, while others provided specialist input, reviewed specific sections or contributed to individual controls and practices.

This experience is directly relevant to VOAP. Lionscraft has already demonstrated its ability to coordinate diverse independent organisations around a shared, open-source security framework, manage contributions and turn that collaboration into published outputs. **VOAP builds on this experience, shifting the focus from developing ValOS to driving its adoption across the Ethereum ecosystem.**

sections.heading: Why a grant: what already exists
sections.markdown:
**ValOS is the result of nearly three years of development and industry collaboration, originally initiated and funded through Lido.**

Beginning with D.U.C.K. in November 2023, the initiative evolved through two phases of development, delivering an open-source security standard, risk and controls framework, assessment resources, toolkits and best practices for Ethereum validator operations. The full ValOS standard launched in September 2026.

The work has already delivered:

- **An open-source standard:** Published security risks, controls, mitigation practices and assessment guidance, available for anyone to use, adapt and extend.
- **Tools and best practices:** Existing resources that support operators in assessing and improving their security and resilience.
- **Industry collaboration:** Contributions from 20 organisations across staking operations, exchanges, cybersecurity, risk and assurance.
- **An independent assessment pathway:** Qualified third-party assessors can evaluate operators against ValOS. Lido will also subsidise part of the assessment costs for four early-adopter node operators.

With the standard, toolkits and best practices now established, the next phase is accelerating adoption across the wider Ethereum ecosystem.

VOAP will leverage existing resources, relationships and adoption pathways to minimise programme overhead and concentrate resources on real-world implementation. Of the $78,000 funding request, $34,000 is directly contingent upon independently verified operational adoption outcomes.

**Public documentation and prior work:** The initiative's development history is documented in the [original D.U.C.K. proposal on Lido Research](https://research.lido.fi/t/d-u-c-k-distributed-utilization-of-configurations-and-knowledge-proposal/5848), with its first published framework available in the [D.U.C.K. Knowledge Base](https://duck-initiative.gitbook.io/d.u.c.k.-knowledge-base). The subsequent development phase is documented in the [ValOS governance, assurance and adoption proposal](https://research.lido.fi/t/strengthen-d-u-c-k-governance-assurance-and-real-world-adoption/9849/4). Lido's continuing support for independent assessments is documented in the [early-adopter assessment subsidy proposal](https://research.lido.fi/t/proposal-funding-request-for-valos-early-adopter-assessment-subsidies/10657). The resulting open-source standard and its development history are available in the [ValOS GitHub repository](https://github.com/lidofinance/valos).

sections.heading: In scope
sections.markdown:
VOAP will deliver a coordinated, open adoption programme across Ethereum's staking and security and assurance ecosystems.

The programme will identify and develop adoption opportunities, recruit prospective adopters, facilitate ValOS integration into existing operations, products and services, and drive the ongoing application of security and resilience practices.

VOAP will prioritise adoption opportunities with credible implementation pathways, meaningful security benefits and the potential for wider ecosystem adoption.

The work is organised into three areas.

**1. Staking Ecosystem: Implementing ValOS in Validator Operations**

VOAP will drive adoption among infrastructure operators and staking organisations through two pathways:

- **Self-assessment:** Recruit and support operators to assess their security practices against ValOS, identify gaps, apply relevant controls and declare their alignment with the standard, without requiring paid third-party certification.
- **Independent assessment:** Connect operators with qualified external assurance providers and facilitate access to ValOS-based independent assessments.

VOAP will target operators of different sizes and staking affiliations, supporting adoption across the wider Ethereum staking ecosystem.

VOAP will also selectively engage staking protocols, pools and institutional stakers where there are credible opportunities to incorporate ValOS assurance evidence into operator selection, oversight and incentives.

The objective is to embed ValOS into how Ethereum staking organisations assess, manage and continuously improve their operational security and resilience.

**2. Security & Assurance Ecosystem: Integrating ValOS into Security Services**

VOAP will drive adoption among organisations that assess, secure, monitor and support Ethereum validator infrastructure. Potential adoption areas include:

- **Assurance & certification:** Integrate ValOS into independent security assessments, certification, control verification and ongoing assurance.
- **Ratings & risk intelligence:** Incorporate ValOS into validator security ratings, operator evaluations and risk analytics.
- **Security monitoring & detection:** Use ValOS risks and controls in monitoring, alerting and ongoing security oversight.
- **Infrastructure security technologies:** Build upon ValOS in validator security tooling, key management, distributed validator technology (DVT) and infrastructure protection services.
- **Incident response & resilience:** Incorporate ValOS into incident preparedness, response, recovery testing and operational resilience services.
- **Financial security & risk protection:** Use ValOS assurance evidence in underwriting, insurance, slashing protection and security-related risk decisions.

VOAP will prioritise integration opportunities based on their implementation feasibility, security impact and potential to extend the benefits of ValOS across multiple Ethereum infrastructure operators.

**Every VOAP-supported integration must address how security practices or assurance remain effective and relevant over time.** VOAP will make continuity a core requirement of its adoption partnerships, including suitable mechanisms for ongoing monitoring, periodic reviews, remediation follow-up or reassessment after material changes and incidents.

The specific mechanisms will be designed, implemented and maintained by the adopting organisations themselves.

The objective is to embed ValOS into the existing services and technologies that help Ethereum infrastructure prevent security failures, detect problems, respond, recover and improve.

**3. Open Adoption: Making Adoption Open, Collaborative and Reusable**

VOAP will operate as an **Open Adoption Programme**, allowing anyone in the Ethereum ecosystem to participate, propose adoption opportunities, contribute to integrations and build upon existing work.

VOAP will:

- **Maintain an open adoption register:** Publish opportunities, their proposed ValOS applications, progress, obstacles and next steps, so others can participate or pursue them independently.
- **Document adoption work as it happens:** Share outreach approaches, integration methods, decisions, outcomes and lessons learned, including unsuccessful efforts, while protecting confidential and security-sensitive information.
- **Publish reusable adoption resources:** Make non-confidential integration examples, practical guidance and relevant materials openly available so other organisations can adapt and extend them.
- **Enable community participation and continuity:** Allow external contributors to propose opportunities, contribute improvements and continue adoption efforts using existing ValOS infrastructure, without depending on Lionscraft.

**The result is an open, reusable body of adoption work that grows with each contribution.** Every adoption can make the next easier, while helping the Ethereum ecosystem independently expand, maintain and improve the use of ValOS.

sections.heading: Commitments
sections.markdown:
- **Operational security adoption:** Drive real-world implementation of ValOS security controls among Ethereum infrastructure operators and integration into existing security and assurance services.
- **Verifiable adoption:** Deliver at least 12 independently verifiable operational adoptions across 9 professional Ethereum node operators and 3 security and assurance providers.
- **Diverse adoption:** Achieve operational adoption across operators of different sizes and staking affiliations, including at least 4 operators with at least 10,000 ETH staked each, at least 3 operators with fewer than 10,000 ETH staked each, and at least 3 Lido node operators, as specified in the adoption milestones.
- **Outcome-based funding:** Allocate $34,000, representing 43.6% of the requested funding, directly to independently verified operational adoption milestones.
- **Open adoption:** Publicly document adoption opportunities, approaches, progress, outcomes and lessons learned, making non-confidential materials openly available for others to reuse and extend.
- **Security and resilience continuity:** Ensure VOAP-supported adoptions address how operational security controls, assessments and assurance will be maintained, reviewed and improved over time.
- **Independent verification:** Provide evidence of completed adoption milestones for independent review, while protecting confidential information and security-sensitive findings.
- **Long-term sustainability:** Enable adopting organisations to maintain their own implementations and allow the wider Ethereum community to continue adoption efforts through existing ValOS infrastructure, independently of Lionscraft.

initiatives.summary:
ValOS (Validator Operations Standard) is an open-source security standard, risk and controls framework, and collection of best practices for secure and resilient Ethereum node operations. Developed with contributors across staking operations, exchanges, risk, cybersecurity and assurance, ValOS evolved through two community releases, the first in 2024 and the full standard in Sep 2026.

The ValOS Operational Adoption Programme (VOAP) will drive adoption across two parts of the Ethereum ecosystem:
- Staking: Node operators and staking pools use ValOS to assess and improve operational security, while staking protocols use ValOS evidence in operator oversight and decisions.
- Security & Assurance: Auditors, ratings providers, monitoring platforms, risk providers, and other security parties incorporate ValOS into their existing security services and products.

Over 18 months, VOAP will coordinate these efforts, targeting 12 independently verifiable operational adoptions across 9 professional Ethereum node operators and 3 security and assurance providers, with mechanisms to maintain security and resilience over time.

Over 43% of the requested funding is directly contingent upon independently verified operational adoption outcomes.

sections.heading: Why this matters
sections.markdown:
Frameworks has significant ongoing maintenance costs and no monetization: practical security know-how stays free for every team. Research, source checks, technical review, updates and releases recur as the reference grows and becomes agent-readable. This grant funds that capacity.

A developer workstation, cloud account or compromised frontend can put users' funds at risk. Chainalysis recorded over $3.4 billion in crypto theft in 2025, including the $1.5 billion Bybit theft. Sygnia traced the attack from a compromised developer workstation through reused AWS sessions to altered JavaScript served from Safe's S3 bucket, leading signers to approve a disguised transaction.

The Nx s1ngularity attack used AI command-line tools to search developer machines for credentials; investigators reported over 2,000 exposed secrets and about 1,700 affected users. Funded sections address developer AI, infrastructure access and frontend delivery. Frameworks publishes machine-readable guidance, extending the reference to agents.

sections.heading: Why this matters
sections.markdown:
Users are safer when every team running a buggy piece of shared code is warned privately and patches before the fix is public. Today nobody holds that list.

- Geth shipped a pre-announced fix for CVE-2021-39137 ([advisory](https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-9856-9gg9-qcmq)) on August 24, 2021. Three days later it was exploited on mainnet, splitting off nodes that had not upgraded ([Geth postmortem](https://github.com/ethereum/go-ethereum/blob/master/docs/postmortems/2021-08-22-split-postmortem.md)).
- Vyper fixed a broken reentrancy lock in December 2021 without realizing its impact, so protocols on old versions were not explicitly notified ([Vyper](https://hackmd.io/@vyperlang/HJUgNMhs2)). In July 2023 attackers took $69.3M from pools compiled with them, $52M after returns ([CertiK](https://www.certik.com/resources/blog/2qbPMcyJpR5UfoKrcjWxlQ-vyper-incident-anaylsis)).
- In December 2023 an ERC-2771 and Multicall flaw affected thousands of contracts, and several pools holding almost 90 ETH were hacked before OpenZeppelin's full public disclosure ([OpenZeppelin](https://www.openzeppelin.com/news/secure-implementations-vulnerable-integrations)).
- In a 2024 study, a GPT-4 agent exploited 87% of 15 disclosed vulnerabilities when handed the public advisory, and 7% without it ([arXiv](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.08144)).

sections.heading: In scope
sections.markdown:
Bidders have complete freedom in how they get there, including their own milestones, within the hard requirements below. Each bid states a hypothesis and a plan of attack for three problems:

1. Who else has it: find who runs the vulnerable code (forks, deployments, chains, node operators) on Ethereum and its L2s.
2. A warning they trust: warn them privately, through a channel where each side can verify the other, so they act.
3. Going public in the age of AI: stage fixes so they land in public repositories without exposing the bug early, release them together, then push operators to update.

One possible approach, the one the milestones below follow: start by hand. The selected team runs real disclosures alongside the teams fixing each bug, races to reach every other affected team before the fix is public, then systematizes what worked. The target clock is 24 hours from bug confirmed to every affected team notified. Example hypothesis: a dependency map built before any bug lets one person list every affected team inside that clock. This RFP is a starting point and will change; the final milestones are agreed with the selected team.

The lasting output is an open, broad disclosure standard (process, comms templates, when and how to go public), informed by SEAL 911 and the cases run. Bugs can come from any source; bids say where. The selected team may use the security contacts published under the companion security-contact RFP and may pass researcher payment to the companion bug broker.

sections.heading: Out of scope
sections.markdown:
- Finding bugs.
- Whitehat rescues.
- Findings only one team must fix (the companion bug broker RFP).

sections.heading: Existing work
sections.markdown:
- [Microsoft Patch Tuesday](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/msrc/faqs-security-update-guide) and [Exploit Wednesday](https://www.manageengine.com/patch-management/exploit-wednesday.html), the day after.
- [SEAL 911](https://securityalliance.org/seal-911) handles live incidents; SEAL's [disclosure framework](https://frameworks.securityalliance.org/vulnerability-disclosure/overview) covers one affected project and tells teams to warn forks before publishing. Bids say whether their standard extends it.
- [linux-distros](https://oss-security.openwall.org/wiki/mailing-lists/distros): Linux distributions' private embargo list, 14 days at most.
- [CERT/CC VINCE](https://sei.cmu.edu/news/certcc-releases-vince-software-vulnerability-collaboration-platform): one shared case space for many vendors.
- [Ethereum Foundation public disclosures](https://github.com/ethereum/public-disclosures): the EF cross-checks client bug bounty reports and shares them with affected client teams.
- [Project Zero's Reporting Transparency trial](https://projectzero.google/2025/07/reporting-transparency.html) targets the "upstream patch gap".

sections.heading: Who we expect to do this
sections.markdown:
A team that client, rollup and protocol security leads already trust with embargoed information: a security alliance, an incident-response firm or a consortium of those leads. Nobody is pre-selected.

Drafted by TheDAO Security Fund from a conversation with EthSec (ethsecurity.org) and Consensys. EthSec, TheDAO Security Fund and Giveth will not bid.

sections.heading: Hard requirements
sections.markdown:
1. Bug details go only to verified contacts at teams that must act. Bids say how they verify them.
2. A public log records each coordinated disclosure after release (what, when confirmed, when each team was notified, share patched), never before.
3. The disclosure standard is published openly for anyone to use.
4. Running costs come from the L2s and protocols served, or from a named home that funds it. Client teams are not expected to pay.
5. **Outside means unaffiliated.** An outside team shares no owner, staff or funding relationship with the selected team. Affiliates count toward no criterion.
6. Ethereum and L2s only.

initiatives.summary: Ethereum is permissionless, so when a bug turns up in shared code nobody knows who else runs it or where. The best-known model for coordinated fixes is Microsoft's Patch Tuesday, one scheduled day a month, and the day after is known as Exploit Wednesday. With AI reading every patch, a scheduled day tells attackers when to look, and waiting for it leaves a known bug live. This RFP asks bidders how Ethereum should coordinate instead, and pays for hand-run disclosures first, then an open standard built from them.
initiatives.title: RFP: What Replaces Patch Tuesday? Coordinated Disclosure for Bugs Shared Across Ethereum

sections.heading: Why this matters
sections.markdown:
Depositors and lenders lose money when an asset they hold or accept as collateral fails, and nothing liquid or transparent prices that risk. Here, an asset defaults under Credora’s definition: holders cannot redeem it for 14 days, or its reserves fall 1% or more short for 7 days. A hack counts when it causes either.

On 18 April 2026, an attacker forged a cross-chain message on KelpDAO’s rsETH bridge, which relied on a single verifier, took [about $292 million](https://www.chainalysis.com/blog/kelpdao-bridge-exploit-april-2026/) of unbacked rsETH and borrowed real ETH against it, leaving Aave facing [$124 million to $230 million](https://www.coindesk.com/tech/2026/04/20/aave-could-face-up-to-usd230-million-in-losses-after-kelp-dao-bridge-exploit-triggers-defi-chaos) of bad debt. That verifier setting was readable on-chain: in an rsETH market, whoever noticed it could have been paid to price the risk higher, warning lenders and DeFi users before anything was lost.

A market pays for finding weaknesses: whoever spots a risk first profits by moving the price, and loses money if wrong. A protocol that reduces its risk sees its price fall, in public.

The price serves DeFi users comparing vaults before depositing, curators and lending protocols setting caps and collateral, insurers testing a rating’s probability of loss, and risk-scoring platforms, one of which has already asked to show it next to its own score.

sections.heading: The team
sections.markdown:
- [Clément](https://x.com/clesaege), Co-founder and CTO. Reviews the market mechanics.
- [0xAlex](https://x.com/alex__eth), Integration Lead. Leads this initiative.
- [JuanRah](https://x.com/JuanRah), Oracle Lead. Point of contact for this initiative.
- [Minh](https://github.com/nvm1410), Engineering, Seer. Builds the market and its interface.
- [Facundo](https://x.com/facundo_trotz), Legal. Drafts the default event rules that resolve the market.

Kleros and Seer pay the development costs; no other grant funds this work. Credora supplies the ratings.

sections.heading: Why a grant: what already exists
sections.markdown:
- The interface is live at [risk.seer.pm](https://risk.seer.pm) with its code in a [public repository](https://github.com/seer-pm/risk-pricing-ui).
- The mechanism is implemented. Each asset has a token paying out if it defaults, plus a "no default" token that pays out if no listed asset does.
- The interface shows Credora’s probability of default, fetched live through its API, next to the market’s, which moves with every trade.
- Seer and Kleros have run and settled markets with a similar stack. [Gitcoin's GG24 Deep Funding round](https://gov.gitcoin.co/t/deep-funding-gg24-web3-tooling-and-infra-round/25040) used Seer's markets to help allocate $350,000 across 98 open-source repositories.
- The user guides are [written and public](https://jagged-ironclad-e1b.notion.site/Default-Risk-Prediction-Markets-Beginner-User-Guide-35da95a2cc7d80fba056c16d17e99303).
- The default event rules are being finalized. With vague rules, traders price the risk of a dispute instead of the risk of failure, so every edge case, such as a failure that starts in one quarter and is confirmed in the next, is settled before trading starts. Kleros Court jurors apply these rules when a payout is disputed.

sections.heading: In scope
sections.markdown:
A new market opens every quarter and asks which listed assets will default during that quarter, so a live price always exists and traders return each quarter. It lists 33 DeFi assets in 4 categories.

Liquidity is the hard part of any prediction market. The pool takes the other side of every trade, so when a better-informed trader moves the price, the pool has sold at the old price. A default costs most, because the pools sold that asset's default token cheaply before the news.

The grant asks $90,000 for liquidity. Each quarter's liquidity is deposited at the rating firm's probabilities, Credora's today, so no market opens at an exploitable price. Kleros Cooperative owns the positions and bears the impermanent loss.

In [Gitcoin's Deep Funding trial](https://gov.gitcoin.co/t/deep-funding-gg24-web3-tooling-and-infra-round/25040) on Seer, about 14% of $44,000 was lost this way, which the round's operators called "the cost to obtain information".

When each market settles, Kleros redeposits what remains in the next quarter's market, including after the program ends. The first milestone’s advance seeds the first quarter’s market with $15,000; the rest of the liquidity follows with the milestones, $20,000, $20,000 and $35,000, each deposited in the following quarter's market.

The grant also asks $10,000 for trading credits for DeFi risk teams and communities, vault curators, security researchers, and traders from earlier Seer markets, usable only in these risk markets.

Deliverables:
- An application to trade the probability of default of 33 DeFi assets, with the grant’s liquidity and trading credits deployed.
- A public API of current and historical market-implied probabilities that anyone can read without an account.
- A quarterly public report: each asset's opening and closing probability and whether it defaulted, plus volume, traders, cost of liquidity and every divergence from the rating, and what followed it.

sections.heading: Out of scope
sections.markdown: Producing initial ratings (Credora does), underwriting cover, or any claim that a listed asset is safe.

sections.heading: Commitments
sections.markdown:
- Grant funds go only to liquidity and trading credits.
- Kleros publishes its liquidity, trading and credits addresses, so third-party activity can be told apart on-chain.
- Kleros Cooperative maintains the markets, the public API and the report for 12 months after the final milestone at no further cost.
- The interface code is open source under the MIT license in its public repository.

initiatives.summary: A DeFi rating is one firm’s estimate of how likely an asset is to fail; the firm has no skin in the game, and nobody can take the other side. Seer prices that probability in an open prediction market, following Vitalik Buterin’s design for trading on many highly improbable events, and the result is a probability of default, free to read, so any lender or depositor can check it. The markets run on Ethereum Mainnet, open at Credora by RedStone's probability of default ratings and are settled by the Kleros oracle. They will also deploy on the Ethereum Economic Zone, a ZK rollup settling on Ethereum, once it is live.
initiatives.title: Kleros x Seer: Open Risk Pricing for DeFi, a Public Price for Default Risk

sections.heading: Why this matters
sections.markdown:
Depositors, liquidity providers and lenders on AMMs and lending markets lose money to economic logic bugs: rounding in the attacker's favour, an action that skips a health check, a share price moved by a donation, a flash loan that comes back short.

- **Euler** lost about $197 million in March 2023. A donation function skipped the health check, and the attacker then liquidated their own position ([Chainalysis](https://www.chainalysis.com/blog/euler-finance-flash-loan-attack/)).
- **Cream** lost about $130 million in October 2021 to collateral whose share price a donation had doubled ([Immunefi](https://immunefi.com/blog/bug-fix-reviews/hack-analysis-cream-finance-oct-2021/)).

Each protocol writes these checks from scratch, or skips them. Public property packs cover token standards ([crytic/properties](https://github.com/crytic/properties), [a16z/erc4626-tests](https://github.com/a16z/erc4626-tests)), not the economics of pools and markets. On this board, the Community Fuzzing RFP funds fuzzing infrastructure and the Echidna grant funds the engine; both put writing protocol invariants out of scope. This fills that gap: a team writes one adapter (10 functions for a pool, 15 for a market) and gets every property.

sections.heading: The team
sections.markdown:
- **Jean Rausis**, co-founder: serial entrepreneur and cybersecurity specialist with a background in ethical hacking, architect of the team's DEX designs and delta-neutral synthetic assets ([LinkedIn](https://www.linkedin.com/in/jeanrausis/))
- **Eric Rabl**, co-founder: EPFL-trained mathematician with a background in quantitative finance and algorithmic market making, leads protocol math ([LinkedIn](https://www.linkedin.com/in/eric-rabl-6708a570))

Both co-founded RA2 Capital. RA2 TECH SA (Montreux, Switzerland, registered since 2019) employs 25+ in-house engineers and researchers who build Everything (everything.inc), a DeFi protocol where lending, borrowing, leverage and swaps share a unified pool per asset pair, and the SmarDex ecosystem. Those engineers wrote and run the invariant suite this pack generalises.

RA2 has self-funded more than $20 million of R&D over five years. No other funder pays for this scope.

sections.heading: Why a grant: what already exists
sections.markdown:
- **The pack is built:** 37 properties across AMM pools (18), lending markets (17) and ERC-3156 flash lenders (2), MIT licensed. 24 generalise the invariant suite of Everything's UniPool v1 contracts; 13 are new. It already handles virtual-share markets (OpenZeppelin ERC-4626, Morpho Blue).
- **It is tested.** Three fuzz campaigns pass 16,384 calls each against reference pools. Five mutant contracts each carry one bug class (withdrawal rounding, redemption rounding, an unpaid flash fee, a flash loan repaid short, a missing health check). The fuzzer catches every one with no hints, within 35 calls, and CI checks both on every push.
- **It caught a bug nobody planted.** On its first run it flagged a stale `totalAssets` view in our own reference market, fixed before publishing.

This costs less than a from-scratch build because the property design, the adapter model and the mutant harness are finished. The money goes to the missing bug classes and to onboarding other teams.

sections.heading: In scope
sections.markdown:
- Position-based lending (Aave and Morpho style accounts) alongside loan-based markets
- Reference adapters for Uniswap V2, Morpho Blue and Euler V2, published in the repo and run in its CI
- New properties for the Euler and Cream classes: no user action leaves the caller's own position liquidatable, a donation cannot raise the value a market assigns to collateral, and a liquidatable position is always profitable to liquidate
- Echidna and Medusa entry points for every pack
- The money's main work: onboarding. An adapter guide, and hands-on help writing the adapter with each adopting team until it runs in their CI

sections.heading: Out of scope
sections.markdown:
- Auditing any protocol, or writing a protocol's full invariant suite beyond its adapter
- Fuzzing compute or hosting
- Formal verification
- Properties specific to Everything's design (virtual reserves, its vault routing), which stay in its private suite

sections.heading: Commitments
sections.markdown:
- All code, properties and adapters under MIT.
- We maintain the pack for 12 months after the last milestone at no further cost. Everything's own contracts run it in CI, so we keep it working for ourselves.
- Every new property ships with a seeded mutant that proves it fires.
- Pinned target: at least 6 outside protocol teams running the pack in their own CI.

initiatives.summary: Open-source invariant properties that check the economics of AMM pools, lending markets and flash lenders under fuzzing: no withdrawal above its share, no redemption rounding in the user's favour, no healthy loan liquidated, no flash loan repaid short. 37 properties already exist, and they catch five seeded bug classes with no hints. This grant adds the bug classes behind the Euler and Cream exploits, position-based markets and Echidna and Medusa support. Its largest milestone pays only when at least 6 outside protocol teams run the pack in their own CI.

sections.heading: Why this matters
sections.markdown:
Protocol users are safer from the second drain: the same exploit working again after the team says it is fixed.

- The Verus bridge on Ethereum lost about $11.5 million on 18 May 2026. Most of it was returned for a bounty and put back into the same bridge on 8 July. On 23 July it lost $7.54 million through the same contract path and bug class ([CoinDesk](https://www.coindesk.com/tech/2026/07/23/bitcoin-ethereum-linked-protocols-lose-usd35-million-in-multiple-attacks-hours-apart)).
- TRM Labs counted a record 207 hacks in the first half of 2026, 125 of them exploiting smart-contract code ([TRM Labs](https://www.trmlabs.com/resources/blog/h1-2026-crypto-hacks-reach-record-high-as-losses-fall-below-usd-1-billion)).

Verus is why a fix gets re-tested before the money goes back in.

sections.heading: The team
sections.markdown:
**Farseen Shaikh**, founder of SCAR AI, works on it full time (github.com/FarseenSh). In this fund's first round, SCAR received $6,275 (linked). Its open datasets, including a 231,269-contract Solidity corpus, have over 1,800 Hugging Face downloads (linked). SunSec (DeFiHackLabs) used SCAR's retrieval model in auditing and credited it with higher recall in a first-place OneSavie Bastet Kaggle entry (linked).

An independent reviewer, named in the grant agreement, signs off every case and milestone. No other funder pays for this scope; E2B and Daytona credits cover part of the compute.

sections.heading: Why a grant: what already exists
sections.markdown:
- **Fix Verifier** (Apache-2.0), with four test cases today (one Ethereum mainnet exploit, three on BNB Chain). It grades a fix on security checks its author never sees, plus normal-use checks, and CI re-grades every control fix.
- **48 published receipts** for control fixes we wrote to test the checker. 26 stop the replayed exploit, yet 15 of those still fail: they leave another path open or break normal use. A replay-only check passes all 15.
- **Revision checks**, previewed on four public OpenZeppelin and Safe changes: 10 of 10 valid versions accepted, 6 of 6 planted faults rejected.

What is thin: one test case from Ethereum mainnet, and no outside reviewer or user of the verifier yet. The harness, receipts and CI exist, so this is not a from-scratch build.

sections.heading: In scope
sections.markdown:
- **24 test cases built from past exploits** on Ethereum mainnet or L2s with over $200 million secured on L2BEAT, 16 public and 8 private until the scoreboard freezes. Each packages the real exploit on frozen chain state, the related attack paths, normal-use checks, a working reference fix and two faulty fixes (one incomplete, one that breaks normal use), so the checker is tested on known answers.
- **A workflow teams run themselves**: Foundry import, command line, CI job and coding-agent adapter.
- **A public scoreboard** grading AI agents' fixes on the private test cases.
- **Onboarding**: intake template, self-serve guide, and hands-on setup of the checks for each adopter's first two fixes (fork, exploit replay, normal-use checks, reviewer sign-off).

Cost basis: one founder full time for 7 months on engineering, case building, onboarding and support ($45,000), 110 reviewer hours at $175 ($19,250), 12 exploit reproductions from outside contributors at $500 ($6,000), archive RPC, hosting and compute ($8,000), tools and bounties ($4,500), contingency ($7,250).

sections.markdown:
- Proofs or whole-contract certification
- Build systems other than Foundry
- A hosted commercial service
- Retrieval and model-training research
- Chains other than Ethereum and its L2s

sections.heading: Commitments
sections.markdown:
- New code under Apache-2.0, case write-ups under CC BY 4.0; third-party material keeps its own terms.
- Farseen maintains the funded release for 6 months after the last milestone at no further cost; after that, revenue from paid checks and support pays for it.
- A verdict never says "safe" or "audited": it states what was replayed and checked, with inputs and a hash anyone can re-run.

- Private test cases are published after the scoreboard freezes, with a tagged release.
- Pinned target: at least 4 outside organizations using the check on 8 real fixes.

initiatives.summary: SCAR helps protocol teams and auditors check whether a smart-contract security fix blocks the known attack without breaking normal use. It replays the real exploit and its variants against the patched contract on a fork of Ethereum, checks normal use still works, and gives a verdict anyone can re-run before the fix ships or funds go back in. This grant pays for 24 test cases built from past Ethereum exploits, a public scoreboard that grades AI-written fixes on them, and four outside organizations using the check on eight real fixes of their own.
initiatives.title: SCAR: Test security fixes against the real exploit before they ship
