sections.heading: Why this matters
sections.markdown:
Ethereum nodes prune blob contents after 18 days by default, and with PeerDAS nodes sample availability without storing full blobs. Older blob data then lives only in a few archives.

Who is safer: users of rollups whose state can only be rebuilt and checked from blob data. From what: losing that data when a single archive fails. Base ($14.15B), Arbitrum One ($9.35B), OP Mainnet ($1.48B) and Mantle ($1.21B) alone secure about $26 billion, according to L2BEAT on 6 November 2026.

Rollup software already depends on these archives:

- **Optimism:** a node that syncs from data older than 18 days needs an archive source, and a fault-proof dispute over a block older than the retention window needs a blob archiver.
- **Arbitrum:** new nodes, and nodes back from a long time offline, need historical blob data.
- **Aztec:** its documentation points operators to archive services such as Blobscan.

Our own logs show the same. Between 7 October and 6 November 2026, 92% of the 3.9 million distinct blobs requested from Blobscan's API were older than 18 days, data Ethereum's own nodes had already deleted. Live nodes of at least three L2s read new blobs from it within the hour, and today all of that depends on a single node.

The archiver Optimism's documentation recommends, base/blob-archiver, was archived by its owner on Oct 9, 2026. Our endpoint serves the route op-node requests (`/eth/v1/beacon/blobs/{slot}`), so an operator can add it as a fallback beacon URL.

EthPandaOps also runs a blob archive endpoint. Both add resilience, and ours lets anyone keep their own copy.

sections.heading: The team
sections.markdown:
- **Paulo Colombo**: web3 developer, 6+ years, DAO tooling and dApp UIs (Gardens, EVMcrispr, TEC Hatch). https://github.com/PJColombo
- **Pablo Castellano**: senior DevOps engineer, 15+ years running scalable systems. https://github.com/PabloCastellano

EF funded the analytics workstream of the same Blobscan project; its Dagster pipeline also computes the archive-health metrics in this grant. No other funder pays for this scope. Blobscan is the team's own codebase.

sections.heading: Why a grant: what already exists
sections.markdown:
Built with the team's own funds:

- The Blobscan explorer and API are live: about 6.5M API requests a month, excluding retry loops, and about 1.2 TB served.
- An IPFS (Kubo) node runs in production. All mainnet blobs are migrated to it, the backend writes new blobs to it, and Blobscan users download blobs from it.
- The IPLD generator builds a deterministic DAG per epoch and exports CAR v2 archives: https://github.com/Blobscan/blobscan-ipld

That single node is the only copy today, so our own archive is a single point of failure. This grant fixes that first.

sections.heading: In scope
sections.markdown:
- Two more archive servers hosted by supporters in other locations, so every mainnet blob sits on three Blobscan-run nodes in different places
- A public CID registry with the network root published via IPNS, and a status page with archive-health metrics (pinned coverage per epoch, copies per blob) and a public alert when any blob falls below 3 copies
- A DAppNode package: independent operators pin the rollups and the disk space they choose
- A beacon-API-compatible blobs endpoint (`/eth/v1/beacon/blobs/{slot}`, `genesis`, `spec`) with a free rate-limited tier and paid tiers (API keys, quotas, x402 payments): an archive sync tier for history syncs, and a rollup node tier with an SLA, sold as an independent fallback next to a team's main beacon provider
- Paid full and custom CAR exports (by rollup or date range) over HTTP; the full mainnet archive is close to 3 TB
- Paid bulk metadata exports: per-rollup index, KZG commitments and decoded batch metadata
- Explorer decoders for Base, Arbitrum One (and Orbit chains such as Robinhood Chain), OP Mainnet and Mantle blobs
- Analytics: new blob metrics, dashboard and address pages (funded by EF)

sections.heading: Out of scope
sections.markdown:
- Gnosis Chain and any other non-Ethereum chain
- Mantle data from before its Arsia upgrade (16 April 2026), when it posted to EigenDA

sections.heading: Commitments
sections.markdown:
- Code stays AGPL-3.0.
- Each blob is stored as one raw IPFS block (CIDv1, sha2-256, the full 131,072 bytes), so its CID matches any other archive that stores blobs as raw blocks.
- The free tier, including the blobs endpoint at a rate limit, stays free. Any blob can also be fetched free from IPFS by its CID in the public registry.
- The Blobscan team maintains the archive, the blobs endpoint, the DAppNode package and the decoders after the last milestone, paid for by API tier revenue.

initiatives.summary: The blob archiver that Optimism's documentation recommends to rollup node operators was archived on Oct 9, 2026 and is no longer maintained, while Ethereum nodes prune blobs after 18 days. Blobscan already serves its full mainnet blob archive from IPFS. This grant adds three-node redundancy, lets community DAppNode operators pin copies, and serves the archive through the beacon blobs endpoint rollup nodes already call. It also decodes Base, Arbitrum One, OP Mainnet and Mantle blobs, and funds paid API tiers that cover the running cost.
initiatives.title: Blobscan: Decentralized Archive for Ethereum Blob Data

sections.heading: Why this matters
sections.markdown:
Clear Signing (ERC-7730) is the Ethereum standard for showing users a human-readable summary of what they are about to sign, instead of raw calldata. Descriptors for each contract live in the open registry at github.com/ethereum/clear-signing-erc7730-registry, and wallets read them. A wrong descriptor is worse than none: the user sees a confident summary that does not match what the contract does. The registry's own reviewing guide says its pull request review is a plausibility check, and that the trust layer is the signed attestation an auditor publishes after verifying the descriptor against the contract's source. Wallets choose which attesters to trust and can refuse to render a descriptor nobody has attested. Bybit lost about $1.5 billion in February 2025 after its signers approved a Safe transaction whose displayed contents differed from what they signed ([Bybit incident timeline](https://www.bybit.com/en/learn/this-week-in-bybit/bybit-security-incident-timeline), [NCC Group analysis](https://www.nccgroup.com/research/in-depth-technical-analysis-of-the-bybit-hack/)).

Attestation lags far behind authoring. On 2026-10-31 the registry had 739 descriptors and 166 attestations, all signed by one firm under Ethereum Foundation funding. Sourcify's live dashboard at erc7730.sourcify.dev ranks verified mainnet contracts by calls that are not plain ETH or standard token transfers: the top 100 carry 75% of those calls, 20 of them have a descriptor, and 0 of those descriptors are attested. Descriptor authoring for the rest is under way through the clear signing working group. Nobody is funded to verify and sign the result, and no second firm has put its name behind any descriptor.

sections.heading: In scope
sections.markdown:
This RFP pays one security firm for verification and signature. The firm's reputation is the deliverable: every attestation is published under the firm's own key and name.

- Review each descriptor for a target contract against the registry's auditor guide
- Publish an EAS offchain attestation (ERC-8176 schema) for each descriptor that passes, as a PR to the registry's sigs folder
- For each descriptor that fails, post the defects on the registry PR or as an issue, and attest the corrected version once it is merged
- For 12 months after each attestation, review every fix, addition or change to that contract's descriptor and re-attest it, or post the defects, within 30 days, so the registry's dropped-attestations list stays empty for this batch
- Migrate every attestation the firm has published to a new version of ERC-8176 or of the registry's attestation format within 60 days of the registry adopting it, during the engagement or the 12 months that follow, at no extra cost
- Publish a batch page: each target contract, its descriptor, review status, defects found, attestation UID and date

The target set is the top 100 verified contracts on erc7730.sourcify.dev by calls that are not filtered out (ETH, standard token transfers, closed source, bots etc) 7-day window, archived on the day the firm starts (based on final agreement with argot to allow for small manual fixes to the list). Descriptors for those contracts are written by others; the firm attests what exists and what lands during the engagement, and keeps reviewing what changes for 12 months after each attestation.

ERC-8176 is being reworked to be easier for developers to use, so a new version may land during the engagement.

The submitter is allowed to update the list (with consent from TheDAO at milestones after 30 contracts attested and 80 contracts attested).

sections.heading: Out of scope
sections.markdown:
- Writing descriptors. The firm does not attest a descriptor it authored.
- Contracts without verified source, and contracts outside the agreed list
- Wallet-side code, schema changes, registry tooling

sections.heading: Existing work
sections.markdown:
- The registry's auditor guide (auditors/README.md): the 5-step review, the ERC-8176 hash, the EAS schema, and the sigs folder format, built on the clearsig CLI (github.com/Cyfrin/clearsig)
- The 166 attestations already in the registry, as the format and bar to match
- Sourcify's clear-signing library, which lets a wallet name trusted attesters and fall back to raw calldata when no trusted attestation exists

sections.heading: Who we expect to do this
sections.markdown:
Nobody is pre-selected. We want one firm whose whole business is security and whose name a wallet would accept as a trusted attester: a smart contract audit firm, or a firm in monitoring or incident response with published Ethereum work. Today one firm signs every attestation in the registry; this RFP adds a second, independent name. A strong bid shows at least 3 years of published Ethereum security work, names the reviewers who will sign, and comes with public backing from a major wallet that plans to accept the firm's attestations.

Co-drafted by the submitter with TheDAO Security Fund. The submitter is a listed co-author of ERC-7730, convened the clear signing working group meetings until the Ethereum Foundation took over that role. The submitter and his employer will not bid on this initiative.

sections.heading: Hard requirements
sections.markdown:
1. **Security firm, in public.** The bidder is a company whose primary business is security, with at least 3 years of published Ethereum security work and at least 20 public audit or incident reports, linked in the bid.
2. **By the book.** Every review follows the registry's auditor guide in full, and no attestation is issued for a descriptor that formats a function whose displayed intent the guide says v2 cannot express.
3. **Under its own name.** Attestations are signed with a key the firm publicly declares as its own, in ERC-8176 format, merged into the registry's sigs folder.
4. **Independent.** The firm attests no descriptor it wrote, and discloses any commercial relationship with a protocol whose descriptor it reviews.
5. **Defects in public.** Every failed review is posted on the registry PR or as a registry issue before any attestation of the corrected version.
6. **Support for 12 months.** For 12 months after each attestation, the firm reviews every fix, addition or change to that contract's descriptor, including changes that follow a contract upgrade, and re-attests it or posts the defects within 30 days, at no extra cost.
7. **A major wallet backs the bid.** The bid includes a public statement from at least 1 of MetaMask, Rabby, Trust Wallet, Ledger, Trezor, Phantom or Fireblocks that it plans to name the firm as a trusted attester, linked in the bid. A bid without it is ignored.

initiatives.summary: Pay one established security firm to review, under its own name, the ERC-7730 clear signing descriptors for the 100 most-used verified Ethereum contracts and publish a signed attestation for each one, so wallets can trust what they render. The registry holds 739 descriptors, 166 carry an attestation, every one of those is signed by a single firm, and none of the top 100 contracts has an attested descriptor. The firm keeps each attestation current for 12 months. A major wallet backs the firm from the start, and payment lands on published attestations and on wallets that act on them.
initiatives.title: RFP: Clear Signing: Independent Attestations for the ERC-7730 Descriptors of Ethereum's 100 Most-Used Contracts

sections.heading: Why this matters
sections.markdown:
Users should know what they're trusting before they deposit. Today a protocol shows "audited by X", and that's where the information stops. It doesn't say how much of the live code the audit covered, whether the audit was three years ago and the code has been rewritten since, or whether the only change was one line. A determined user can piece this together for one protocol, but there's no public database that has it for every protocol in one place.

Ackee Blockchain found that 92 of 157 protocols on the Rekt list were hacked through unaudited or out-of-scope code, often while showing "audited by" logos ([Ackee, 2023](https://ackee.xyz/blog/why-we-need-to-start-using-erc-7512-onchain-audit-representation-right-now/)).

Afterwards:
- **Users and risk teams** can see, for any Ethereum DeFi protocol, which fund-holding contracts run code that no public audit covers, with every claim linked to its source.
- **Security researchers** get a list of post-audit changes no audit covers, ranked by TVL, as a place to start looking.
- **Protocols and audit firms** are accountable in public for what was actually reviewed and what shipped.

sections.heading: The team
sections.markdown:
- **SEAL (Security Alliance)** runs the project and publishes the results. SEAL is a nonprofit that shares threat intelligence and sets security standards for crypto. It runs SEAL 911, a free 24/7 incident hotline that has handled 3,300+ tickets; Safe Harbor, which lets whitehats step in to rescue funds during a live exploit; and SEAL Certifications, an operational security standard protocols are assessed against. Its frameworks and research are at [securityalliance.org](https://securityalliance.org/).
- **Dickson Wu** leads it: the method, the tooling and reviewing results. Dickson helps run SEAL's Safe Harbor and SEAL Certifications programs.

sections.heading: Why a grant: what already exists
sections.markdown: A working prototype already runs the full pipeline on Ethereum: it maps core contracts and proxies, collects public audits with their stated commit and scope, rebuilds the audited code and compares it to live bytecode. A public preview covers the 20 largest Ethereum DeFi protocols: [ethereum-audit-register-demo.dicksonwu.xyz](https://ethereum-audit-register-demo.dicksonwu.xyz). The grant pays to extend it to every protocol over $1 million, publish it and keep it current.

sections.heading: In scope
sections.markdown:
Every Ethereum DeFi protocol over $1 million in TVL on DeFiLlama: DEXs, lending, liquid staking, restaking, stablecoins, bridges and the rest. Together they hold 99.9% of Ethereum DeFi TVL, and new protocols are added as they cross $1 million. For each one:
- Map the core contracts, resolve proxies to their current implementations, and record who can upgrade them.
- Collect the public audits and record the commit and scope each report states.
- Rebuild the audited commit with the deployed compiler settings and compare it to the live bytecode, accounting for metadata, immutables and linked libraries. Each difference is classed as cosmetic, covered by a later audit, or not covered by any public audit.
- Publish audit statistics: share of core contracts covered by an audit, number of audits, time since the last one, and auditor working days where reports state them.
- Roll contract results up into one protocol verdict, so an uncovered fund-holding contract can't hide behind the rest.
- A public site with every protocol page and its sources, plus the full dataset, free to query.
- A monthly refresh of every protocol that picks up new audits and upgrades, with a last-checked date on each record and a public corrections channel.

Some protocols and audit firms don't publish reports, keep repos private, or leave contracts unverified, so full coverage isn't possible everywhere. Where that blocks a comparison, the record says exactly what's missing, and those gaps are published too.

sections.heading: Out of scope
sections.markdown:
- Rollup and L2 risk, which L2BEAT already does an excellent job covering.
- Other chains: this grant covers Ethereum mainnet.
- Protocols under $1 million in TVL. A protocol that falls below $1 million after it's added stays covered.

sections.heading: Commitments
sections.markdown:
- **License:** the dataset under CC BY 4.0, with the method published.
- **Maintenance:** every covered protocol is refreshed monthly for at least 12 months after launch, and SEAL keeps the dataset running after that.

initiatives.summary: An open, sourced record of every Ethereum DeFi protocol over $1 million in TVL, about 400 today: what each one had audited, what was in scope, what is running onchain now, and what changed through upgrades since. Each live contract is rebuilt from its audited commit and compared to the deployed bytecode, so anyone can see which live code no public audit covers. It needs no cooperation from protocols or audit firms, so it can cover the whole ecosystem.
initiatives.title: SEAL Audit Transparency: every DeFi protocol's audits, mapped to the code running onchain today

sections.heading: Why this matters
sections.markdown:
An audit tells you which code was reviewed. Your wallet asks you to approve a transaction using the code deployed today, and it doesn't tell you whether they're the same.

We analysed 12 Ethereum transactions involving 97 contract calls (https://proofofaudits.com/demos/proof-before-sign). Only 2 calls had a recorded byte-for-byte match to a reviewed build. Another 74 ran code in files named in audit reports, and 21 had no matching public audit in our records.

Those are very different levels of evidence, and none of that difference is visible when someone presses Confirm.

Proof Before Sign brings that evidence into the wallet. Before the user signs, it shows what matches reviewed code, what has changed and what remains unverified. AI agents can also be required to follow the owner's evidence rules.

A matching audit is not a guarantee of safety, but users should at least know what they are relying on.

sections.heading: The team
sections.markdown:
I'm M K Veerendra Vamshi, founder of Proof of Audits and a smart-contract security researcher. I placed first in Sherlock's Allbridge Core Yield audit contest in 2025.

I started Proof of Audits to solve a problem I kept seeing in Web3 security: teams spend heavily on audits, but users still cannot tell whether the contracts they're interacting with are the code that was reviewed.

We've built a working transaction-analysis service, a MetaMask Snap and a public Ethereum evidence explorer. We've also started onboarding auditors to the platform, so we're building both the technology and the researcher network behind it.

At Devcon and DSS Mumbai, I connected with people from Sigma Prime, ChainSecurity, corpus.core and other Ethereum security teams. These conversations opened opportunities to explore integrations, share audit evidence and work together. They are relationships we're developing, not partnerships we're claiming are already signed.

I lead the product, security research and engineering. The grant will allow us to bring in specialist engineering and independent security review capacity, while I remain responsible for delivery and adoption.

**Track record:**

https://audits.sherlock.xyz/watson/veerendravamshi

https://github.com/MKVEERENDRA
https://proofofaudits.com

sections.heading: Why a grant: what already exists
sections.markdown:
We've already done the work needed to show this problem can be solved. Now we need to make the solution reliable enough for other teams to use, and get it into the wallets where it matters.

Our live analyzer has checked 12 real Ethereum transactions involving 97 contract calls. Only 2 had recorded byte-for-byte matches to reviewed code. Another 74 were linked to audit scope, while 21 had no matching public audit evidence.

We've also built an explorer covering 656 functions across ten major Ethereum protocols, reproduced deployed Aave V4 and Uniswap V2 code from reviewed commits, and developed a MetaMask Snap that displays this evidence before signing. The code is public, although the independent evidence release process and ordinary MetaMask distribution are not complete.

We're not starting from zero on distribution either. Auditors have already joined our platform, we have an API for audit firms to publish their evidence, and Devcon gave us direct connections with security researchers, audit firms and Ethereum infrastructure teams interested in exploring the product.

**The next challenge is getting this into everyday use.**

The grant will fund three things:

- **Finish the product:** Complete the difficult execution-path checks, strengthen evidence verification, commission independent security reviews and prepare the wallet and agent integrations for production use.
- **Bring in the evidence:** Work with auditors, audit firms and protocols to connect reviewed source code, findings and fixes to the contracts running on Ethereum.
- **Get it into wallets:** Turn our Devcon connections into technical pilots, give external wallet and agent teams integration support, and prove that they use the checks in real Ethereum workflows.

We already have the product foundation and the relationships to begin this work. A new team would need to build that foundation before attempting the same integrations.

The final $25,000 of this grant is tied to adoption: at least two independent wallet or agent teams must use the evidence checks in live Ethereum workflows for 30 days, including at least one established provider. An independent reviewer will verify that use.

We're not asking TheDAO to fund another audit dashboard. We're asking it to help put existing audit evidence in front of people at the moment they are about to trust a contract with their funds.

**Existing work:**

https://proofofaudits.com/demos/proof-before-sign

https://proofofaudits.com/explorer/functions

https://github.com/ProofOfAudits/proof-before-sign-snap

sections.heading: In scope
sections.markdown:
- Reproduce the proposed transaction at a pinned Ethereum mainnet state, naming the external calls, proxy implementations and dependencies it reaches.

sections.heading: Why this matters
sections.markdown:
BlockThreat told teams where the attacks were going before they got there:

April 2026: after the KelpDAO and Drift hacks, it told teams to treat nodes, relayers and signers as part of the protocol, and to "stop using every day machines to sign multi-million-dollar transactions" (April).
July 2026: its outlook named the next target: "the next likely frontier will be signer infrastructure", the systems that approve and sign high-value transactions (July).
September 2026: it predicted that the next big exchange hack would start with social engineering, and told teams to audit their signing services and treat source control access like signing keys (September).
October 29: attackers went from a fake job interview to an engineer's laptop to Binance's wallet signing service, which signed 50 EIP-7702 authorizations and emptied its main Ethereum hot wallet. The loss was $6.3B (Cointelegraph, Week 44).
First week of November: 9 of the 13 incidents BlockThreat tracked across the industry, and about 97% of the $53.2M lost, came from outside smart contracts, led by $48.6M of validly signed withdrawals at one exchange (Week 45).

An audit covers none of this, and a defense built for last quarter's attacks is already behind. The warnings are public but scattered across hundreds of blogs, X threads, chatrooms and disclosures that no security team has time to read. BlockThreat reads them, re-ranks the threats every week and month, and says what to change.

Who is safer: security teams at Ethereum and L2 protocols, exchanges, custodians and wallets, against the attack vectors in play right now, such as compromised signing infrastructure and keys, fake-interview malware, frontend and DNS hijacks, and known bugs in forked code. Afterwards, anyone can point to teams that changed a defense because of a BlockThreat recommendation, and to teams that stopped a real attack with it.

sections.heading: The team
sections.markdown:
Peter Kacherginsky (@iphelix) does the work: editor of BlockThreat since 2019, sourcing, analysis and impact tracking. He has more than 20 years in security and founded Coinbase's blockchain security team. He has spoken at DeFi Security Summit for the past four years, most recently on "The State of DeFi Security - 2026", and seven years of his editions are public at blockthreat.com.

BlockThreat earns money from reader support, advertising, Enterprise subscriptions and Peter's advisory work for protocols (blockthreat.com/vciso). The Ethereum Foundation and TheDAO Security Fund each sponsored it once before, and neither funds this scope. No other funder pays for this work.

sections.heading: Why a grant: what already exists
sections.markdown:
* Seven years of weekly editions without a gap, plus monthly outlooks with loss statistics, the top 10 attack vectors and emerging threats, all free to read since November 2026.

* The readers are the defenders: 13,000+ subscribers at 1,900+ organizations, among them exchanges, custodians, protocols and audit firms. Past advertisers include Immunefi, Chainalysis, Trail of Bits and OpenZeppelin.

* One edition covers a defender's whole week. Week 44 had 30 incidents, 5 vulnerabilities and 18 research papers and tools, plus DPRK, malware and scam reporting.

* The sourcing: 294 feeds, 972 X accounts, 48 chatrooms and 15 newsletters. That is 32+ hours of reading a week, filtered with an in-house classification tool, reviewed by hand, and delivered as a 10-minute edition.

* The data behind the statistics: 2,313 incidents tracked, growing by 10 to 15 a week.

A new threat intelligence desk would have to build all of this first. Here the fund pays $6,000 a month for the Ethereum share of one editor's time, and readers and sponsors pay for the rest.

sections.heading: In scope

* 12 months of weekly briefings: the attack vector behind every Ethereum and L2 incident, the vulnerability disclosures, research, tools and threat-actor reporting that matter to Ethereum teams, and what to do about them (what to patch, what control to add, what to test for, who is on notice)

* 12 monthly outlooks: Ethereum loss statistics, the re-ranked top 10 attack vectors, and the threats to prepare for next

* Impact tracking, which is new work: a reporting link in every edition, follow-up with teams that act on a recommendation, and a quarterly impact report

* Building the sponsor base that pays for BlockThreat after the grant, at prices already published.

sections.heading: Why this matters
sections.markdown: Address poisoning plants dust transfers from look-alike addresses in a victim's history, hoping they copy the wrong one. Scam Sniffer tracked a $50 million loss in December 2025 and a $12.2 million loss in January 2026 ([Cointelegraph](https://cointelegraph.com/news/over-62m-lost-address-poisoning-since-december-scam-sniffer)). Blockscout offers only an admin-managed scam badge today. Afterwards, any wallet can check an address against a public score before a user sends funds.

sections.heading: Why this matters
sections.markdown:
Ethereum wallets, protocols, and autonomous AI agents handle sensitive information, including private keys, signing secrets, cryptographic operations, and transaction data. Yet timing variations and other side-channel signals can expose this information even when software behaves as designed. Conventional security testing often overlooks these vulnerabilities because it focuses on functional correctness rather than unintended information leakage.

LeakDetectAI closes this gap by bringing AI-powered side-channel detection into real-world Ethereum security workflows. It enables developers and security teams to identify and reproduce hidden vulnerabilities, validate fixes, and introduce regression tests that prevent them from returning. This makes it possible to detect and remediate security weaknesses that conventional testing may miss, strengthening the protection of Ethereum wallets, protocols, and AI agents.

sections.heading: Why a grant: what already exists
sections.markdown:
LeakDetectAI has an existing open-source foundation in automated side-channel analysis, machine-learning-based leakage detection, and hardware-wallet security testing. This is not a proposal to build side-channel analysis from scratch: the team has already published and made available the underlying research code and experimentation infrastructure. Public work includes:

Hardware-wallet testing and Ethereum/Web3 security: https://github.com/SEC4AI-AI4SEC/autosca-hw-wallet-tester 
The active development repository for automated side-channel security testing, including hardware-wallet analysis.

Deep-learning side-channel analysis: https://github.com/SEC4AI-AI4SEC/deep-learning-sca
An existing research and reproducibility codebase for automated side-channel analysis.

Quantitative information-leakage detection: https://github.com/SEC4AI-AI4SEC/AutoMLQuantILDetect 
An existing package applying AutoML and information-theoretic methods to detect and quantify leakage.

Project resources and demonstrations: LeakDetectAI project github site, project dashboard and and public research discussions: 
https://github.com/SEC4AI-AI4SEC/deep-learning-sca/discussions/3 and https://x.com/libp2p/status/2119770702907871743 

Partners: https://leak-detect-tooling.lovable.app/#partners 
Giveth Update: https://leak-detect-tooling.lovable.app/#giveth 
Devcon Update: https://leak-detect-tooling.lovable.app/devcon 
 
Prior ecosystem validation: LeakDetectAI was selected for the Ethereum Security Quadratic Funding round, with support from Giveth and TheDAO Security Fund. The selection and community discussion are publicly documented at https://x.com/manusheel/status/2054083699298472238 and https://github.com/SEC4AI-AI4SEC/deep-learning-sca/discussions/3 

The grant is priced below a from-scratch build because it reuses existing research, code, experimental methods, and testing infrastructure rather than funding the development of foundational side-channel analysis and AutoML capabilities again. The requested work is the focused next step: adapting and validating these capabilities against Ethereum wallet and agent threat models, building reproducible Ethereum-specific benchmarks, and working with ecosystem projects to turn findings into verified fixes and regression tests. The existing repositories provide a starting point; the Ethereum-specific integrations, validation, and adoption outcomes remain the work to be delivered by this grant.

sections.heading: In scope
sections.markdown:
LeakDetectAI will deliver the adoption of an open-source security testing and remediation capability across Ethereum wallets, hardware wallets, AI-agent frameworks, and Layer 2 ecosystems. The funding will support the integration of LeakDetectAI into the actual security-testing and development workflows of participating projects, collaboration with their maintainers to identify and reproduce exploitable side-channel weaknesses, and engineering support to implement and verify fixes. The central deliverable is not simply a tool that detects potential information leakage, but demonstrable security improvements in Ethereum projects that use it.

Adoption will be pursued across six areas. First, LeakDetectAI will be adopted for desktop, mobile, and hardware-wallet security testing, covering real-world key-management, transaction-signing, and authorization workflows. The work will engage relevant wallet developers and hardware-wallet testing environments to identify reproducible weaknesses, provide actionable remediation guidance, and support fixes and regression tests. Second, the existing Ethereum field deployments, including the Ethereum Layer 1 and 2 based hardware-wallet testing workflow using Ledger, will be used to apply LeakDetectAI in practical environments. The objective is to translate findings from these deployments into documented, actionable security improvements in the participating applications and their associated workflows.

Third, adoption will extend across Ethereum agent and protocol ecosystems, including relevant teams and applications within Optimism and Arbitrum. LeakDetectAI will be applied to agent execution, transaction authorization, signing, and protocol-integrated workflows, with participating developers supported in reproducing and remediating confirmed weaknesses. Fourth, we will work with Ethereum wallet developers, with prospective targets including MetaMask, Rabby Wallet, and Safe, to identify side-channel vulnerabilities affecting wallet security and support maintainers in implementing fixes. Fifth, we will engage Ethereum agent-framework developers, with prospective targets including Coinbase AgentKit and ElizaOS, to identify weaknesses in agent execution and transaction workflows and support code-level remediation and regression testing. These are prospective adoption targets, not confirmed commitments; engagement and remediation will be pursued in coordination with the relevant maintainers.

The sixth area will consolidate these efforts into ecosystem-wide adoption and verified security remediation. We target adoption by at least three named Ethereum wallet or agent-framework projects and at least three implemented security improvements in participating codebases, including wallet and agent-framework environments. Each counted improvement must be linked to a reproducible weakness identified through LeakDetectAI and supported by verifiable evidence of remediation, such as a merged patch, released fix, downstream code change, or equivalent maintainer-confirmed implementation, together with a regression test or repeatable validation showing that the weakness has been addressed. Deliverables will include documented integrations, vulnerability reproduction reports, remediation records, regression tests, and a public adoption report, subject to responsible-disclosure requirements.

The $60,000 requested will fund the adoption work required to achieve these outcomes: deployment and testing across desktop, mobile, and hardware-wallet environments; integration into existing Ethereum field deployments; engagement with Ethereum and Layer 2 agent and protocol teams; direct collaboration with wallet and agent-framework maintainers; vulnerability reproduction and remediation support; implementation of security fixes and regression tests; and independent verification and documentation of the resulting improvements. Of the total request, $50,000 (Milestones B to D) pays only on outside teams using LeakDetectAI and merging its fixes. This allocation will support the engineering effort and maintainer coordination needed to move identified vulnerabilities through to implemented fixes.

The success of the initiative will be measured by security improvements in real Ethereum projects, rather than downloads, user counts, demonstrations, or the number of testing runs. By completion, participating projects will have used LeakDetectAI to identify actionable side-channel weaknesses and address them through implemented fixes and regression tests. This will make Ethereum safer by reducing opportunities for attackers to exploit observable execution behaviour to infer sensitive information, strengthening the protection of wallet keys and signing operations, improving transaction authorization security, and reducing the exposure of AI-agent workflows to side-channel attacks. All non-sensitive tooling, remediation guidance, and verification evidence will be published as reusable open-source resources so that other Ethereum developers can adopt the same protections.

sections.heading: Out of scope
sections.markdown:
LeakDetectAI will not undertake general-purpose privacy research, academic research without a direct Ethereum security application, or the development of new foundational machine-learning or side-channel analysis algorithms unrelated to the project's defined objectives. The initiative is not intended to build a general-purpose privacy auditing platform, surveillance or user-monitoring system, or a commercial security product. It will not cover non-Ethereum ecosystems, or other unrelated blockchain networks; the scope is strictly limited to Ethereum, its Layer 2 ecosystems, and the wallets and agent frameworks serving them.

The grant will not fund the development of new wallets, blockchain protocols, consensus clients, agent frameworks, or general-purpose AI infrastructure. It will not include broad penetration-testing engagements, smart-contract auditing unrelated to the identified side-channel risks, formal verification of entire applications, or remediation of vulnerabilities outside the project's defined threat model. It will also not fund speculative vulnerability research that cannot be connected to a concrete Ethereum security risk or actionable remediation.

Finally, the project will not publicly disclose exploitable vulnerabilities before maintainers have had a reasonable opportunity to address them. Sensitive findings, exploit details, and affected code will be handled through responsible-disclosure processes. Funding is specifically for the development and application of Ethereum-focused detection capabilities, vulnerability validation, maintainer-supported remediation, and independently verifiable improvements to Ethereum wallet and agent security; activities outside these boundaries are excluded.

sections.heading: Commitments
sections.markdown:
LeakDetectAI commits to releasing all grant-funded, non-sensitive software, detection tooling, benchmark suites, test cases, documentation, and integration examples under an OSI-approved open-source license, preferably Apache-2.0, with source code and development history publicly available in the project's GitHub repositories. Any existing components with different licenses will retain their original licenses, and their licensing compatibility will be reviewed before integration. No grant-funded core functionality will be made exclusively available through a proprietary service.

We commit to maintaining the open-source repositories after the grant period, including preserving documentation, addressing critical bugs, reviewing community contributions, and keeping the detection and regression-testing infrastructure usable. We will make reasonable efforts to coordinate ongoing maintenance with the relevant Ethereum wallet, agent-framework, and open-source maintainers. The project will also document installation, testing, and integration procedures so that other developers can independently use and extend the work without depending on the original team.

For ecosystem adoption, we commit to pursuing the named targets MetaMask, Rabby, Trust Wallet, Safe, Coinbase AgentKit, and ElizaOS. The adoption objective is verified remediation in at least three named projects, including at least one Ethereum wallet and one agent framework. Evidence will consist of publicly verifiable issues, maintainer-reviewed fixes, merged pull requests or downstream commits, and regression tests, subject to responsible-disclosure requirements. These projects are pinned adoption targets for engagement and evaluation, not claimed partnerships or guaranteed commitments from their maintainers. Where a target has no reproducible vulnerability within the project's scope, or its maintainers decline participation, we will document the outcome and pursue another relevant Ethereum wallet or agent framework with equivalent adoption potential.

We are not requesting an exception to the open-source licensing or public-goods commitments. The only qualification is that existing third-party components retain their original licenses and security-sensitive vulnerability details may remain confidential until responsible disclosure permits publication. We will not use confidentiality as a reason to withhold non-sensitive grant-funded deliverables or the evidence needed to verify completed security improvements.

Its success will be measured through independently verifiable adoption, maintainer-accepted vulnerabilities, merged fixes, and regression tests across the Ethereum ecosystem.

sections.heading: Why this matters
sections.markdown:
Safe owners, DAO voters and wallet users approve calldata, and the result can differ from what they expected: state moves after signing, and calldata can hide what it does. An assertion writes the expected outcome into the transaction, such as a minimum balance after a swap, and the transaction reverts when the outcome is different. Signers are protected from a wrong result even when they cannot read the calldata.

OP Mainnet's next upgrade ([superchain-ops eth/084](https://github.com/ethereum-optimism/superchain-ops/tree/main/src/tasks/eth/084-U21-op-ink-soneium-uni)) is one Safe transaction that gives 25 contracts new code across four chains, including the vault holding over 180,000 ETH of bridge deposits. Its signers see a delegatecall and a wall of hex, and the task's README lists checks to run after it executes. We wrote those checks into the transaction instead, with the ones the Builder reads from the chain: 60 checks, all passing on a mainnet fork, and if one fails nothing executes.

Two gaps remain, and this grant closes them:

- **Signers take the author's word.** The description of the checks comes from whoever built the batch. The Viewer rebuilds it from the transaction.
- **Checks compare against fixed numbers.** Notations records a value while the transaction runs, so a check can say "this transaction takes out at most 50,000 USDC" whatever the balance is.

sections.markdown:

- [Sem](https://github.com/sembrestels), lead engineer: author of the Assertions contracts, the EVMcrispr compiler and the Assertion Builder, and of the [launch transaction](https://etherscan.io/tx/0x462475a38cd8a3b75b2732db28ea21a7addfce059af03ea4f638f461c707bf10) of TheDAO Security Fund.

Blossom Labs is the round operator of TheDAO Security Fund Round 2, and Rodrigo works at Giveth, which administers the fund, so the independent technical reviewer for these milestones is named in the grant agreement and is not Blossom Labs.

No other funder pays for this scope. TheDAO Security Fund Round 1 [paid about $7,186](https://thedao.fund/transparency/assertions-eth-on-chain-transaction-guards-for-ethereum) for the existing contracts.

sections.heading: In scope
sections.markdown:
- **[Notations](https://github.com/BlossomLabs/Assertions/issues/10)**: the contract that records a value while a transaction runs, for later checks to compare against, and deploys the compiled assertions.
- **[EVMcrispr](https://github.com/BlossomLabs/Assertions/issues/10)**: a `set` whose value is read when the batch executes, which a Safe and a DAO vote need because sometimes they execute days after they are written. Our own review of the Safe module, so it leaves experimental status.
- **Assertion Builder**: adapted to use the new features.
- **Protect your transactions**: a public board at assertions.eth listing every mainnet transaction checked by the Assertions contracts, with three values measured from onchain data: the money the transaction transfers, the money the originating account holds, and the money that account controls (for a bridge admin, the assets in the bridge it can upgrade). Each value links its addresses and its query.
- **[Assertion Viewer](https://github.com/BlossomLabs/Assertions/issues/13)**: open a pending or executed transaction and read each assertion as a plain sentence, checked against the calldata and deployed code.

sections.heading: Why this matters
sections.markdown:
Researchers need one clear pathway to every team. A report that never reaches the team leaves users exposed until an attacker finds the same bug.

- Researchers now hunt with AI agents. An agent can route and encrypt a report automatically only when every team publishes the same machine-readable record in the same place. AI can also chain low-severity bugs into critical ones, so every finding needs a route.
- The worst bugs need more than a public address: every extra hop is a chance to leak. In a web of trust a finding goes straight to a verified security lead, who knows the sender is real amid AI-generated junk reports.
- Our count (November 23, 2026) checked the website DeFiLlama lists for each entry.

sections.heading: In scope
sections.markdown:
Bidders have complete freedom in how they get there, including their own milestones, within the hard requirements below. What matters is three outcomes: one agreed standard for what teams publish and where; every Ethereum and L2 team with real value at stake publishing it; and a private web of trust that reaches those teams' security leads fast. This RFP is a starting point and will change; the final milestones are agreed with the selected team.

One possible approach, the one the milestones below follow:

- Settle the standard: what every project publishes (a contact, a private channel such as an encryption key, and a vulnerability disclosure policy, or VDP, with scope, expected response and safe harbor) and where (security.txt, SECURITY.md with GitHub private reporting, an onchain record such as ERC-5437), endorsed by groups that send and receive reports.
- Hunt teams down one by one: direct outreach, pull requests to their repositories, whatever tactics work.
- Build the web of trust with SEAL: start from the contacts SEAL and other groups already have, verify each team's security lead and a backup on a video call, connect them over encrypted channels, let members vouch for researchers so teams know a report is real, and keep it current with call-tree drills.
- A public campaign, for example on X, naming who has published and who has not.
- A simple public tracker, a checkmark per record per project, mainly to track this grant's progress and give teams a gold star.

sections.heading: Out of scope
sections.markdown:
- Running bug bounties.
- Validating or handling reports (the companion bug broker RFP).
- Emergency response to live hacks ([SEAL 911](https://securityalliance.org/our-work/seal-911) does that).

sections.heading: Existing work
sections.markdown:
- [RFC 9116](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9116): security.txt, with fields for a contact, an encryption key and a policy.
- [SEAL's vulnerability disclosure framework](https://frameworks.securityalliance.org/vulnerability-disclosure/overview): tells teams to publish one consistent set of contacts everywhere researchers look, with a [SECURITY.md template and sample security.txt](https://frameworks.securityalliance.org/vulnerability-disclosure/security-contact) and a policy template. The natural starting point.
- [disclose.io's dioterms](https://github.com/disclose/dioterms): public-domain VDP and safe harbor templates.
- [ERC-5437](https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-5437): an onchain contact with an encryption key, status Stagnant.

sections.heading: Who we expect to do this
sections.markdown:
One person or a small team that SEAL and researchers already trust, good at relentless, polite outreach and loud public campaigns. A strong bid shows SEAL will work with it. Nobody is pre-selected.

Drafted by TheDAO Security Fund from conversations with EthSec (ethsecurity.org) and Consensys. EthSec, TheDAO Security Fund and Giveth will not bid.

sections.heading: Hard requirements
sections.markdown:
1. **Verified means project-controlled.** A record counts only when the project publishes it itself: on its domain, in its repository or from its admin or governance address.
2. **Encrypted to count.** Only records with a published encryption key or a private reporting form the project controls count.
3. **Open and maintained.** The standard is published under CC0 or CC BY 4.0, and a home outside the selected team commits in public to maintain the standard and the web of trust after the grant. The tracker's data is open, each checkmark linked to the project's own record.
4. **Names only, never bugs.** Campaigns and the tracker show only whether a project published the records, never a vulnerability, finding or report.
5. **Private stays private.** Web-of-trust members' direct contacts are never published; only vouched members can use them, under access rules the bid states.
6. **Outside means unaffiliated.** An outside team shares no owner, staff or funding relationship with the selected team. Affiliates count toward no criterion.
7. Ethereum and L2 projects only.

initiatives.summary: Ethereum is permissionless, so teams publish security contacts many ways or not at all, and researchers and their AI agents cannot reliably find where a bug goes or how to encrypt it. Of the 50 largest DeFi entries on Ethereum, 37 serve no security.txt, and only 2 publish one with an encryption key. AI is finding bugs fast, so this needs solving now. This RFP pays one person or a small team to get every team to publish one standard and to build, on what SEAL and other groups already have, a private web of trust that reaches each team's security lead fast.
initiatives.title: RFP: Hunt Down Every Ethereum Team Until It Publishes a security.txt and Joins a Web of Trust

sections.heading: Why this matters
sections.markdown:
Ethereum applications depend on interacting technical and operational systems.
A security failure can begin in a software dependency or operator session, alter
transaction construction, pass through legitimate signing, and reach onchain execution.
Understanding those relationships is necessary to design effective protections.

Historical incident reports contain valuable evidence, but comparing them requires
repeated interpretation of terminology, system boundaries, causes, and consequences.
Onchain Risk Map will share that work through a maintained reference model and
reproducible dataset.
Auditors, wallet developers, projects, and incident responders will be able to find
comparable incidents, inspect affected trust boundaries, and assess proposed defenses.
The scope addresses wallet experience, smart contract security, infrastructure, and
incident response in the Ethereum Foundation’s linked Trillion Dollar Security report.

sections.heading: Why a grant: what already exists
sections.markdown:
The [public preview](https://map.okcontract.com) provides the starting point.
OKcontract Labs’ existing package includes typed topology definitions, incident
annotations, source snapshots, explicit merge and exclusion decisions, catalog
validation, and deterministic generators.
The source package is currently private.

The grant pays for publication, stronger provenance, independent review, and external
use. Completed prototype work is excluded from the budget.
A from-scratch build would also need to create the existing model, catalog, and
generators. The first milestone makes these foundations publicly inspectable through a
versioned source release.

sections.heading: In scope
sections.markdown:
1. Publish the graph specification: node and relationship semantics, incident surface
   roles, confidence levels, and primary-cause assessment rules.
   Include JSON schemas, TypeScript interfaces, migration guidance, and examples.
   Distinguish architectural relationships, observed incident relationships, and analyst
   hypotheses.
2. Strengthen provenance and incident identity.
   Attach references and review rationale to individual surface, relationship, and cause
   assertions. Record reviewer identities, dates, disagreements, and corrections.
   Normalize chain identifiers and support multiple transactions per incident.
   Separate source observations from canonical incidents to prevent duplicate incident
   counts and loss totals.
3. Publish a reviewed Ethereum L1 and L2 corpus spanning contract exploitation, signing
   deception, supply-chain compromise, governance, custody, bridges, and delegated
   authorization. Publish selection criteria and coverage gaps.
   Preserve unknown and disputed findings.
4. Assess defensive controls, including transaction verification, restricted delegation,
   release integrity, independent approval channels, and upgrade restrictions.
   Record enforcement location, assumptions, and whether each control prevents, detects,
   or limits the failure mechanism.
   Separate demonstrated protection from hypothetical applicability.
5. Release downloadable datasets, a query CLI, executable examples, and a small
   reference viewer. Publish mappings to [OAK identifiers](https://onchainattack.org/)
   and a field-level
   [STIX 2.1](https://docs.oasis-open.org/cti/stix/v2.1/os/stix-v2.1-os.html)
   compatibility note, including unmapped fields.
   Link available upstream exploit reproductions.
   Include machine-readable query outputs for defensive AI-agent workflows.
6. Recruit external users, support use in their work, and compare source-only and
   graph-assisted workflows.
   The grant covers onboarding, workflow support, evaluation design, and public evidence
   collection. Publish completion time, factual errors, missing evidence, and feedback,
   including neutral or adverse results.

The planning budget is $42,000 for 7 person-months at $6,000, $6,000 for independent
incident review and technical verification, and $2,000 for hosting and releases.
Milestone allocations are: specification, $9,000 labor, $2,000 review, $1,000
operations; corpus and tools, $9,000 labor, $3,000 review; viewer and handoff, $8,000
labor, $1,000 operations; adoption, $16,000 labor and $1,000 evidence verification.
These are planning allowances.

sections.heading: Out of scope

Exhaustive incident coverage, live monitoring, emergency response, newly developed

Historical frequency and recorded losses will not be presented as calibrated
probabilities of future compromise.

are excluded from public downloads.

sections.heading: Why this matters
sections.markdown:
Smart contracts can pass large unit test suites and still fail after an unexpected sequence of calls, actors, prices, timestamps, upgrades, or token behaviors. Echidna attacks that gap with stateless and stateful property-based testing. It generates transaction sequences from a contract ABI and searches for inputs that falsify user-defined properties or Solidity assertions.  
Echidna already combines coverage guidance, corpus mutation, source integration, automatic test minimization, Foundry reproducers, hevm cheatcodes, and optional symbolic execution. Its next challenge is reliability at the seams: EVM behavior changes, campaign and worker coordination, symbolic-execution edge cases, agent control and improved performance. Those are the areas that determine whether auditors can trust a long-running campaign and reproduce what it found.

sections.heading: The team
sections.markdown:
Gustavo Grieco does the work, in the public [Echidna repository](https://github.com/crytic/echidna).  
He was the lead developer of Echidna and the lead author of [the ISSTA 2020 paper](https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3395363.3404366) that introduced it. He was a security engineer at Trail of Bits from September 2017 to April 2025, junior to principal, across blockchain audits, fuzzing, and tool development, and has been independent since. He has been [elected Audit Committee Technical Expert for the Arbitrum DAO since July 2025](https://snapshot.box/#/s:arbitrumfoundation.eth/proposal/0x131574819442cb6da293795ee9faeec4754a5af664b535b654b3d9d3d53f47e1). He co-authored the [Slither paper](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1908.09878) and echidna-parade, and before Echidna he built another fuzzer: [QuickFuzz](https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/2976002.2976017). Echidna lives in the crytic GitHub organization, which Trail of Bits runs. Even after he left Trail of Bits, Gustavo is still a volunteer to keep Echidna maintained.

sections.heading: Why a grant: what already exists
sections.markdown:
The recipient has the decisive head start. The work touches Echidna's Haskell engine, release process, hevm and Slither integrations, symbolic execution, Foundry compatibility, and the existing MCP preview. A new vendor would first spend months on implementation details and EVM edge cases.  
The [2026-2027 roadmap discussion](https://github.com/crytic/echidna/issues/1612) is the maintainer's planning thread, where users prioritize the goals. The 2.3 [releases](https://github.com/crytic/echidna/releases) added optional symbolic verification, multiple SMT solvers, Foundry reproducers, and an experimental MCP interface. The [public fuzzing campaigns list](https://github.com/perimetersec/public-fuzzing-campaigns-list) shows the tool in real audit work, and Recon Invariant Testing Extension and scfuzzbench are external users or integration targets.  
**Example roadmap outcomes**, to show the expected scope. The milestones name the class of outcome, so the issue can change.

> * Fork support like [issue \#1623](https://github.com/crytic/echidna/issues/1623): the relevant fork's execution-layer changes supported in hevm and Echidna, with fork-specific and conformance tests.  
> * Symbolic verification like [issue \#1625](https://github.com/crytic/echidna/issues/1625): difficult properties proved by combining fuzzing and symbolic execution, with replayable counterexamples.

sections.heading: Commitments
sections.markdown:
> 1. **Open source and public development.** All grant-funded code, tests, documentation, and examples are published under AGPLv3 or another OSI-approved license, through public issues, pull requests, and tagged releases.  
> 2. **Roadmap delivery.** Each roadmap outcome ships in a tagged release whose notes explain the improvement and link to the test, reproducer, or benchmark behind it.  
> 3. **Substitution and 2026 carry-over.** A blocked roadmap item may be replaced by one of equal or greater security value and scope, with the reason, the replacement, and its acceptance evidence published first. Unfinished 2026 roadmap work counts if it happens in 2027, was not funded elsewhere, and is of comparable scope and importance.  
> 4. **Current EVM support.** Finalized EVM and toolchain changes in the work period are covered by public regression tests. No milestone depends on an Ethereum upgrade shipping on a fixed date: if a fork slips, the fork-dated target moves with it.

> 6. **Post-grant maintenance.** The recipient keeps maintaining Echidna after the grant (releases, triage, security reports, user support on the public channels), without follow-on funding and at a pace set by his other paid work.  
> 7. **Pinned targets, counted from the first payment.** EVM fidelity and campaign reliability: within 90 days after the next Ethereum mainnet fork activates. Symbolic verification and agent workflows: within 7 months. Roadmap completion and handoff: within 10 months. Adoption: within 12 months.

sections.heading: Why this matters
sections.markdown:
Security remains a major challenge for Ethereum developers. While professional smart-contract audits are essential, they are expensive, time-consuming, and typically conducted at specific stages of development. Existing automated security tools help identify potential vulnerabilities, but often produce false positives or struggle to recognize issues requiring deeper contextual reasoning. This creates a gap between basic automated scanning and the security analysis developers need throughout the development lifecycle.
Kann Audits is addressing this gap through Kann AI, a proprietary AI model developed specifically for Solidity vulnerability detection and supported by a specialized security dataset. Rather than simply adding an interface to a general-purpose AI model, we are developing and improving the underlying security-focused model itself. With grant funding, we will improve detection accuracy, reduce false positives, strengthen vulnerability reasoning, and introduce CI/CD integrations that enable automated security scanning on code changes and pull requests. This will help Ethereum developers identify potential vulnerabilities earlier, investigate findings more efficiently, and incorporate security checks into everyday development workflows without replacing professional manual audits.

sections.heading: The team
sections.markdown:
Kann AI is developed by Kann Audits, a smart-contract security firm combining hands-on security research, professional auditing experience, and AI engineering expertise.

Erkan Alaydinov - Founder, Kann Audits

Erkan has worked in smart-contract security since 2023, with experience in professional security audits, independent security research, public audit contests, private code reviews, and large-scale AI-generated finding triage. He leads the security research direction of Kann AI, including vulnerability analysis, dataset quality, and the practical evaluation of model-generated findings.

LinkedIn: https://www.linkedin.com/in/erkan-erolov/

Kann Audits track record

Kann Audits has completed 71 smart contract security audits and secured more than $2 billion in TVL.

Our AI security tooling has also been used by projects including Manifest Finance, HyperLend, and Mystic Finance.

This combination of practical security research and AI engineering gives Kann Audits the expertise needed to develop a specialized vulnerability detection model and evaluate its performance against real-world smart-contract security issues.

Funding and relationships

Kann AI has been developed through Kann Audits' own resources. Kann Audits is committing $12,500 toward the initiative, alongside the requested $50,000 grant.

The protocols mentioned above are examples of previous users of our security tooling. Their inclusion does not imply that they are funding the initiative or formally endorsing this application.

sections.heading: Why a grant: what already exists
sections.markdown:
Kann AI is already an operational product rather than a concept awaiting initial development.

Kann Audits has developed a proprietary AI model specialized in detecting security vulnerabilities in Solidity smart contracts. The model is supported by a dedicated vulnerability dataset informed by real-world security research, historical vulnerability patterns, audit findings, and manually reviewed security issues.

An Alpha version of Kann AI is already deployed and publicly accessible at:

https://scan.kannaudits.com

Developers can use the existing platform to submit Solidity code for AI-assisted security analysis and review potential vulnerability findings.

Our advantage comes from the security expertise supporting the model. Kann Audits has conducted 61 security audits involving protocols representing more than $2 billion in TVL. This experience helps us understand real vulnerabilities, distinguish meaningful findings from noise, and continually improve the quality of the model's training and evaluation process.

The grant will not finance development of a new product from scratch. The initial model, core infrastructure, security research methodology, and public scanning platform have already been established through Kann Audits' own investment.

Instead, grant funding will accelerate improvements to the existing model, expand and refine the vulnerability dataset, strengthen evaluation against previously unseen contracts, improve inference reliability, and introduce production-ready CI/CD integrations.

This existing foundation allows the requested $50,000 to be concentrated on measurable technical improvements and practical developer adoption rather than initial product research and infrastructure development.

sections.heading: In scope
sections.markdown:
The initiative will focus on improving Kann AI's Solidity vulnerability detection capabilities and making automated smart-contract security analysis easier to integrate into Ethereum development workflows.

Solidity AI model improvement

We will expand and improve the proprietary vulnerability dataset using real-world Solidity vulnerabilities, exploit examples, secure contract implementations, and difficult negative examples. The improved dataset will support further model training, with an emphasis on increasing vulnerability detection accuracy, strengthening contextual reasoning, and reducing false positives and false negatives.

Development will prioritize major Solidity security risks, including access-control vulnerabilities, reentrancy, unsafe external interactions, accounting inconsistencies, and complex authorization issues.

Evaluation and benchmarking

We will establish a held-out security benchmark containing vulnerable and non-vulnerable Solidity contracts excluded from model training.

The current Kann AI Alpha will serve as the baseline for measuring improvements. Evaluation will report precision, recall, false-positive rates, false-negative rates, and performance across relevant vulnerability categories.

We will document important failure modes, publish the evaluation methodology, and share benchmark results so that improvements can be assessed independently.

CI/CD security integrations

We will develop integrations that allow Ethereum development teams to run Kann AI vulnerability scans automatically within their existing development workflows.

The initial integration will target GitHub Actions, enabling scans during pull requests and code pushes.

The integration will support:

Automated Solidity vulnerability scanning.

Security results associated with code changes.

Machine-readable findings suitable for CI/CD pipelines.

Configurable severity thresholds.

Automated warnings or failed checks when configured security thresholds are exceeded.

Integration guides, configuration examples, and developer documentation.

Production infrastructure and adoption

We will improve the reliability and scalability of the existing Kann AI scanning infrastructure and deploy updated models through the publicly accessible platform.

We will support adoption by independent Ethereum development teams, with a target of at least 20 projects or teams successfully integrating Kann AI into real CI/CD workflows.

Use of funding

Grant funding will support AI model development and training, security dataset curation, benchmarking, CI/CD engineering, inference infrastructure, developer tooling, testing, and documentation.

All funded work will directly support the improvement and practical adoption of Kann AI as a Solidity smart-contract security tool.

sections.heading: Commitments

Kann Audits commits to making Kann AI a practical and accessible AI-assisted security tool for Ethereum developers while maintaining clear boundaries around proprietary technology and public deliverables.

Public access

Kann AI will remain publicly accessible through https://scan.kannaudits.com throughout the funded development period and for at least 6 months after completion of the final milestone, subject to reasonable usage limits, infrastructure capacity, and operational safeguards.

The improvements developed through this grant will be made available through the public Kann AI scanning platform.

Open-source commitments

We will publish relevant security evaluation methodology, benchmark results, and technical documentation so developers and security researchers can understand the system's capabilities and limitations.

Proprietary technology

The core Kann AI model weights, proprietary training methods, and privately curated vulnerability dataset will remain the intellectual property of Kann Audits.

We request an explicit exception to any grant requirement that would otherwise mandate publication of the underlying model weights or complete proprietary training dataset.

Where licensing, confidentiality, and security considerations permit, we will publish relevant research findings, benchmark artifacts, and supporting evaluation materials.

Maintenance

Kann Audits will maintain the publicly deployed Kann AI platform and funded CI/CD integrations for at least six months following acceptance of the final milestone. Maintenance will include reasonable bug fixes, operational support, and compatibility updates.

sections.heading: Why this matters
sections.markdown:
Ethereum is built around verification. In practice, transaction signing still depends heavily on blind trust.

Before approving a transaction, a user typically trusts an RPC for chain state, a verification service or explorer for the ABI, the dapp for what the action means, and often a remote tx simulator for what the transaction will do. The wallet eventually asks the user to approve bytes, but the context that makes those bytes understandable usually comes from external systems, if it comes at all.

Independent verification is already possible, easy, and cheap. So why not add a second or third factor check to what you are about to sign, and check if they agree on everything? We are used to have 2FA in every parts of our lives but not in the most sensitive step in crypto.

The problem is usability. Doing it properly today means stitching together several tools and manual checks, so almost nobody does it for ordinary transactions. 

Onay turns that into a second sanity check that can run on every signing request. It independently reconstructs the facts the user needs before approving: the chain state, the code actually deployed, the contracts reached during execution, and the human-readable intent of the transaction. 

The application does not hold any keys and is view only. So it can safely leverage a multitude of services and display any information that will enrich the signing process. It does this locally, without replacing the wallet or taking custody of keys. 

This gives hardware-wallet users, multisig signers, treasury operators, and ordinary Ethereum users a practical way to compare what a dapp is asking them to sign against an independently verified view.

Ethereum already makes verification possible. Onay makes it easy enough to actually use.

Onay puts every security-relevant fact through the user's own machine, or highlights what’s missing:

- Chain state is proof-verified by a local Helios client where the chain supports it (Ethereum, the OP Stack family, Linea), and read from an RPC the user chooses everywhere else, with a permanent notice about the trust that implies.
- Sourcify's verification claim is not trusted blindly. The app downloads the sources, recompiles them with the pinned solc binary, and compares the result byte for byte with the on-chain code.
- The transaction runs in a local EVM to reconstruct the call tree, so every contract it touches goes through the two checks above, and ERC-7730 descriptors turn the verified ABI into readable intent. It does full ABI decoding with NatSpec comments when clear-signing is not possible.
- After confirmation the app shows the ERC-8213 digest. A wallet that implements the standard shows the same hash, which proves the wallet received exactly the bytes the user reviewed, and that the dapp or the transport was not compromised in between.

Afterwards a multisig signer, a treasury operator or any hardware wallet user can check what they sign with no trusted intermediary and no hosted service.

sections.markdown:
**Sourcify** does the work: Manuel Wedler, Kaan Uzdogan and Marco Castignoli, all full-stack developers on the Sourcify team, which runs the verification service and its libraries (lib-sourcify, the clear-signing library) at a scale of millions of requests. Sourcify is part of the Argot Collective.

- https://sourcify.dev

Relationships to codebases named here: the team maintains Sourcify, lib-sourcify as well as the ERC-7730 clear-signing library and the ethereum/clear-signing-erc7730-registry repo that Onay recompiles and renders with.

sections.heading: Why a grant: what already exists
sections.markdown:
A working prototype exists and anyone can run it: https://github.com/sourcifyeth/project-independence, a Tauri desktop app with an embedded Helios light client, the local Sourcify verification gate, proxy and diamond resolution, ERC-7730 clear signing, local EVM simulation, Ledger signing, post-mining verification, activity history and an address book. The browser build runs at https://explorer.sourcify.app against live contracts on mainnet.

The prototype was written quickly to prove the idea end to end and none of its code is trusted as-is. We received positive feedback from our close circle of external stakeholders and want to continue shipping this into production.

The rebuild plan, the full UX mock of release 1 with fake data, and the transport design (native messaging with encrypted pairing) are done. Two of the four libraries the verifier depends on, lib-sourcify and the clear-signing library, are the team's own code.

sections.heading: In scope
sections.markdown:
Release 1 is the transaction verifier. This grant pays for:

- **The extension.** A hand-written, zero-dependency script that wraps the page's EIP-1193 provider, catches eth_sendTransaction and signing requests, and forwards them to the app over native messaging. The host manifest allows only this extension, the channel is sealed with X25519 keys exchanged on first approval, and the app verifies the browser binary before accepting.
- **The app.** Helios light-client state for supported chains and user-chosen RPC state for every other EVM chain, the local EVM call-tree reconstruction, the local verification gate over every contract in the tree, ERC-7730 rendering, the confirm-or-reject review, and the ERC-8213 digest display after confirmation.
- **Other ways to input a transaction.** Not through the browser extension. Raw transactions, calldata and EIP-712 payloads pasted by hand, and ERC-4527 animated QR codes from air-gapped wallets (Keystone, OneKey, AirGap).
- **Supply-chain hardening.** Pinned and release-age-delayed dependencies, lifecycle scripts disabled, cargo-deny and cargo-vet, Socket and OSV scans in CI, hash-checked solc binaries, reproducible extension builds diffable against the git tag, releases built only from CI, and a software bill of materials with every release.
- **Distribution.** Signed desktop builds, and the extension published on the Chrome Web Store.

sections.heading: Out of scope
sections.markdown:
- Holding keys. The verifier never generates or hold the user's key; the user's wallet does.
- Any hosted service. Nothing runs on a server the team operates; Sourcify and the ERC-7730 registry are untrusted download sources that the app re-verifies.
- Effects preview (balance changes, storage writes, events), the transaction builder, Ledger signing, post-mining verification and the Firefox port. They belong to later releases.
- Non-EVM chains.

- Maintenance: the Sourcify team maintains Onay after the last milestone as part of its tooling, for at least 12 months at no further cost.
- Pinned target: release 1 available for download, with the extension on the Chrome Web Store, within 6 months of the first payment.
- Analytics are off by default and switched on by one explicit toggle. They exist to measure usage for this grant (below) and for nothing else. The prompt that offers the toggle says exactly this.

We want this tool to be really used so the grant payout is heavily skewed on the adoption goals.

initiatives.summary:
Ethereum is built to be verifiable, and verification is cheap. Yet most users still sign transactions without independently checking what they are approving. A second sanity check on the tx is a low-hanging fruit and Onay makes that second check seamless: it verifies the transaction locally, explains what it does, and lets the user compare against their wallet before signing.

Onay is a local desktop app with a thin browser extension that sits between the dapp and the wallet. It intercepts the signing request, verifies chain state through an embedded Helios light client, recompiles and verifies the source code locally, simulates the transaction, renders its intent in readable form with ERC-7730 clear signing, and finally displays the ERC8213 calldata digest for an equivalence check.
initiatives.title: Onay: Local signing companion
