sections.heading: Why this matters
sections.markdown:
AI is making it faster to attack software, giving attackers a meaningful edge. The answer is to put AI on the defending side too: AI that writes machine-checked proofs that a contract's stated properties hold, with humans only checking the theorems. Formal verification is widely considered the strongest guarantee of software correctness, and it is the one place where AI output can be checked mechanically rather than trusted.

This grant creates an open-source framework for Solidity verification (Verity, built on Lean 4, with an AI proof-writing skill) and increases formal verification adoption across the Ethereum ecosystem. Success is measured by the TVL covered by formally verified properties.

sections.heading: The team
sections.markdown:
The recipient is Verity Labs. This is a grant rather than an RFP because its team has spent the past few months doing unbounded formal-verification work with leading Ethereum protocols. Its public work covers 40+ protocols, among them popular names like Lido, Morpho, and Safe (see Existing work below).

This experience shows where real protocols need unbounded proofs, where modeling gaps block use, and what needs to become repeatable for developers and audit firms. The Ethereum Foundation has already funded part of Verity's product roadmap via a grant.

sections.heading: Why a grant: what already exists
sections.markdown:
- Verity Labs: https://veritylabs.dev and the Verity product page https://veritylabs.dev/projects/verity
- Verity compiler, MIT licensed: https://github.com/lfglabs-dev/verity
- verity-benchmark, the AI proof-generation benchmark built with ecosystem protocols: https://github.com/lfglabs-dev/verity-benchmark
- Technical docs, including the Solidity-to-Verity porting guide: https://veritylang.com
- Public verification case studies (Lido V3 vault solvency, Safe owner list invariants, Morpho, Balancer, 1inch, Pendle and others): https://veritylabs.dev/research
- Paper, "A Formally Verified Smart Contract Compiler in Lean 4", accepted at ETHReS 2026: https://veritylabs.dev/research/verity

sections.heading: In scope
sections.markdown:
- Product work on Verity's compiler, Solidity coverage, reusable proof infrastructure, benchmark, documentation, developer onboarding, AI proof-writing skill, and a deterministic Solidity-to-Verity transpiler that reduces modeling gaps.
- Public releases that document supported workflows, trust assumptions, version pins, known limitations, and how teams and formal audit firms can use the tooling.
- Adoption through protocol teams using Verity in-house and formal audit firms using it in their own work.
- Measuring adoption primarily through the TVL of contracts whose stated properties are formally verified.

**What this pays for:**

This is not a program to select public contracts and publish formal verifications of them. It pays for two connected things:

- **Product work:** continue the open-source Verity tooling, benchmark, documentation, developer onboarding, AI proof-writing skill, and deterministic Solidity-to-Verity transpilation work.

- **Adoption work:** make Verity usable by protocol teams in-house and formal audit firms in their own work. Success is led by the value covered by the verified properties.

Our success will only be judged on adoption, cause that is the only things that matters.

sections.heading: Out of scope
sections.markdown:
- Verifying the Solidity compiler itself.
- A proprietary product, hosted-only workflow, or exclusive access for a single provider.
- Counting users or github stars as the main measure of adoption. We consider real impact in TVL.

sections.heading: Commitments
sections.markdown:
1. **Open to everyone.** Verity product code, benchmark artifacts, documentation, and CI are public under an OSI-approved license. No proprietary runtime, hosted service, account, or paid provider is needed to use the tooling or reproduce a proof.
2. **Reproducible.** A stranger can reproduce each headline product claim from a clean checkout, documented command, public CI, and version pins, without admitted proof gaps.
3. **TVL-led adoption.** Adoption evidence names the participating protocol team or formal audit firm, provides public confirmation of use, and gives the public TVL source and snapshot date for each value included in the aggregate.
4. **Clear scope on verified TVL.** Each reported verification states the code revision, properties proved, trust assumptions, and known limits in plain language.

sections.heading: Why this matters
sections.markdown:
- Users and protocols lose money to code nobody reviewed. ack3's H1 2026 incident dataset (Gattermayer, Kalivoda and Bašović, https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.13792) covers 135 DeFi incidents in the first half of 2026. Of the 68 where a pre-incident audit was found, 46 were hit through code outside every audit's scope, and out-of-scope paths account for 94.4% of those 68 incidents' losses.
- An "audited" badge does not say which contracts a report covered. That answer sits in PDFs on 60 firm websites, each with its own words for severity and status, and new reports appear every week.
- On Trustblock today, fewer than half of all reports name a deployed contract address (46.5%), and only about 1 in 5 protocol audits do (18.4%, 1,225 of 6,644). Many name a repository instead, so the link from a report to the live contract has to be made, and kept current: a report missing for three months is a gap a user cannot see.
- Every effort that compares deployed code with audits needs the same input first: which report reviewed which commit, which files and which addresses. This grant produces that input for every public Ethereum and L2 audit and makes it free to look up, record by record.
- Afterwards, a wallet user about to sign, a risk team listing collateral or an explorer visitor can look up which public reports named this exact contract and commit, with each finding's severity and status as the firm wrote it, or see that no report names it. Every record links to the firm's own PDF, so anyone can check it.

- Relationships: Trustblock works with the security firms that publish on it, including Quantstamp, QuillAudits, Hacken, Zokyo, and ack3 (formerly Ackee Blockchain), whose incident dataset is cited above. Etherscan and Blockscout show Trustblock's card through their own integrations. None of them funds this work unless listed as a backer, and Trustblock does not rank or score firms.

Already built, all public:
- A publishing platform for security firms: verified firm accounts publish reports, scope and findings through a dashboard or the API. Today it holds over 10,800 public audit reports from 60 firms, on more than 7,200 projects: https://app.trustblock.run

- An audit card on the contract pages of 26 block explorers, including Etherscan, and on Blockscout: open the Cards tab of the Uniswap token link above.
- A reading pipeline: new reports are read twice, blind, and a finding goes in only when both readings agree on its severity and the firm's own status word ("Mitigated" stays "Mitigated"). A third reading settles any disagreement.
- A free API tier, embeds for firms and projects, public project, firm and audit pages, and a sitemap and llms.txt for search engines and AI agents.
- Grants delivered: Starknet Foundation (25,000 USDC, 2024; Starknet support shipped in January 2025) and AngelHack x Polygon (80,000 POL, 2025; three milestones reported complete in December 2025).
- The platform, the explorer integrations and the reading pipeline are already paid for. What costs money every month is the reading itself: following 60 firms' sites, reading each new PDF twice, checking it, and keeping the card and API answering. This grant pays for the scope pinning, six months of that reading work on Ethereum and L2, and the open release, at a fraction of what a build from scratch would cost.

sections.heading: Why this matters
sections.markdown:
- **Who is safer:** validators and node operators who run official client releases, and the users who rely on them.
- **From what:** an attacker who breaks into a client team's build machine or release account and ships a tampered release, while the public source code still looks clean. The xz-utils backdoor in 2024 worked this way: the malicious code was only in the release files, not in the public repository [1].
- **What anyone can point to afterwards:** official client releases that rebuild from source to exactly the same file, the accepted fixes in each client's repository, and a public webpage that explains how to repeat the check.

We found no client whose official releases are checked by anyone outside its own team. Two clients check their own builds, some say their builds are reproducible without anyone verifying it, and the rest have done part of the work or none. No tampered client release is known so far. These clients secure all staked ETH.

sections.heading: The team
sections.markdown:
- [Vivi Andersson](https://github.com/vivi365), engineer: PhD student at KTH. Built Geth Rebuild, a tool that checks whether official Geth releases match their source code [2].
- [Sofia Bobadilla](https://sofiabobadilla.github.io/), coordinator and engineer: PhD student at KTH and member of mab.xyz, works on Ethereum and smart contract security.
- [Raphina Liu](https://github.com/Stamp9), engineer: PhD student at KTH. Took part in Ethereum Protocol Fellowship cohort 7.
- [Julien Malka](https://luj.fr/), engineer: postdoc at KTH. Studies build reproducibility across whole software distributions, and showed how one tampered build tool can infect an entire Linux distribution [8].
- [Martin Monperrus](https://www.monperrus.net/martin/), advisor: Professor of Software Technology at KTH.
- [Javier Ron](https://github.com/javierron), advisor: postdoc at KTH. Researches how running several different clients keeps Ethereum resilient [4].
- [Aman Sharma](https://github.com/algomaster99), engineer: PhD student at KTH. Studies why building the same software twice gives different files, and how to fix it [3].

Other funding: CHAINS, a KTH research project financed by the Swedish Foundation for Strategic Research, funds the PhD research of the four KTH students. It does not pay for this engineering work, so this grant pays for the engineers' time. The Ethereum Foundation funded our earlier research on client diversity [5].

sections.heading: Why a grant: what already exists
sections.markdown:
Our team has already done this for Geth, the most used execution client, and has studied the problem at scale:

- **Geth:** Geth Rebuild checks whether an official Geth release matches its source code [2]. While building it, Vivi Andersson reported two problems to the Geth team: file paths from the build machine were left inside the release, and the wrong compiler version was used. The Geth team fixed its builds in 2024 and tagged her on the fix [6][7].
- **Attacks on build tools:** with Julien Malka, we showed that a single tampered build tool can silently spread to nearly all the software of a Linux distribution [8]. It is the kind of attack that hides in the build, not in the source code.
- **Java clients:** our published study of thousands of Java packages explains the common reasons builds differ and provides a tool that removes some of them [3]. The clients Besu and Teku are written in Java.

What is missing is the same work for the other 11 clients: finding what makes their releases differ and getting the fixes accepted. Some client teams have started on their own, such as Reth and Lighthouse [9][10], but none has yet reached an official release that anyone outside the team can rebuild and check.

**References:**

[1] Report of the xz-utils backdoor. https://www.openwall.com/lists/oss-security/2024/03/29/4

[2] Geth Rebuild: Verifiable Builds for Go Ethereum. https://www.diva-portal.org/smash/record.jsf?pid=diva2%3A1908608

[3] Causes and Canonicalization of Unreproducible Builds in Java. https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.21679

[4] Proving and Rewarding Client Diversity to Strengthen Resilience of Blockchain Networks. https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.18401

[5] Ethereum Foundation 2024 Academic Grants. https://blog.ethereum.org/2025/01/17/academic-grants-recipients

[6] Geth issue on reproducible builds. https://github.com/ethereum/go-ethereum/issues/28987

[7] Geth fix for reproducible builds. https://github.com/ethereum/go-ethereum/pull/30321

[8] Trusting-Trust Attack against an Entire Linux Distribution through Binary Manipulation. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.24888

[9] Reth: reproducible build profile. https://github.com/paradigmxyz/reth/pull/10459

[10] Lighthouse: reproducible builds. https://github.com/sigp/lighthouse/pull/6799

By official release we mean the file operators download from the client's release page.

The 12 clients: Geth, Nethermind, Besu, Erigon, Reth and Nimbus-eth1 (execution), and Prysm, Lighthouse, Teku, Nimbus, Lodestar and Grandine (consensus).

initiatives.summary:
Ethereum runs on client software such as Geth, Lighthouse and Prysm, which node operators download from each client's repositories.
Today, operators have to trust that each download was built from the public source code untampered.
This proposal aims to make the 12 main clients reproducible: anyone can rebuild a release from its source, and get exactly the same binary as the one in the repository.
We work with the client teams to achieve reproducibility, and we publish a webpage explaining how anyone can verify a release themselves.

sections.heading: Why this matters
sections.markdown:
Ethereum already has extensive testing infrastructure. PRSpec does not replace EEST, Hive, or existing client tests.
The missing piece is a practical way to connect specification requirements with their corresponding implementation points across independent clients.
When an EIP changes, engineers must manually trace affected requirements, identify relevant code paths, and determine whether each client has implemented the change consistently.
PRSpec helps automate this process through three complementary capabilities:
- **Deterministic checks:** Extract measurable requirements from pinned EIP revisions and verify them against client-code anchors, without requiring an LLM.
- **Fork Watch:** Compare specification revisions, identify changed parameters, and map their impact to relevant verification rules and client files.
- **Semantic analysis:** Use LLM-assisted analysis and adversarial verification to identify potential implementation divergences. Findings remain candidates for engineering review, not automatic bug confirmations.
The goal is to help client teams identify issues earlier, investigate them with reproducible evidence, and decide where additional tests or implementation changes are needed.

sections.heading: The team
sections.markdown:
**Safi El-Hassanine — Founder and Lead Developer**
PRSpec is independently built and maintained by Safi El-Hassanine, a software developer focused on Ethereum infrastructure, protocol verification, and developer tooling.
He designed and developed the project's architecture, multi-client analysis engine, deterministic verification system, Fork Watch, and CI pilot.
PRSpec's public development history includes technical discussions with Nethermind, Ethereum Foundation execution-specs contributors, Besu, and go-ethereum.
The grant will directly support continued engineering and open-source development. Safi will be responsible for delivering the milestones and publishing their supporting evidence.

sections.heading: Why a grant: what already exists
sections.markdown:
PRSpec is a working open-source project, not a proposal to build a tool from scratch. Its V2 implementation includes:

**1. Four execution-client integrations**
Source-code mappings for Geth (Go), Nethermind (C#), Besu (Java), and Reth (Rust). The semantic analysis registry covers 10 EIPs across the clients, with Reth currently covering 7.

**2. Deterministic verification**
The witness engine currently includes EIP-1559 and EIP-4844 rulebooks.
- 34 cross-client checks: 34 matched, 0 mismatched, 0 incomplete.
- Two additional rule/client combinations are explicitly marked as lacking verified code anchors.
- A historical EIP-4844 replay correctly identifies three constants changed by a real specification commit.

**3. Fork Watch**
Implemented and tested against a historical EIP-4844 change, identifying modified parameters, affected verification rules, and relevant client files.

**4. Semantic analysis and adversarial verification**
A published mutation experiment tested 10 pre-registered implementation deviations:
- 6 confirmed, 1 flagged, 3 inconclusive.
- 0 missed and 0 errors.
The clean baseline produced 33 raw issues, all rejected during automated verification.
This is a single experiment on one pinned client revision, not a statistically established detection or false-positive rate.

**5. Working CI pilot**
On November 12, 2026, PRSpec completed an end-to-end GitHub Actions pilot on a Besu fork. It produced a report artifact and reproducible evidence, including a terminal transcript and screen recording.
The pilot is advisory and non-blocking. It is not installed in the official Besu repository.

**6. Engineering and reproducibility**
The V2 codebase includes:
- Installable CLI and Dockerfile with pinned dependencies.
- Local OpenAI-compatible model support and a `--no-cloud` privacy guard.
- Fail-closed exit codes.
- JSON, Markdown, and HTML reports.
- 210 passing automated tests, with 2 skipped tests requiring an API key.

**Explore the implementation and evidence:**
- GitHub: https://github.com/Fosurero/PRSpec
- Verification record: https://github.com/Fosurero/PRSpec/blob/main/VERIFICATION.md
- Roadmap: https://github.com/Fosurero/PRSpec/blob/main/ROADMAP.md
- Besu pilot evidence: https://github.com/Fosurero/PRSpec/tree/main/docs/evidence/2026-11-12/besu-fork-e2e

sections.heading: In scope
sections.markdown:
The initiative focuses on making PRSpec V2 independently deployable, reproducible, and practical for execution-client teams.

1. **Production packaging:** Finalize the CLI and Docker distribution, pinned environments, installation instructions, and reproducible examples.
2. **Deterministic verification:** Expand witness coverage beyond EIP-1559 and EIP-4844, improve fork-aware rules and client-code anchors, and evaluate EEST-format witnesses against EELS.
3. **Local model execution:** Validate open-weight models through OpenAI-compatible endpoints, publish hardware requirements and inference costs, and preserve the `--no-cloud` guard.
4. **Client CI integration:** Turn the Besu pilot into a reusable integration kit, add PR-level reporting, and work with client teams on advisory, non-blocking trials.
5. **Finding quality:** Maintain transparent triage records covering confirmed findings, disputed findings, false-positive candidates, and incomplete analyses.
6. **Maintainability:** Document how to add EIPs, forks, client mappings, and rules, and provide an integration guide and technical walkthrough.

sections.heading: Out of scope
sections.markdown:
PRSpec is an additional verification layer, not a replacement for existing testing infrastructure.
This initiative does not promise:
- Complete EIP compliance or proof that an implementation is bug-free.
- Replacement of EEST, Hive, ethereum/tests, or existing review processes.
- Automatic confirmation of LLM-generated findings.
- Consensus-layer client support.
- Deterministic verification of every semantic requirement.
- Mandatory transmission of proprietary source code to external AI providers.
- Official client adoption or endorsement without public confirmation.
- Perpetual maintenance beyond the grant period.

sections.heading: Commitments
sections.markdown:
**Open source:** PRSpec and its documentation will remain available under the MIT license.
**Privacy:** Teams can run PRSpec in their own infrastructure. Local model support and `--no-cloud` will remain available, with external data flows and costs documented.
**Reproducibility:** Results will identify the relevant EIP revision, client commit, and model configuration where applicable. Incomplete analyses will not be presented as successful checks.
**Finding quality:** Findings will be reported as review candidates, with confirmed, disputed, false-positive, and incomplete results tracked separately.
**Adoption transparency:** Only publicly evidenced integrations will count as adoption. Trials and technical discussions will be reported separately.
**Independent review:** PRSpec will seek independent execution-client engineering review of its methodology, finding quality, and integration safety. Review will not be presented as endorsement.
**Continuity:** A public maintenance guide will explain how to extend coverage and reproduce existing results. The repository will remain publicly accessible after the grant period.

initiatives.summary:
Ethereum relies on multiple independent execution clients implementing the same protocol specifications consistently. Yet specifications evolve, implementations differ, and conventional tests only cover explicitly defined scenarios.
PRSpec adds a complementary verification layer that connects EIP requirements directly to client source code, combining deterministic checks with LLM-assisted semantic analysis.
Its V2 release introduces deterministic witnesses, specification change tracking (Fork Watch), adversarial verification, and reproducible evidence tied to exact specification revisions and client commits.
PRSpec already supports Besu, Geth, Nethermind, and Reth, with a working CI pilot demonstrated on a Besu fork.
This initiative will turn the existing implementation into a practical, privacy-conscious workflow that client teams can independently evaluate and integrate.

sections.heading: Why this matters
sections.markdown:
Multisig thefts at [Bybit](https://www.theblock.co/post/343530/lazarus-appears-to-compromise-safe-developer-machine-in-lead-up-to-1-5-billion-bybit-hack-report) (February 2025, about $1.5 billion) and [Radiant Capital](https://decrypt.co/286728/radiant-capital-exploited-50-million) (October 2024, about $50 million) show that a compromised interface can display a routine transfer while the wallet signs a different transaction. Clear signing lets users understand the transaction payload in a human-readable way with hashes to compare against an independent source (e.g. "Deposit $100 into Aave" vs. an unintelligible hexadecimal string). As an industry, we can't expect to onboard the masses if the expectation is for them to decode raw transaction data themselves or otherwise lose their life savings.

As of October 8, 2026, none of the 32 hardware and software wallets listed passes Walletbeat's transaction legibility test.

sections.heading: Why this matters
sections.markdown:
Autonomous agents move user liquidity across DeFi on Ethereum and its L2s. A model, a prompt, a hot key, an operator, every protocol touched: any one can lose the funds. Depositors (individuals and institutions) cannot tell a careful agent from a reckless one.

No agent has lost user funds yet. But during the KelpDAO rsETH exploit (April 2026, $124 million to $230 million of bad debt on Aave) and the Resolv USR depeg (March 2026, about $25 million extracted), Zyfai's agents exited early while depositors sat frozen in Aave (sources: https://www.bankless.com/read/agents-and-x402-make-defi-safer, https://x.com/Zyfai_/status/2036119040528375853). The same autonomy loses funds when screening, key management or incident response is weak. Afterwards, anyone can open the public board and see a current assessment of every integrated agent, re-checked at least every 14 days.

sections.heading: Why this matters
sections.markdown:
Ethereum security depends on the people controlling accounts, devices, software and signing permissions. Convincing messages, impersonation and malicious requests can persuade someone to bypass otherwise sound protections. The [FBI documents targeted social engineering against crypto employees](https://www.ic3.gov/PSA/2024/PSA240903).

People need practical ways to verify requests, recognise uncertainty and respond safely. Zealynx Defence connects structured training with guidance when a suspicious situation actually happens. Learners practise decisions and demonstrate understanding on unfamiliar examples. Completion shows the skills assessed; it does not guarantee immunity from deception.

It includes 30 reviewed case records and 12 practical exercises, with legitimate counterparts, explanations, corrective feedback and fresh assessments. The curriculum can grow as threats and learner needs change.

**A case assistant connected to training.** Users describe or paste a suspicious message or situation. The assistant explains supported warning signs, identifies missing information, suggests protective steps and recommends relevant lessons. It makes uncertainty explicit and does not declare something safe merely because it finds no known scam pattern.

**One paid subscription.** Access includes the standard paid course library, updates and a bounded assistant allowance. Individuals receive three free checks. Team access adds training assignment and completion records.

**Free educational resources.** Provide videos with Carlos's narration and Zealynx explanatory cards. Reviewed research also supports course updates, case guidance and newsletter material, with source dates and human review before publication.

The proposed fifteen-month schedule is approximately three months for the initial release, followed by twelve months to demonstrate paid adoption and sustainable operation.

sections.heading: Why this matters
sections.markdown:
A Safe verifies signatures, not whether its owners signed freely. Physical coercion can turn a valid signing quorum into an attack path. Treasury operators need a separate emergency action that can interrupt transfers without giving another party custody or spending authority.

The guard lets a registered emergency credential start an on-chain freeze. With the required configuration, it blocks owner and module transfers and new ERC-1271 signature validation during the incident. A restricted recovery path lets owners replace a compromised signer with a pre-approved recovery owner. Normal operation resumes after the configured lockdown and recovery periods. An optional transaction delay provides time to activate the freeze before a coerced transaction executes. The contracts have no team administrator or privileged unlock key. The protection has documented boundaries, including existing token allowances and previously valid signatures; it does not guarantee an attacker's behaviour or a person's physical safety.

sections.heading: The team
sections.markdown:
The team behind Runtime Capital, a DeFi fund, developed the guard and funded its development. This is its contribution to Ethereum's public security infrastructure: reusable code, public specifications and an independent audit that any compatible Safe operator can use. Runtime Capital handles auditor coordination, remediation, release documentation and ongoing maintenance. Public project contact: contact@runtime.capital.

The project has been awarded a subsidy of up to $6,500 through the Ethereum Security Subsidy Program, a joint initiative involving the Ethereum Foundation's Trillion Dollar Security Initiative, Chainlink Labs, Nethermind, participating audit firms and Areta Market. The subsidy is delivered as a discount from participating audit providers, covering at most 30% of an eligible quote. At our $20,000 gross audit ceiling, it reduces the cost by $6,000, leaving $14,000 to fund. Participation is not an endorsement or recommendation by the program partners. This discount is already deducted from the amount requested here.

These are documented results for that candidate, not a substitute for an external audit. The candidate is not yet externally audited or released for value-bearing production use.

Runtime Capital already owns the implementation work and can resolve findings directly. Development costs are already paid; the request covers the remaining external audit bill. The auditor has not been selected. Selection will use an eligible marketplace provider, a confirmed scope, remediation review and a public report, within the $20,000 gross ceiling.

sections.heading: Why this matters
sections.markdown:
Wake combines Solidity testing, fuzzing, static analysis, and code intelligence in a Python framework. Maintaining that stack requires continued work as Solidity, Python packages, EVM implementations, and Ethereum hard forks change. Unresolved compatibility problems and user-reported defects make security tests harder to reproduce and maintain.

AI can reduce the mechanical work involved in writing fuzz tests, as ack3 explains in [why AI-assisted smart contract testing belongs in Python](https://ack3.ai/research/why-ai-assisted-smart-contract-testing-belongs-in-python/), but useful tests still need explicit invariants, correct state models, and reviewable execution results. This initiative improves the parts of Wake that support that workflow. Developers and auditors will have a maintained Wake v5 release, clearer AI-assisted fuzzing paths, and public fixes for problems reported through GitHub.

sections.heading: The team
sections.markdown:
**ack3** does the work. [Michal Převrátil](https://github.com/michprev) is the author of Wake and leads its tooling work. [Naoki Yoshida](https://github.com/meditationduck) focuses on fuzz testing and making complex failures reproducible. [Jan Kalivoda](https://github.com/jaczkal) works on smart-contract security research and review methodology. [Josef Gattermayer](https://x.com/jgattermayer) provides project oversight.

The team built Wake and uses it in Ethereum security reviews. ack3 works with clients including [Lido](https://lido.fi/) and [Safe](https://safe.global/), and Wake fuzzing was used in the [public Lido NEST security work](https://ack3.ai/research/lido-nest-audit-summary/). The team's public track record is available at https://ack3.ai, https://github.com/ack3-ai/wake, and the linked fuzzing benchmark. No other funder currently pays for this scope.

sections.heading: Why a grant: what already exists
sections.markdown:
Wake is an existing open-source framework built and maintained by the team now operating as ack3. Wake v5 already provides Python-based Solidity testing, property-based fuzzing, [manually guided fuzzing](https://ack3.ai/research/introducing-manually-guided-fuzzing-a-new-approach-in-smart-contract-testing/), static-analysis detectors, typed Solidity representations, coverage, call tracing, and an EVM execution backend. Its documentation and releases are public.

ack3 also uses Wake in security work and has already tested AI-assisted fuzzing approaches. The linked benchmark records a concrete agent-written harness experiment, while the Wake documentation contains the testing and fuzzing foundations this initiative will extend. A new team would first need to learn the compiler pipeline, generated Python types, EVM backend, fuzzing runtime, static-analysis model, and release process. The $20,000 goal funds focused maintenance and improvements to the existing framework rather than a new framework build.

sections.heading: In scope
sections.markdown:
- Maintain the Wake v5 release line and address compatibility changes affecting Solidity compilation, Python support, EVM behavior, testing, fuzzing, and static analysis.
- Resolve GitHub issues that affect Wake reliability and usability, with fixes or documented resolutions linked from public issue threads.
- Improve Wake interfaces and workflows used for AI-assisted fuzz-test preparation and execution.
- Update documentation and publish runnable examples showing how AI-assisted fuzzing fits into Wake tests.
- Publish tagged releases and release notes for completed work.

sections.heading: Out of scope
sections.markdown:
- A fully autonomous audit system.
- A guarantee that fuzzing finds a fixed number of vulnerabilities or reaches a fixed coverage percentage.
- A Wake v6 rewrite or an unrelated replacement framework.
- Dedicated consulting, integration support, or developer onboarding as a milestone.
- Documentation of private user activity.
- New detector families unrelated to the maintenance and AI-assisted fuzzing scope.

sections.heading: Why this matters
sections.markdown:
Ethereum teams increasingly use TEEs for proving, signing and confidential execution. They need to establish more than whether an attestation has a valid signature: whether the workload is authorized, whether its inputs and host interfaces are safe, whether recovered state is current, and whether the deployed binary corresponds to reviewed source. The Handbook already explains TEE architectures and common failures; this expansion turns those foundations into checks engineers can execute.

[Taiko's postmortem](https://paragraph.com/@taiko-labs/taiko-security-incident-a-postmortem-and-next-steps) documents a debug-policy gap. Bluethroat's [published dstack research](https://bluethroatlabs.com/reveries/missing-tcb-status-check) addresses missing TCB-status enforcement. These cases demonstrate why authentic hardware evidence and safe application policy are separate concerns. The proposed chapters connect public incident analysis to rejection tests, review checklists and recovery exercises that Ethereum developers can apply to their own systems.

sections.heading: The team
sections.markdown:
**Rahul Saxena**, founder of Bluethroat Labs and the [Handbook's maintainer](https://bluethroatlabs.com/docs/contributors), leads technical research, reproduction validation and final editorial review. Phala's [security update](https://phala.com/posts/dstack-security-update-attestation-pipeline-hardening) publicly credits Rahul and Bluethroat for attestation-pipeline research and remediation collaboration.

**Wehi**, a Bluethroat Labs research intern, supports evidence collection, drafts, teaching examples and contribution records under Rahul's technical review. Funded contributions will be attributed in the public repository and release records.

Rahul operates the proposed recipient. Bluethroat has conducted security research involving Secret Network and collaborated on disclosures involving Phala/dstack. Existing Handbook contributors, including people identified on its contributors page as Coinbase-affiliated, are credited for past work; this proposal does not claim new participation or endorsement from them or their employers. The Handbook has been self-funded to date, and no external funding is committed to this proposed cycle. An independent technical reviewer will be appointed through the grant process; no reviewer is represented as already committed.

sections.markdown:
The [public Handbook](https://bluethroatlabs.com/docs/executive-summary) already contains platform explanations, a Nitro workflow, implementation failure patterns and layered defenses. Bluethroat maintains that material and has published relevant original security research. The grant builds on an existing resource and delivery team instead of paying to establish one from scratch.

The Docusaurus migration is scheduled for September 16, 2026 and remains planned at submission. It will support version history, attributed contributions and an open contribution workflow. Existing content and that migration are not charged as new grant deliverables. The linked GitHub repository is the current website source; the migrated Handbook will identify its canonical content repository and licensing at publication.

sections.heading: In scope
sections.markdown:
- **Verifier engineering:** a practical acceptance-policy chapter covering debug state, measurements, TCB policy, collateral, freshness, key binding and failure behavior, with good/bad verification fixtures.
- **Malicious-host interfaces:** a casebook chapter covering concrete failures in host-controlled inputs or enclave interfaces, with an attacker-to-impact trace and vulnerable/fixed teaching example.
- **State continuity and recovery:** a chapter and exercise distinguishing authenticated storage, rollback, cloning, revocation and recovery after loss of the original host.
- **Source-to-deployment verification:** a pinned build walkthrough connecting reviewed source and build inputs to an attested deployment measurement, including an intentional mismatch.
- Four associated review checklists, independent review records, contribution/version records, corrections and six monthly maintenance updates.
- Documented use of the materials by independent Ethereum-facing teams, with a public evidence index and feedback-driven corrections.

The case material will draw on published Bluethroat research, cleared Secret Network lessons and public incident reports. Taiko is an initial verification-policy example. [Base Azul](https://blog.base.dev/introducing-base-azul) is a relevant comparison for proof-path and fallback assumptions. Any conclusion about a named implementation will identify the version and supporting evidence.

The planning allocation is $9,000 for Rahul's technical work, $4,000 for Wehi's research and writing, $4,000 for independent technical and milestone review, and $1,000 for test infrastructure and publication. These allocations support the milestone outcomes; they are not payments to users for reporting adoption.

- A physical-hardware attack campaign or a commitment to cover the entire longer-term research backlog.

sections.heading: Why this matters
sections.markdown:
Ethereum’s public mempool reveals transaction details before their order is finalized, creating opportunities for front-running, transaction copying, censorship, and other forms of harmful MEV.

More than $1.8 billion has extracted from Ethereum users through MEV since 2020, much of it through tactics including front-running and sandwich attacks. Encrypted mempools can reduce this attack surface by keeping transaction information hidden until ordering has been fixed.

LUCID provides a path to doing this at the Ethereum protocol level while preserving an open and permissionless transaction pipeline. Resolving optionality is an important remaining security requirement before LUCID can be proposed for inclusion in I*.

sections.heading: The team
sections.markdown:
The recipient is brainbot, a core contributor to Shutter Network.

- Jannik Luhn, Developer. Author of EIP-8105 and contributor to LUCID development.
- Luis Bezzenberger, Project Manager. Coordinates encrypted mempool development and ecosystem work.

Both have worked on encrypted mempools through Shutter Network for several years.

The team also helps coordinate the Encrypt the Mempool coalition, which brings together Ethereum researchers, client teams, builders, and infrastructure providers working to advance encrypted mempools for Ethereum.

brainbot receives monthly funding from Shutter DAO 0x36 for broader encrypted mempool work. That funding does not cover this milestone.

sections.heading: Why a grant: what already exists
sections.markdown:
brainbot and Shutter Network have years of encrypted mempool research and implementation experience. Jannik authored EIP-8105, and the team is actively contributing to EIP-8184.

Shutter has also deployed encrypted mempool technology on Gnosis Chain and previously launched a Shutterized OP Stack testnet on Sepolia. The work here builds directly on existing specifications, implementations, and relationships with Ethereum client teams.

sections.heading: In scope
sections.markdown:
- resolving the optionality problem
- defining the role and security model for independent key publishers
- developing the public threat model, economic analysis of key withholding, and test vectors for both execution and consensus layers
- obtaining independent security review of the optionality design
- revising EIP-8184
- technical review with Ethereum researchers and client teams
- preparing LUCID to be proposed for consideration in I*

sections.heading: Out of scope
sections.markdown:
- guaranteeing acceptance or inclusion of EIP-8184 in I*, which is determined through Ethereum’s protocol upgrade process
- full production deployment on Ethereum Mainnet
- long-term operation of encryption or decryption service providers
- development of unrelated private order-flow or MEV mitigation systems

sections.heading: Commitments
sections.markdown:
- work funded by this initiative will be open source.
- brainbot will continue maintaining its contributions to EIP-8184 and coordinating LUCID development through its ongoing encrypted mempool work.
- Client implementations remain maintained by their respective upstream client teams.

initiatives.summary:
EIP-8184, LUCID, proposes encrypting transactions as they move through Ethereum’s public mempool and revealing them only after their ordering has been committed.

The design has progressed significantly. The main remaining security barrier is the optionality problem: the party responsible for revealing a decryption key may have an opportunity to withhold it after a transaction has already been committed.

A promising approach is to use independent key publishers, with validators helping identify reliable providers. This would also enable a competitive marketplace for encryption and decryption service providers rather than relying on a single provider.

The goal of this initiative is to resolve the optionality problem, update the LUCID specification, obtain independent security review of optionality design, and formally propose EIP-8184 for inclusion in Ethereum’s I* hard fork.
initiatives.title: Shutter: Preparing encrypted mempools for inclusion in the earliest EIP possible

sections.heading: Why this matters
sections.markdown:
On 16 Nov 2026 a Safe lost about $6.45 million. [Cointelegraph](https://cointelegraph.com/news/safe-wallet-reportedly-loses-millions-after-key-compromise) put the transfer at about 4.39 million USDC and 1.72 million syrupUSDC, through a Zodiac Roles modifier, and quoted Zodiac's co-founder: the policy allowed the call, and the role member's key was most likely compromised. [Safe said no owner signed](https://coinmarketcap.com/academy/article/safe-multisig-zodiac-roles-key-compromise).

[Zodiac Roles](https://roles.gnosisguild.org) is where a team edits that policy. A co-signer still cannot hand someone a block-pinned link that a second person re-runs and matches.

Co-signers of mainnet Safes that use Delay or Roles v2.1.1 get that link. The page shows who can already act, and it leaves unread authority as unknown. The 16 Nov module is a Roles version this reader identifies and does not interpret. The loss shows the class of incident. This grant does not claim that loss would have been stopped.

A stranger can open [www.saviours.xyz/audit](https://www.saviours.xyz/audit) and the repo. One team proof, the Term Safe at block 26435999, is there so the read can be repeated. It does not count as an outside user.

sections.heading: Why this matters
sections.markdown:
- **Who is safer:** Ethereum and L2 protocol users whose security teams must investigate reported vulnerabilities and assess proposed fixes.
- **From what:** False or inconclusive vulnerability reports, ineffective fixes, regressions that disrupt legitimate transactions, and new vulnerabilities introduced during repair.
- **What anyone can point to afterwards:** Openly documented workflows, reproducible evaluations on Ethereum incidents, and evidence that independent auditing teams used the workflows on real findings.

sections.heading: The team
sections.markdown:
- **Sofia Bobadilla, lead:** PhD student at KTH, member of CHAINS and mab.xyz, with expertise on smart contract security, particularly on exploit validation, automated vulnerability repair and transaction replay. Homepage: https://sofiabobadilla.github.io/
- **Martin Monperrus, advisor:** Professor of Software Technology at KTH and co-founder of mab.xyz. Homepage: https://www.monperrus.net/martin/

Other funding: WASP (Knut and Alice Wallenberg Foundation) and the Swedish Foundation for Strategic Research support Sofia's PhD research. This grant supports applied workflow research, portable implementation examples, reproducible evaluation and external adoption, distinct from the existing research funding.

sections.heading: Why a grant: what already exists
sections.markdown:
Our team has already published research and developed open tools addressing three stages of smart contract vulnerability response:

- **Behavior preservation:** PonDeReplay, our open-source replay framework, compares patched contract behavior with historical Ethereum transactions [1]. This mechanism is key for revealing unintended effects; for example, a tested guard that stops an attack on Yearn yDAI also blocks 88 legitimate keeper calls [2].
- **Exploit validation:** PoCo studies how AI agents turn vulnerability reports into runnable Foundry proofs of concept and how to verify that those tests actually demonstrate the reported issue [3].
- **Patch effectiveness:** Our study of automated smart contract fixes evaluated whether patches stopped real exploits, showing why passing conventional checks is not sufficient evidence of security [4].

These results are publicly available, and our work on exploit validation and automated repair has been peer-reviewed. Our findings have also informed AI-related guidance for Ethereum Foundation grants [5].

The missing piece is not another standalone agent or replay tool, but independently evaluated guidance for combining these checks in real audits. We will study which workflows improve decisions across different setups, where they fail, and when human review is necessary. We will publish reusable specifications, integration examples, and evidence of adoption by independent auditing teams.

**References:**

[1] PonDeReplay (open-source replay framework).
https://github.com/ASSERT-KTH/PonDeReplay

[2] Smart Contract Invariants Protect Against Cybercriminals.
https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.13191

[3] PoCo: Agentic Proof-of-Concept Exploit Generation for Smart Contracts.
https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.02780

[4] Do Automated Fixes Truly Mitigate Smart Contract Exploits?
https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.04600

[5] Ethereum PhD Fellowship on AI-Powered Protocol Security: Research, Auditing, and Vulnerability Detection.
https://web.archive.org/web/20260211213355/https://esp.ethereum.foundation/rounds/phdfp26/phdfp-rfpd1

sections.heading: In scope
sections.markdown:
- Workflow specifications for three decisions: whether a vulnerability is reproducible, whether a patch stops the exploit while preserving expected behavior, and whether a patch introduces security regressions.
- Explicit inputs, outputs, verification steps, uncertainty states, escalation criteria and evidence formats for each workflow.
- Portable agent skills and reference examples that can be adapted to different models, agent frameworks, and existing auditor toolchains.
- Reproducible empirical evaluation on public Ethereum cases, including failure analysis and comparisons with existing individual-tool approaches.
- Hands-on integration and feedback with independent audit firms and security teams using real Ethereum or L2 findings.

sections.heading: Out of scope
sections.markdown:
- Building a hosted service or requiring teams to adopt one agent framework or vendor.
- Guaranteeing that all workflows outperform existing practice; negative and inconclusive findings will be documented.

sections.heading: Commitments
sections.markdown:
- MIT for code and agent skills; CC BY 4.0 for workflow specifications, public benchmarks and published evaluation results.
- Sofia Bobadilla will maintain the published reference materials and fix reproducibility-breaking issues for 18 months after the final milestone.
- Public benchmarks will use public incidents. Confidential adopter cases can be validated using redacted evidence supplied to the independent technical reviewer.

initiatives.summary: This initiative will research, develop and validate reusable workflows for Ethereum vulnerability triage and patch validation. Audit firms, bounty platforms and protocol teams will be able to adapt the open workflows to their own tools and infrastructure. Independent teams will test them on real security work.

sections.heading: Why this matters
sections.markdown:
Builders keep shipping tools that stop attacks: approval revokers, wallets that check signatures and transactions. A tool only protects the users who find it. Users have no central place to learn what exists and how to use it. They scramble to search X, GitHub and Reddit.

Wallet drainers took $494 million from 332,000 addresses in 2024 and $83.85 million from 106,106 wallets in 2025 (Scam Sniffer annual reports, drops.scamsniffer.io). Users who revoke bad approvals, check signatures and verify addresses they interact with can avoid these attacks. The best security layer is the preventive layer.
